cards.title: Can exact weighted all-pairs shortest paths be computed in truly subcubic time?
cards.formal: Is there a constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a uniform randomized algorithm that, for every n-vertex directed graph with real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, outputs all exact shortest-path distances in $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ worst-case time with probability at least 2/3? Use a comparison-addition real RAM: adding, subtracting, and comparing stored real values costs O(1), and standard arithmetic and bit operations on O(log n)-bit index words cost O(1). Unreachable distances must be reported as infinity. Arbitrary real-number encodings or unit-cost floor operations are unavailable.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an algorithm with one fixed positive exponent saving on all valid inputs, or prove that no such randomized algorithm exists in the stated model. An n-cubed bound divided by a subpolynomial factor is progress but is not a positive answer.
cards.context:
Single-source shortest paths produce one row of a distance matrix. All-pairs shortest paths ask for every row, including the effects of intermediate vertices shared by many shortest routes. Running a source algorithm repeatedly is useful, but does not explain how much computation those rows can share.

For example, a path from u to v can be much cheaper than their direct edge even when it visits many intermediate vertices. Restricting attention to one-hop or two-hop routes changes the problem. Negative edges are allowed here, but negative cycles are excluded so that every reachable distance has a finite optimum.

Matrix formulations expose the shared work: combining two path segments uses a minimum over sums, rather than the ordinary sum of products of ring multiplication. Fast algorithms for ordinary matrix multiplication therefore do not automatically give the required bound for arbitrary weighted distances. Subcubic equivalences connect the problem to several other path and matrix tasks.

The distinction between subcubic and truly subcubic is quantitative. Dividing cubic time by a very large subpolynomial factor still leaves an exponent tending to three. The target asks for a fixed positive exponent saving. The 2026 progress on node-weighted triangles does not settle the edge-weighted problem underlying this hypothesis.
cards.why: I include this because exact distances are a basic graph primitive, and this particular exponent question organizes many conditional lower bounds. A resolution would identify either a common algorithmic improvement across equivalent problems or a precise limitation of what those reductions can accomplish.
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its adjacency matrix, with a special symbol for absent edges. Output contains one distance for every ordered pair, including zero self-distances. Negative-cycle detection outside the promise is not required. Space and preprocessing are included in the algorithm’s ordinary running time. The probability guarantee applies to the complete output matrix on each fixed input. This is a classical sequential model; quantum and parallel work/depth bounds are separate targets.

Williams gives a randomized real-RAM algorithm with time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$, demonstrating a substantial subpolynomial saving while leaving a fixed exponent improvement unresolved.

Akmal and Fischer solve the node-weighted zero-triangle problem in matrix-multiplication time; their introduction explicitly distinguishes it from the edge-weighted variant governed by the APSP hypothesis.

cards.title: An entanglement entropy area law for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every fixed local dimension q≥2, interaction range r≥1, interaction incidence bound g≥1, norm bound J>0, and spectral gap Δ>0, is there a finite constant C=C(q,r,g,J,Δ) such that every Hamiltonian H described below, on every square lattice Λ_L, has unique ground state ψ satisfying S(ρ_A)≤C|∂A| for every A⊆Λ_L?
cards.definitions: Let L≥1 be an integer, Λ_L={1,…,L}² with open boundaries, and the Hilbert space be the tensor product of C^q over its sites. Write H=Σ_a h_a, where each h_a is Hermitian and acts only on a nonempty support X_a⊆Λ_L of diameter at most r in the maximum-coordinate metric. Each site belongs to at most g supports, counting terms with the same support separately, and the operator norm of every h_a is at most J. Suppose H has a unique normalized lowest-energy eigenvector ψ and its next eigenvalue is at least Δ above the lowest eigenvalue. This is a gap of the entire Hamiltonian; no spectral-gap condition is imposed on subregions or subsets of terms. For A⊆Λ_L, let A^c be its complement in Λ_L and ρ_A=Tr_(A^c)(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|) and S(ρ_A)=−Tr(ρ_A log_2 ρ_A), with 0 log_2 0=0. The boundary ∂A is the set of nearest-neighbor lattice edges with exactly one endpoint in A; its cardinality is the boundary length in lattice units. Empty and full regions have entropy zero. The local parameters and C must be independent of L, A, and the actual interaction matrices. Interactions may vary from site to site and with L. They need not commute or share a simultaneous minimum-energy state; translation invariance and frustration freeness are not assumed. No approximation or state-preparation algorithm is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform entropy bound for all fixed choices of local parameters, or produce a family with the same q,r,g,J,Δ throughout and regions A for which S(ρ_A)/|∂A| is unbounded. A gap that closes with lattice size, growing local dimension or term norms, or degeneracy allowing a highly entangled choice of ground state does not refute this formulation. A bound with an extra unbounded logarithmic or subpolynomial factor is progress but does not establish the strict area law stated here.
cards.context:
A region with m spins has enough Hilbert-space dimension for entropy m log_2 q. For a square block of side length ℓ, that is proportional to ℓ², whereas this conjecture allows only a constant times ℓ. The physical idea is that finite-range interactions and a gap should constrain how much quantum information crosses the boundary. Fixing both interaction strength and the gap prevents an artificial rescaling from making a gapless family appear uniformly gapped.

In one dimension, Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped local systems. Since an interval has only a constant number of boundary points, its entropy remains bounded as the chain grows. Matrix-product-state approximations then connect this structure to classical numerical methods. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not directly extend the theorem: each new site has dimension q^L, which grows exponentially with the width.

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound n^(1+O((log n)^(−1/5))) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. context_blocks.text: A region with m spins has enough Hilbert-space dimension for entropy m log_2 q. For a square block of side length ℓ, that is proportional to ℓ², whereas this conjecture allows only a constant times ℓ. The physical idea is that finite-range interactions and a gap should constrain how much quantum information crosses the boundary. Fixing both interaction strength and the gap prevents an artificial rescaling from making a gapless family appear uniformly gapped.

In one dimension, Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped local systems. Since an interval has only a constant number of boundary points, its entropy remains bounded as the chain grows. Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound n^(1+O((log n)^(−1/5))) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

cards.title: Is nonuniform TC⁰ strictly smaller than nonuniform NC¹?
cards.formal: Is TC⁰⊊NC¹ for the nonuniform circuit classes defined below? Equivalently, does there exist a Boolean function family f=(f_n:{0,1}^n→{0,1}) in NC¹ such that for every fixed depth d≥1, exponent k≥1, and constant M≥1, there is an n for which every depth-at-most-d majority circuit computing f_n exactly has size greater than M(n+1)^k?
cards.definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes x_1,…,x_n, optional constants 0,1, and one output. Depth is the maximum number of gates on an input-to-output path. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires; if an input is repeated at a gate, each occurrence counts as a wire. A majority circuit has AND and OR gates of arbitrary positive fan-in, NOT gates of fan-in one, and MAJ gates of arbitrary positive fan-in m, with output 1 exactly when strictly more than m/2 inputs equal 1. TC⁰ consists of all families with such circuits of size M(n+1)^k and depth at most d for every n, for some constants M,k,d depending on the family. NC¹ consists of families with circuits over AND, OR, NOT, with fan-in at most two (one for NOT), size M(n+1)^k, and depth at most b log_2(n+1), for fixed M,k,b. Circuits may share intermediate gates. Both classes are nonuniform: an arbitrary separate circuit may be chosen for each input length, without any requirement to compute its description. The output must be correct on every input; no randomness, approximation, promise, or distributional error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some NC¹ family has no polynomial-size majority circuits of any fixed depth, or prove NC¹⊆TC⁰, which would give equality because TC⁰⊆NC¹ is known. Excluding only one or finitely many depths, or proving a fixed polynomial lower bound, is not by itself a separation. A lower bound for an E^NP language without NC¹ membership does not provide the required family. Results for uniform classes alone must not be substituted for this nonuniform question.
cards.context:
The two models trade different resources. A majority gate can aggregate arbitrarily many bits in one step, whereas a binary Boolean gate sees only two. NC¹ permits logarithmically many layers of binary computation. A majority of polynomially many bits can itself be computed by a polynomial-size logarithmic-depth Boolean circuit, so a constant number of majority layers gives TC⁰⊆NC¹. The open issue is whether counting in a fixed number of layers can also replace every logarithmic-depth computation.

Arithmetic tasks are an instructive warning against judging depth from familiar sequential algorithms. Hesse, Allender, and Barrington prove that integer division and iterated multiplication have even DLOGTIME-uniform TC⁰ circuits. A binary long-division procedure takes many dependent steps, but that procedure does not establish a lower bound on all circuits for division. These arithmetic problems therefore cannot serve as the missing separation.

There are concrete complete problems on the NC¹ side. Evaluating a Boolean formula, and evaluating a product of elements of the fixed permutation group S_5, capture NC¹ under very simple reductions. S_5 consists of the 120 permutations of five objects, with permutation composition as its operation. Thus the problem can be approached through a fixed finite algebraic operation repeated on a long input, without requiring complicated individual gates. Chen and Tell study these complete problems in their lower-bound amplification results.

Their result shows that surprisingly mild improvements in known bounds could suffice. Suitable wire lower bounds of the form n^(1+c^(−d)) for an NC¹-complete problem, uniformly strong enough as the constant depth d grows, would imply a full separation. The depth dependence of the exponent is essential: obtaining a superlinear bound at an isolated depth is a much weaker statement.

Dawar and Evans give an algebraic characterization of uniform NC¹ using typed monoids in FSTTCS 2025, extending earlier work on uniform TC⁰. Typed monoids allow infinite algebraic structures while restricting recognition through finitely many types. This supplies another mathematical language in which to compare the classes. Their theorem is a characterization, not a separation, and its uniform scope must be kept distinct from this card’s formulation.

Chen, Tal, and Wang’s 2026 result proves n^(2.5−ε) gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits computing an E^NP function. Linear-threshold gates test weighted sums against a threshold, unlike the unweighted majority gates fixed in the definition above. Beyond this gate convention, the result addresses a single depth, a polynomial bound, and a much larger ambient class for the hard function. Those distinctions explain why the new lower bound does not resolve TC⁰ versus NC¹.
cards.why: One of the central small-circuit questions: whether a constant number of counting layers can perform every logarithmic-depth Boolean computation. A resolution would clarify the power of threshold circuits, finite-group computation, and the role of sequential dependence in parallel computation.

importance.reason: A flagship unresolved containment between basic circuit classes, with explicit complete problems and connections to arithmetic, algebraic automata theory, and lower-bound amplification.

progress.text: Hesse, Allender, and Barrington place division and iterated multiplication in DLOGTIME-uniform TC⁰, demonstrating the arithmetic power already available at constant depth.

Chen, Tal, and Wang prove superquadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two weighted threshold circuits for an E^NP function; the result does not supply an NC¹ separation against every constant depth.

cards.title: Does every VC class admit linear-size sample compression?
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class H⊆{0,1}^X of finite VC dimension d≥1 admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying k+b≤Cd, in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
cards.definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept h∈H is a total function X→{0,1}. A finite set A⊆X is shattered if {h|_A:h∈H}={0,1}^A; d is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set S⊆X×{0,1} agreeing with some h∈H. A scheme consists of deterministic maps κ and ρ, which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable S, κ(S)=(T,z), where T⊆S is an unordered labeled subset with |T|≤k and z∈{0,1}^b. The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor ρ(T,z):X→{0,1} agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a bound k+b≤Cd with C independent of H, X and the sample size, or refute the existence of every such constant by concept classes whose minimum scheme size divided by their positive VC dimension is unbounded. A bound depending on the number of examples, an exponential bound in d, or a theorem for selected classes does not settle this question. Requiring exactly d retained examples with no side information, or requiring proper reconstruction, specifies a stronger variant.
cards.context:
The stored object is a small selection of examples that lets a fixed decoding rule recover every training label. It need not identify the unknown target function on points never observed. For example, consider indicators of closed intervals on the real line. Retain the leftmost and rightmost positive examples, or the empty set if there are no positives. Decode to the interval between those retained points, or to the all-zero function in the empty case. Realizability ensures that no negative example lies between the extreme positives. Thus an arbitrarily large sample can be represented by at most two examples.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A real-valued example may itself require arbitrarily many bits to describe; sample compression charges one unit for retaining it. Conversely, permitting an arbitrary uncharged side message would trivialize the problem, because that message could encode the whole sample. The fixed reconstructor and the explicit bound b prevent this loophole. The question concerns the combinatorial information carried by selected observations, rather than ordinary lossless compression of their numerical representations.

Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every finite-VC binary class has a scheme of size 2^{O(d)}, settling the earlier existence question. Their argument combines learning with an approximate minimax principle. More precisely, their bound also involves the dual VC dimension: this reverses the roles of domain points and concepts, treating each point as its pattern of membership across the concepts. Since the dual dimension can be exponential in d, that result leaves a substantial quantitative gap. Their corrected 2015 version retains the binary theorem while withdrawing an erroneous multiclass extension.

An influential proposed route was to place a class inside a better-structured extremal class of comparable VC dimension and compress there. Chase and coauthors show that such embeddings can require an exponential increase in dimension. Their COLT 2024 result rules out that general route to a linear bound; it does not show that the original class itself needs exponential compression. A failed intermediate representation is different from a lower bound against every compressor.

The problem also has concrete graph instances. Fix a graph and label sampled vertices according to membership in an unknown metric ball. Bourneuf and coauthors give proper schemes of size O(t log(t+1)) when the graph has treewidth at most t, and an analogous bound for cliquewidth. Proper means that decoding produces another ball, a stronger requirement than this card imposes. Their April 2026 work supplies structured examples and explicitly leaves the general linear-VC conjecture open.

Attias, Hanneke, and Ramaswami show how binary compression results transfer to multiclass, regression, and robust-learning settings, with additional factors or additional requirements on the binary scheme. Consequently, a solution could have consequences beyond binary prediction, but those transfers have hypotheses. In particular, their Open Problem 28 is about adversarially robust compression; the standard conjecture used here appears in their introduction.
cards.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

importance.reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.

progress.text: The framework of Littlestone and Warmuth led to the conjecture that compression size can be linear in VC dimension; the general conjecture remains explicit in the 2025 survey of reductions.
Moran and Yehudayoff prove a general 2^{O(d)} bound for binary classes. The corrected arXiv v2 is the appropriate preprint; the journal version appeared in JACM in 2016.
Chase and coauthors prove an exponential dimension obstruction to embedding arbitrary VC classes in extremal classes, limiting a major proposed approach without refuting sample compression itself.
Bourneuf and coauthors obtain almost-linear proper compression in treewidth and cliquewidth for graph-ball classes, while retaining the general conjecture as open.

The latest version of arXiv:2603.23561, which had earlier claimed a compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result, is withdrawn. Its authors identify an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. This is not a resolution.

cards.title: Does public-key encryption imply oblivious transfer?
cards.formal: In the classical plain model, does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme for bits imply the existence of a polynomial-time 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious-transfer protocol secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party? Both primitives have negligible error and computational security as defined below. The implication may use arbitrary non-black-box techniques and a polynomial number of communication rounds.
cards.definitions: The security parameter is λ, supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; adversarial distinguishers are polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0, μ(λ)<λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Public-key encryption consists of KeyGen(1^λ)=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,m;r), and Dec(sk,c), for m∈{0,1}; decryption fails with negligible probability over key generation and encryption coins, for each m. IND-CPA means that no such adversary given pk distinguishes Enc(pk,0) from Enc(pk,1) with nonnegligible advantage; public encryption is available to it. In OT, sender S has bits (m_0,m_1), receiver R has a choice bit c, and R must output m_c except with negligible probability for every input triple; S has no output. The parties follow their prescribed algorithms but keep their entire views, including inputs, random tapes, and messages. There must be uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators Sim_S(1^λ,m_0,m_1) and Sim_R(1^λ,c,m_c) whose outputs are computationally indistinguishable from the corresponding real views for every sequence of input triples. Thus S learns nothing about c and R learns nothing beyond (c,m_c). The parties have independent private randomness and exchange classical messages directly. There is no trusted setup, common reference string, random oracle, pre-shared correlated randomness, trusted hardware, or quantum resource.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without a second unproved hardness assumption, or refute that unrelativized implication. A construction may inspect and use the code of the encryption algorithms and use non-black-box security arguments. An oracle separation or a lower bound restricted to black-box reductions is a barrier, not a negative resolution of this question. A construction requiring an additional property of encryption must also derive that property from arbitrary IND-CPA encryption to settle the card.
cards.context:
Ordinary encryption protects a message from someone who lacks the secret key. Oblivious transfer must arrange a more selective situation: the receiver can read one of two messages, cannot read the other, and does not disclose which one it selected. This combines privacy for both participants. Merely encrypting both messages under a key generated by the receiver fails, because that receiver can decrypt both ciphertexts. Asking the receiver to reveal which key it can decrypt would instead reveal its choice.

Some encryption schemes offer the missing structure. If a receiver can create two indistinguishable-looking public keys while knowing a decryption key for just one, it can place the decryptable key in position c. The sender encrypts the two messages under the corresponding keys. Such an argument needs a suitable oblivious-sampling property, including security even given the sampler’s retained randomness. Gertner and coauthors identify sufficient properties and also prove an oracle separation between general PKE and even semi-honest OT. Their historical separation uses uniform adversaries.

That result constrains a style of construction, rather than deciding the unrestricted implication. In an oracle argument all algorithms are given access to an additional idealized operation. A construction based on the actual implementation of an encryption scheme may use features that do not survive replacement by an arbitrary oracle. Consequently, the qualifier allowing non-black-box techniques is substantive; removing it would turn the card into a question already addressed by known barriers.

The semi-honest target is already powerful. Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. context_blocks.text: Ordinary encryption protects a message from someone who lacks the secret key. Oblivious transfer must arrange a more selective situation: the receiver can read one of two messages, cannot read the other, and does not disclose which one it selected. This combines privacy for both participants. Merely encrypting both messages under a key generated by the receiver fails, because that receiver can decrypt both ciphertexts. Asking the receiver to reveal which key it can decrypt would instead reveal its choice.

Some encryption schemes offer the missing structure. If a receiver can create two indistinguishable-looking public keys while knowing a decryption key for just one, it can place the decryptable key in position c. The sender encrypts the two messages under the corresponding keys. Such an argument needs a suitable oblivious-sampling property, including security even given the sampler’s retained randomness. Gertner and coauthors identify sufficient properties and also prove an oracle separation between general PKE and even semi-honest OT. Their historical separation uses uniform adversaries.

That result constrains a style of construction, rather than deciding the unrestricted implication. In an oracle argument all algorithms are given access to an additional idealized operation. A construction based on the actual implementation of an encryption scheme may use features that do not survive replacement by an arbitrary oracle. Consequently, the qualifier allowing non-black-box techniques is substantive; removing it would turn the card into a question already addressed by known barriers.

The semi-honest target is already powerful. Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. The fairness result has its own model and does not constitute a proof against all non-black-box OT constructions.

cards.title: Does ordinary polynomial-hard LWE suffice for circuit obfuscation?
cards.formal: Does the decisional LWE assumption with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, leakage-resilience, or circular-security assumption? The target is a classical polynomial-time obfuscator secure against classical polynomial-size adversaries.
cards.definitions: Fix q(n) to be the least prime at least n^4 for every integer n≥2. Let χ_n be the discrete Gaussian on Z with probability of e proportional to exp(−πe²/n²). The assumed LWE statement is: for every polynomial m(n), the ensembles (A,A s+e mod q) and (A,u) are computationally indistinguishable, where A is uniform in Z_q^(m×n), s is uniform in Z_q^n, the m coordinates of e are independent χ_n samples, and u is independent uniform in Z_q^m. Indistinguishable means every polynomial-size classical circuit family has negligible advantage in n; negligible means smaller than n^(−c) eventually for every constant c>0. No secret-dependent leakage is supplied. An obfuscator O is a uniform probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in λ+|C| that outputs a Boolean circuit O(1^λ,C) of polynomial size. Circuits are finite acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuits with fan-in at most two, a specified list of input and output bits, and explicit binary descriptions; |C| is description length. For every polynomial p, there is negligible μ_p such that for every |C|≤p(λ), with probability at least 1−μ_p(λ) over the obfuscator’s coins the output circuit agrees with C on ALL inputs. For every pair of circuit sequences C_0,λ and C_1,λ with polynomially bounded, equal description lengths, the same input/output lengths and identical functions, their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable against all polynomial-size circuit families. Both functionality and security quantify over all such circuits, without requiring an efficiently checkable proof of equivalence. There is no oracle, trusted setup, quantum state, or restriction to a special circuit family.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated LWE-to-iO existence implication, allowing arbitrary non-black-box constructions and proofs, or refute that unrelativized implication. A result assuming subexponential hardness, a different LWE parameter regime, circular security, additional leakage resilience, pairings, or another independent assumption settles this card only if the extra requirement is derived from the specific LWE assumption here. A construction for a restricted circuit class or a barrier against one proof technique is partial progress.
cards.context:
Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of exactly the same function. After obfuscation, an efficient observer should not tell which implementation was used. Equality of size prevents a trivial distinction from the amount of code supplied; padding can put implementations under a common size bound. This definition does not say that every secret written into an arbitrary program is hidden. A secret that the function itself reveals through its outputs remains visible.

That distinction is necessary. Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement, which would make code reveal no more than oracle access to its function. Their impossibility theorem does not rule out indistinguishability obfuscation. The weaker comparison between equivalent implementations has therefore become a central target, rather than an informal promise to make arbitrary software unreadable.

LWE supplies a particularly concrete potential foundation. Its samples are linear equations modulo a public integer, perturbed by small independent errors. Exact equations would reveal the secret by linear algebra; the errors obstruct that approach. Regev introduced reductions connecting LWE to worst-case lattice problems and used it to build public-key encryption. This card fixes a particular ordinary decisional-LWE ensemble so that the noise distribution, modulus, number of samples, and adversarial resources cannot vary silently.

Jain, Lin, and Sahai established general-circuit iO from a combination of four assumptions: LWE, LPN over large fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and a bilinear-group assumption. Their theorem uses stronger quantitative security than mere polynomial hardness. Its Journal of the ACM version appeared in February 2026, following the STOC 2021 work. That publication is an important foundation for iO, but is not a 2026 construction from plain LWE alone.

A follow-up by the same authors removes LWE from that combination, leaving the other three assumptions. Eliminating LWE from a sufficient set is logically different from eliminating all the other assumptions while retaining LWE. The follow-up explicitly poses the possibility that LWE alone might suffice, without claiming a resolution.

Brakerski, Döttling, Garg, and Malavolta give another route using LWE-based encryption with circular randomness-leakage resilience. This provides a plausible route to post-quantum obfuscation under the stronger assumption. Its security experiment exposes structured information related to keys and encryption randomness, whereas ordinary LWE supplies only the noisy linear samples defined above. Calling the construction LWE-based therefore does not remove the extra security hypothesis.

A solution would unify the assumptions behind many uses of obfuscation with an established lattice-learning problem. The specific target here is deliberately demanding: ordinary polynomial security and a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio. Even a construction from plain LWE with stronger quantitative hardness would be substantial progress, but the security loss would still need attention before it established this exact implication. The question concerns mathematical feasibility; it does not impose practical code size or execution speed.
cards.why: Asks whether a single basic noisy-linear-equation assumption supports general program obfuscation. Resolving the implication would clarify the strength of LWE and the assumption cost of a broad family of cryptographic constructions that currently use iO as a separate resource.

importance.reason: A central assumption-minimization problem for general obfuscation, with consequences throughout cryptography and a crucial distinction between ordinary LWE and strengthened LWE-based assumptions.

progress.text: Barak and coauthors establish impossibility for general virtual-black-box obfuscation while introducing weaker obfuscation notions, including the indistinguishability target.
Regev develops LWE, lattice-hardness connections and public-key encryption; these results supply the standard noisy-equation foundation, rather than general obfuscation.
Jain, Lin, and Sahai construct general iO from four well-founded assumptions with the quantitative security specified in their theorem. The JACM publication does not reduce the list to LWE.
Their follow-up removes LWE, obtaining iO from LPN over prime fields, DLIN, and local PRGs under subexponential security. It explicitly leaves minimal assumption sets open.

Brakerski and coauthors obtain iO from circular-security properties of LWE-based encryption, including randomness-leakage resilience. They also repair a limitation in a previous exponentially-efficient-obfuscation transformation.

cards.title: Can every two-way NFA be determinized with polynomially many states?
cards.formal: Do universal constants C,k≥1 exist such that, for every n≥1, every finite nonempty input alphabet Σ and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over Σ with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most C(n+1)^k states satisfying L(D)=L(A)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word w∈Σ*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in {−1,0,+1}; moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such a universal polynomial bound, or prove that no universal polynomial bounds the minimum number of states of an equivalent 2DFA. A negative answer means that for every C,k there is an A for which every equivalent deterministic two-way automaton exceeds C(|Q_A|+1)^k states. An exponential lower bound would suffice but is not necessary. Lower bounds against sweeping or few-reversal targets, simulations only for bounded-length words, or simulations by machines that rewrite input do not resolve this formulation.
cards.context:
All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over {0,1}, consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least 2^r states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses O(r) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with n^{O(log n)} states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to NL⊆L/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with L=NL.

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in a_1*⋯a_t* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

importance.reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.

progress.text: Sakoda and Sipser formulate the polynomial-state simulation questions and conjecture that nondeterminism cannot always be removed with polynomial cost.
The Geffert–Mereghetti–Pighizzini simulation gives n^{O(log n)} states for unary two-way NFAs. It leaves a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial gap.
Kapoutsis characterizes polynomial-state simulation on short inputs by NL⊆L/poly, carefully distinguishing input-length restrictions and advice.
Clerici Lorenzini and coauthors obtain a polynomial-size normal form for two-way NFAs accepting letter-bounded languages.
Guillon and coauthors give polynomial-size complementation using self-verifying 1-limited automata, with rewritable annotations; the unrestricted read-only determinization question remains open.

cards.title: Are word equations with linear length constraints decidable?
cards.formal: Is there a Turing machine that halts on every finite input consisting of a system of word equations U_i=V_i and a system of integer linear equalities and inequalities on the variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when a simultaneous solution exists in the free monoid Σ*? The alphabet, equations, variables, and arithmetic coefficients are part of the input, with the conventions below.
cards.definitions: Σ is a finite nonempty alphabet of constant symbols and X={X_1,…,X_k} is a disjoint finite set of variables. Each U_i,V_i is an explicitly written finite word over Σ∪X; repeated occurrences of a variable must receive the same substitution. A solution assigns a finite word σ(X_j)∈Σ* to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing every letter of Σ. The empty word is allowed. Every substituted equality σ(U_i)=σ(V_i) must hold as a literal equality of words. The additional constraints are a finite conjunction of atoms sum_j a_j|σ(X_j)|≤b or sum_j a_j|σ(X_j)|=b, where all coefficients and constants are signed binary integers. Length is the number of alphabet symbols. There is no product of two variable lengths, letter-frequency counter, regular-expression predicate, string-to-integer conversion, or universal quantifier. The requested decider need not run in polynomial, elementary, or any specified computable time bound, but must terminate on satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs alike. Nonempty-substitution requirements can be imposed using |σ(X_j)|≥1.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove decidability by a correct algorithm terminating on every instance, or prove undecidability for this exact input language. Enumerating satisfying substitutions is only a semidecision procedure. A hardness lower bound for any decidable complexity class does not prove undecidability. A procedure for a syntactically restricted fragment, bounded solution lengths, or a stronger theory with additional predicates does not by itself settle the problem.
cards.context:
The two ingredients are individually manageable: plain word equations are decidable by Makanin’s theorem, and integer linear arithmetic is decidable. Their combination is difficult because string equality constrains how letters align, while arithmetic constrains the lengths of pieces across those alignments. A decision procedure for either component does not automatically decide their interaction. Ciobanu’s survey identifies this specific combination as a major remaining question.

Taking lengths gives useful necessary conditions, but can lose decisive information. For distinct letters a and b, the equation Xa=bX yields the harmless length identity |X|+1=1+|X|. Nevertheless, it has no finite-word solution. If X is nonempty its first letter must be b, and cancelling that b leaves the same equation for a shorter word; eventually one obtains the false equality a=b. This example shows why satisfying the induced linear equations alone cannot certify a word solution.

There is an elementary way to recognize every YES instance eventually: enumerate all tuples of finite words and test the equations and length constraints. If a solution exists, this search reaches it. For a NO instance, however, there is no prescribed point at which enumeration can stop. A computable bound on the size of some solution to every satisfiable input would therefore be sufficient for decidability. The existence of large witnesses by itself does not establish undecidability.

Several nearby theories have a different status. Constraints on the numbers of individual letters, or on the full vector of letter counts, can make word-equation satisfiability undecidable. Those predicates carry information beyond total length. Similarly, results with alternating quantifiers concern a stronger logical language. Importing either kind of undecidability theorem into this purely existential length-only question would change the problem.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic word equations in at most two unknowns, using a connection with matrix-semigroup reachability. Quadratic means each unknown has at most two occurrences across the equation. The two-unknown restriction is essential to the result stated in their RP 2025 paper. Its abstract also explains that sets of possible solution-length vectors need not be semilinear, so representing every such set by ordinary Presburger arithmetic cannot simply be assumed.

Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 work analyzes when extended Nielsen transformations terminate. These transformations reason about prefixes of variable values while tracking partial length information. Their cut graph records dependencies between occurrences, giving a sufficient termination criterion and a partial converse. This advances a procedure used in string solvers, but neither guarantees termination for every input nor decides the unrestricted problem.

Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez’s July 2026 preprint claims NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints, already over two letters. This strengthens the PP-hardness stated in its first version. Its NEXP-completeness theorem is for arithmetic with divisibility, not for unrestricted word equations with lengths. Positive Boolean formulas can be expanded into finitely many conjunctions for purposes of decidability, but that expansion need not be polynomial. The result therefore records a substantial complexity barrier without establishing a general decider or undecidability.

cards.title: Is positivity of integer linear recurrences decidable?
cards.formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, on every input consisting of an integer d≥1, integer initial values u_0,…,u_{d−1}, and integer coefficients a_0,…,a_{d−1}, halts and decides whether u_n≥0 for every n≥0, where u_{n+d}=sum_{i=0}^{d−1}a_i u_{n+i}? The order d is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound.
cards.definitions: All integers are given exactly in signed binary, and the coefficient and initial-value lists are explicit. The recurrence is homogeneous and its coefficients are constant in n. The requested property includes every term from u_0 onward and allows zero terms. It is enough to require a_0≠0: zero trailing coefficients can be removed after separately checking a finite prefix. No promise of distinct characteristic roots, reversibility, eventual nonnegativity, or bounded order is imposed. The recurrence supplied need not be of minimal order. Computation uses the ordinary Turing model, with no real-number or number-theoretic oracle. No polynomial-time or other specified running-time bound is required, but the machine must halt for both possible answers. A simple sequence has a minimal characteristic polynomial with no repeated complex roots.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a total, correct algorithm deciding the stated all-indices nonnegativity property, or prove that this exact problem is undecidable. Detecting a negative term by enumeration only semidecides the NO instances. Deciding whether all sufficiently late terms are nonnegative, or handling every sequence within a fixed restricted subclass, does not by itself settle the question.
cards.context:
A recurrence is a finite description of an infinite trajectory. One can compute any requested term exactly, but checking every term asks for a finite justification covering unbounded time. This makes positivity a basic test case for the limits of algorithmic verification. The July 2026 survey still lists its general decidability among the central unresolved problems. The word positivity is conventional here: the inequality is non-strict.

The connection to linear dynamics is direct. Store d consecutive values in a vector x_n. A fixed integer companion matrix M then gives x_{n+1}=Mx_n, and the first coordinate of M^n x_0 is u_n. The question is whether that coordinate ever enters the negative half-line. Even though the transition is linear and deterministic, the trajectory can combine growth, decay and oscillation through its characteristic roots.

No universal finite amount of simulation certifies the desired answer. For any chosen integer N, the sequence u_n=N−n satisfies u_{n+2}=2u_{n+1}−u_n, is nonnegative through index N, and becomes negative afterward. Of course this particular family is easy to analyze. Its role is to distinguish sampling a long prefix from proving a bound that is computed from an arbitrary input and is sufficient for that input.

Ouaknine and Worrell decide positivity for all sequences of order at most five. Their analysis combines effective estimates from Diophantine approximation with decision procedures for real algebraic conditions. At order six, decidability would already imply that certain approximation constants associated with transcendental numbers are computable. This is a precise mathematical consequence, rather than a proof that no algorithm can exist.

Removing repeated characteristic roots improves the known frontier: positivity is decidable for simple sequences through order nine.

A separate theorem decides ultimate positivity for simple sequences of every order, in polynomial space. Ultimate positivity asks whether some finite prefix contains all negative terms. The algorithm need not provide an effective cutoff beyond which the terms are nonnegative. Without such a cutoff, the theorem cannot be turned into a positivity decider by checking the remaining prefix.

There are larger decidable orders under a different structural promise. An integer recurrence is reversible when its extension to all negative indices also has integer values. Kenison and coauthors decide positivity through order eleven for reversible sequences, and through order seventeen when they are also simple. The extra integrality in backward time matters; these bounds do not apply to arbitrary integer recurrences of those orders.

A general solution would also decide the Skolem problem, which asks whether an integer recurrence ever equals zero. Integer recurrence sequences are effectively closed under termwise products and subtraction of a constant. Thus w_n=u_n²−1 is another such sequence, and it is nonnegative at every index exactly when u has no zero. Negating the answer to a positivity decider would decide Skolem. This reduction explains why positivity has consequences beyond sign analysis itself.
cards.why: A basic infinite-time safety question for finite linear descriptions. Its resolution would establish a major decidability boundary connecting verification, discrete dynamical systems and effective number theory, and would also settle general Skolem decidability.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational decision problem with an elementary input model, strong links to verification, and consequences for the separate Skolem problem; unrestricted decidability is unknown before any efficiency requirement is imposed.

progress.text: Ouaknine and Worrell establish positivity decidability through order five, and Diophantine consequences of extending it to order six.
For simple sequences, positivity is decidable through order nine.
Ultimate positivity is decidable for simple sequences of arbitrary order in PSPACE, and in polynomial time at each fixed order; this does not supply a general effective threshold.
Kenison, Nieuwveld, Ouaknine and Worrell establish positivity decidability for reversible sequences through order eleven, and simple reversible sequences through order seventeen.

The new survey retains general positivity as open and gives a concrete order-ten example whose positivity is unsettled. It also presents a reduction from order-five Skolem to positivity of simple order-ten sequences.

cards.title: Can simple stochastic games be solved in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is the following decision problem in deterministic polynomial time? Given an explicitly represented finite simple stochastic game G, a start vertex s, and a binary rational threshold r∈[0,1], decide whether v_G(s)>r, where v_G(s)=sup_σ inf_τ Pr_s^{σ,τ}[eventually reach the target sink 1]. The game and threshold follow the exact conventions below, and time is polynomial in their total bit length.
cards.definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability 1/2, independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; r=a/b is exact with binary integers 0≤a≤b and b>0. Equality v_G(s)=r is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language belongs to P, or prove that it does not. A polynomial-time algorithm for a fixed graph family, an approximate numerical estimate with an uncontrolled error, or a bound depending polynomially on an exponentially large numerical precision parameter is insufficient. Randomization in the game is part of the input semantics and does not grant randomization to the requested algorithm.
cards.context:
This game combines three elementary kinds of branching: a controller chooses, an adversary chooses, or a fair coin chooses. Removing one player gives a Markov decision process; fixing both players’ strategies leaves a Markov chain. The hard case is their interaction across cycles. Condon established that the threshold problem has polynomially checkable certificates on both sides, placing it in NP∩coNP. That classification has not yielded a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Both players have optimal deterministic positional strategies: one successor choice per owned vertex suffices, even though the definition permits history and randomization. A candidate strategy is therefore short. Fixing one player leaves a one-player optimization problem that can be solved in polynomial time, which explains the certificates. The difficulty is finding a suitable strategy among the exponentially many combinations, rather than needing to represent an optimal strategy of enormous length.

The local equations look deceptively simple: a Max vertex takes the maximum successor value, a Min vertex the minimum, and a random vertex their average. In a nonterminating component these equations alone can have multiple solutions. For example, a random vertex whose two slots both lead back to itself satisfies x=(x+x)/2 for every x, but its actual target-reaching probability is zero. A solver must identify the reachability values rather than accept an arbitrary fixed point.

Exact thresholds matter. A chain of k independent fair choices can reach the target with probability 2^(−k), with any failed choice leading to 0. Its graph has only O(k) vertices. Thus an additive error suitable for many numerical applications may be too large to distinguish a positive value from zero or to decide a nearby rational threshold. Polynomially many bits of precision can still require very many iterations if convergence is slow.

Ludwig’s classical randomized algorithm uses an expected 2^{O(√n)} operations on n-vertex games. It demonstrates that straightforward enumeration is not the only way to search the strategy space. It still gives a subexponential bound rather than the polynomial deterministic bound requested here.

Recent progress develops both practical solvers and structural cases. Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger extend sound value iteration to games with end components, maintaining lower and upper bounds while addressing probabilistic cycles.

Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang’s FUN 2026 paper solves stopping binary games on ladders: distance layers toward the sinks contain two vertices, except possibly the last layer. Their algorithm recovers an ordering of optimal values from this special geometry. Neither theorem supplies a polynomial-time solver for unrestricted games.

The consequences extend to more expressive objectives. Berthon, Katoen and Zhou give a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games, using binary representations of transition probabilities. This strengthens the explanatory connection between recurring long-run conditions and a single reachability target. Their paper invokes the known polynomial equivalence of the usual probability encodings; the reduction does not itself remove the open algorithmic bottleneck.
cards.why: A central test of efficient decision-making under both adversarial control and randomness. A polynomial algorithm would solve a canonical NP∩coNP problem and carry through reductions to quantitative verification tasks with more expressive objectives.

importance.reason: An elementary game model with broad consequences for synthesis and stochastic verification; short optimal strategies and efficiently checkable certificates coexist with an unresolved polynomial-time search problem.

cards.title: Can mean-payoff games be solved in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in the total input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a finite directed graph G=(V,E), a partition V=V_Max⊔V_Min, integer edge weights w:E→Z, and a start vertex s, determine whether Max has a strategy σ such that every strategy τ of Min produces a play s=v_0,v_1,… satisfying liminf_{T→∞}(1/T) sum_{t=0}^{T−1} w(v_t,v_{t+1})≥0.
cards.definitions: The graph, its ownership partition, its start vertex and all weights are represented explicitly; weights use signed binary. Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge, so plays are infinite. The owner of the current vertex chooses the next edge with full knowledge of the finite history. Strategies are arbitrary deterministic functions of this history. There are no chance vertices, simultaneous moves, hidden observations or multiple payoff coordinates. Max seeks a nonnegative lower limit of average accumulated weight; equality zero is winning. No bound is imposed on intermediate losses or on the size W=max(1,max_e |w(e)|). The running-time requirement concerns ordinary bit operations, so a polynomial dependence on W is not sufficient. Zero threshold loses no generality: a binary rational threshold a/b with b>0 can be absorbed by replacing w(e) with b w(e)−a, with polynomial growth of the encoding.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that this exact winner-decision language is in P, or prove that it is outside P. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a smoothed or average-case guarantee, or a lower bound for one strategy-improvement rule does not settle the unrestricted worst-case question. Strongly polynomial time would suffice but is a stronger requirement than this card asks for.
cards.context:
Mean payoff measures sustainable long-run performance. Edge weights can represent net resource gains, rewards or the negative of costs; an adversary controls some of the transitions. A finite initial loss disappears from the limiting average, while a repeatedly traversed cycle continues to matter. For example, eventually repeating weights −5 and +7 has mean payoff one, regardless of any fixed initial prefix. This distinguishes the objective from requiring the accumulated sum to remain nonnegative at every step.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players, so a player can make the same choice whenever a vertex is revisited. With both choices fixed, the resulting path eventually repeats a cycle, and its value is the cycle’s average weight. This yields compact certificates and NP∩coNP membership. It does not make the search easy: the number of positional strategy combinations can be exponential. Zwick and Paterson gave the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games.

The size of a weight and the size of its representation differ sharply. A weight 2^b takes only b+1 binary digits. An algorithm using O(nmW) arithmetic operations, where n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges, can therefore take exponential time in the input length. Brim and coauthors obtain such a pseudopolynomial bound for the threshold problem through energy-game progress measures. The result is powerful for small weights, but it leaves the dependence needed for this question unresolved.

Universal graphs provide a way to organize and compare value-iteration algorithms. Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann establish tight bounds within that framework, including improved dependence on the largest weight for a fixed number of vertices. Such a matching lower bound identifies a limitation of the framework being analyzed; it does not rule out an unrelated polynomial-time algorithm for mean-payoff games.

Smoothed analysis gives a different kind of progress. Loff and Skomra’s ICALP 2024 theorem obtains polynomial running time with high probability after sufficiently random independent perturbations of rewards, on ergodic game graphs. Here ergodicity is stronger than ordinary strong connectivity: for every reward assignment, the game value is independent of the start vertex. The theorem helps explain efficiency on perturbed inputs while retaining both a graph restriction and distributional assumptions. It does not decide the present worst-case complexity question.

There are also increasingly direct links to linear optimization. Maat’s September 2025 preprint identifies many strategy-improvement variants with instances of the simplex algorithm under nondegeneracy assumptions. This gives a structural bridge between algorithms and their lower-bound constructions. A correspondence between local improvement methods, however, is not a proof that their number of iterations is polynomial.

A July 2026 preprint by Adenwalla and coauthors connects tropical inequality systems and mean-payoff games with deciding chromatic boundedness for certain classes of graphs defined by equality patterns. context_blocks.text: Mean payoff measures sustainable long-run performance. Edge weights can represent net resource gains, rewards or the negative of costs; an adversary controls some of the transitions. A finite initial loss disappears from the limiting average, while a repeatedly traversed cycle continues to matter. For example, eventually repeating weights −5 and +7 has mean payoff one, regardless of any fixed initial prefix. This distinguishes the objective from requiring the accumulated sum to remain nonnegative at every step.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players, so a player can make the same choice whenever a vertex is revisited. With both choices fixed, the resulting path eventually repeats a cycle, and its value is the cycle’s average weight. This yields compact certificates and NP∩coNP membership. It does not make the search easy: the number of positional strategy combinations can be exponential. Zwick and Paterson gave the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games.

The size of a weight and the size of its representation differ sharply. A weight 2^b takes only b+1 binary digits. An algorithm using O(nmW) arithmetic operations, where n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges, can therefore take exponential time in the input length. Brim and coauthors obtain such a pseudopolynomial bound for the threshold problem through energy-game progress measures. The result is powerful for small weights, but it leaves the dependence needed for this question unresolved.

Universal graphs provide a way to organize and compare value-iteration algorithms. Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann establish tight bounds within that framework, including improved dependence on the largest weight for a fixed number of vertices. Such a matching lower bound identifies a limitation of the framework being analyzed; it does not rule out an unrelated polynomial-time algorithm for mean-payoff games.

Smoothed analysis gives a different kind of progress. Loff and Skomra’s ICALP 2024 theorem obtains polynomial running time with high probability after sufficiently random independent perturbations of rewards, on ergodic game graphs. Here ergodicity is stronger than ordinary strong connectivity: for every reward assignment, the game value is independent of the start vertex. The theorem helps explain efficiency on perturbed inputs while retaining both a graph restriction and distributional assumptions. It does not decide the present worst-case complexity question.

There are also increasingly direct links to linear optimization. Maat’s September 2025 preprint identifies many strategy-improvement variants with instances of the simplex algorithm under nondegeneracy assumptions. This gives a structural bridge between algorithms and their lower-bound constructions. A correspondence between local improvement methods, however, is not a proof that their number of iterations is polynomial.

Its reverse encoding uses a specified succinct representation. This creates another setting in which a solver would be useful. The paper explicitly leaves polynomial-time mean-payoff solving open, and its graph-class reduction should not be mistaken for a polynomial algorithm for games.

cards.title: Is there a polynomial-time simplex pivot rule?
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic primal-simplex pivot algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every rational linear program max{cᵀx: Ax=b, x≥0} with A of full row rank, a finite optimum, and any supplied feasible basis B_0, the algorithm reaches a basis whose reduced costs are all nonpositive using at most p(L) bit operations in total? Here L is the binary input length of A,b,c and B_0, and every basis change must be a legal improving simplex pivot as defined below.
cards.definitions: A has m rows and n columns with 1≤m≤n; all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicit binary integers. A basis B is a set of m columns with invertible A_B. Its basic solution is x_B=A_B^{-1}b and x_j=0 for j∉B, and feasibility means x_B≥0. An entering column j∉B must have reduced cost r_j=c_j−c_BᵀA_B^{-1}A_j>0. Put a=A_B^{-1}A_j. Choose a leaving basic index i attaining θ=min_{k∈B:a_k>0}x_k/a_k, and replace i by j in the basis. The finite-optimum promise ensures that this minimum exists for an improving column. Ties may be resolved by the rule; θ=0 is an allowed degenerate pivot and counts toward the bound. The rule may inspect the whole input and maintain history, with all preprocessing, pivot selection, exact arithmetic, helper computations and memory operations charged to p(L). It must follow these basis exchanges on the supplied LP from B_0: it may not jump to another feasible basis or replace the feasible region by an extended formulation. The required terminal condition r_j≤0 for all j∉B certifies optimality. This is the supplied-feasible-basis optimization version; phase-I feasibility construction is not part of this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a rule and prove its total polynomial bit complexity for every promised input and initial feasible basis, or prove that no such rule exists. Merely bounding the number of pivots while leaving their selection computationally unbounded is insufficient. A lower bound for a prescribed family of rules, or for nonlinear objectives, does not establish the negative answer for all rules here.
cards.context:
Linear programming already has algorithms with polynomial bit complexity, including ellipsoid and interior-point methods. The unresolved question is whether the same guarantee can be achieved while moving through bases by the simplex method. A pivot rule determines which improving direction to expose next and how to break ties. The STACS 2026 paper on ranking-based rules states that the general question remains open.

There are two obstacles to a polynomial guarantee. First, a short route to an optimal basis must exist under the permitted improving moves. Second, the rule must discover such a route efficiently. Knowing the optimum from another computation does not authorize skipping the route: every intervening basis exchange is still required. Likewise, a short path in the undirected graph of a polyhedron need not be a short path along improving edges.

The bit-complexity requirement is deliberately weaker than strongly polynomial simplex. It permits the running time to depend polynomially on the number of bits in coefficients. A strongly polynomial rule would instead bound its arithmetic work polynomially in m and n, together with appropriate bounds on the sizes of numbers used. Therefore this card does not assert that a positive answer alone settles Smale’s strongly polynomial LP problem or a diameter bound depending only on dimension and number of facets.

Degeneracy means several bases can describe the same vertex. A legal pivot with θ=0 changes the basis without improving the objective value, so an algorithm can stall even if the geometric route is short. Kukharenko and Sanità’s March 2026 paper bounds a block of consecutive degenerate pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by n−m−1, given an improving feasible direction. Such a direction can be obtained using an LP solver. This controls local stalling, but does not bound how many different nonoptimal vertices the method must visit.

Positive average-case results are also substantial. Spielman and Teng show polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex algorithm under random perturbations of the input. Smoothed analysis studies the expected behavior around an arbitrary instance as a function of perturbation size. It helps explain good practical performance, but does not give a deterministic worst-case guarantee on every exact rational instance.

The 2026 ranking-based lower bounds exclude broader families than a single greedy rule. One result covers index-ranking rules with a specified limit on their memory states; another covers memoryless rules using rankings by index, reduced cost and objective improvement. Full access to numerical data and unrestricted polynomially bounded history are allowed in this card, so those lower bounds do not cover every candidate.

A striking neighboring result does exclude every pivot rule for the active-set method with a nonlinear objective. Disser and Mosis first use higher-degree polynomial objectives on the hypercube. Bach and coauthors then obtain the phenomenon for maximizing a convex quadratic function, published at SODA 2026. The direction of optimization matters: this is convex maximization. Their construction does not have a linear objective, and the authors explicitly distinguish it from a general simplex lower bound.
cards.why: A fundamental question about whether local, improving basis exchanges can support efficient global optimization. It would explain a central practical algorithm and sharpen the relationship between polyhedral geometry, degeneracy and algorithmic access to an optimum.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem about one of the most important optimization algorithms; the existence and efficient discovery of short improving basis paths remain unresolved even though LP itself is polynomial-time solvable.

progress.text: Spielman and Teng establish polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex algorithm; this is a distributional guarantee rather than worst-case polynomial bit complexity.

Bach, Disser, Huiberts and Mosis strengthen the all-rules active-set lower bound to convex quadratic maximization. The latest preprint version is dated 22 October 2025.
Disser, Loho, Maat and Mosis publish superpolynomial lower bounds for specified ranking-based classes, with explicit information and memory restrictions.

Kukharenko and Sanità publish an antistalling rule bounding consecutive degenerate pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by n−m−1, given an improving feasible direction. It leaves the global pivot count open.
