cards.title: Is exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is the following language in P in the ordinary Turing model: all lists of symmetric rational matrices A_0,A_1,…,A_m∈Q^{n×n} for which there exists a real vector x∈R^m satisfying A_0+sum_{i=1}^m x_i A_i⪰0? Both m and n are unbounded parts of the input, and the algorithm must decide exact nonemptiness in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length.
cards.definitions: Every matrix entry is an explicitly supplied rational number, with signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; all matrices have the same size n≥1. A symmetric matrix M is positive semidefinite, written M⪰0, when zᵀMz≥0 for every real vector z, equivalently when all eigenvalues are nonnegative. The unknown x ranges over all real vectors, not just rational vectors. Singular feasible matrices count as YES. There is no strict-feasibility, boundedness, conditioning, rank, or distance-to-infeasibility promise, and no radius or accuracy parameter is supplied. The output is one bit specifying whether any feasible x exists; an explicit feasible point is not required. An affine subspace given by rational linear equations can be parametrized by rational Gaussian elimination, so this is also the rational-affine-subspace intersection formulation.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic polynomial-time bit algorithm deciding every instance, or prove that this language is outside P. Producing approximately positive semidefinite matrices, deciding only a promised well-conditioned case, or showing that explicit feasible points can have very long encodings does not settle this decision problem.
cards.context:
Semidefinite constraints replace scalar nonnegativity by nonnegativity of a quadratic form in every direction. They include linear inequalities as the diagonal-matrix special case and support powerful relaxations in combinatorial optimization. Approximation algorithms are well developed, but their guarantees require attention to input geometry and numerical precision. De Klerk and Vallentin establish polynomial bit complexity for a short-step interior-point method under appropriate assumptions; their theorem is about controlled approximation, not arbitrary exact feasibility.

The unrestricted problem is decidable. Introduce a real n×n matrix Y and impose A_0+sum_i x_i A_i=YYᵀ. These are finitely many polynomial equations of degree at most two, and a real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when such a factor exists. General real-algebraic decision procedures therefore apply. Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop more specialized symbolic algorithms, including treatment of degenerate feasible sets. None of this supplies polynomial time when both input dimensions vary.

Exact feasibility can differ even from arbitrarily close approximation. The matrix M(t) with rows (0,1) and (1,t) has determinant −1, so it is never positive semidefinite. Yet as t tends to positive infinity, its negative eigenvalue (t−√(t²+4))/2 tends to zero. Thus these infeasible matrices approach the positive semidefinite cone arbitrarily closely. A numerical tolerance alone cannot distinguish this situation from a singular feasible matrix.

Rational input also need not admit a rational witness. Consider a block diagonal matrix with blocks [[x,2],[2,2x]] and [[2,x],[x,1]]. The first block is positive semidefinite exactly when x≥√2, and the second when |x|≤√2. The whole matrix is therefore feasible exactly at x=√2. All coefficient matrices are rational, but searching only rational substitutions would miss the solution. This example explains why the domain of the unknowns is part of the formal question.

Even rational feasible points can be enormous. Conditions x_1≥2 and [[x_{i+1},x_i],[x_i,1]]⪰0 force x_{i+1}≥x_i², hence x_k≥2^{2^{k−1}}. A block diagonal LMI encodes the chain compactly, while writing its final coordinate in ordinary binary needs exponentially many digits in k. Pataki and Touzov analyze how such growth arises beyond isolated examples, including connections to singularity degree. Large explicit witnesses obstruct a naive search algorithm; they do not prove that deciding existence is hard.

Ramana’s exact dual provides an alternative feasibility system of polynomial description size without regularity assumptions. In the Turing model, it implies that semidefinite feasibility belongs to NP if and only if it belongs to coNP. It does not establish either membership individually. The corresponding NP∩coNP theorem over exact real-number machines belongs to a different computational model. This distinction prevents a common overstatement of what SDP duality proves about bit complexity.

Pataki’s October 2025 work gives a new derivation and a fuller description of the feasible set of Ramana’s dual using facial reduction.

A separate STOC 2026 result by Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer obtains small approximate solutions for minimizing convex polynomials over polyhedra. That result concerns polynomial objectives with linear constraints; the authors explicitly contrast it with the large-solution obstacle for semidefinite programs. It does not settle general exact semidefinite feasibility.
cards.why: A basic boundary between numerical convex optimization and exact efficient computation. Resolving it would clarify what semidefinite programming can guarantee without hidden regularity or witness-size assumptions, with consequences for optimization relaxations, algebraic certificates and verification.

importance.reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.

progress.text: Ramana constructs an exact dual without regularity assumptions and proves simultaneous NP/coNP membership in the Turing model, without proving membership in either class.
De Klerk and Vallentin establish Turing-model polynomial approximation complexity for a short-step interior-point method under their stated assumptions.

Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop symbolic homotopy for degenerate feasible sets. Generic auxiliary choices and objectives remain in their algorithmic analysis; fixed-parameter arithmetic bounds are not a general polynomial bit bound.
Pataki and Touzov publish a structural analysis of exponentially large feasible solutions and partial approaches to representing them compactly.
Pataki’s preprint gives a combinatorial treatment of Ramana’s exact dual and its feasible set, preserving the unresolved Turing-model complexity distinction.

Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer prove polynomial bit-length bounds for approximate optima of convex polynomial minimization over polyhedra. The result does not cover exact feasibility of arbitrary linear matrix inequalities.

cards.title: The deterministic k-server conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer k≥1, every metric space (M,d) with at least k+1 points, and every initial placement C_0 of k servers, does there exist a deterministic online serving rule A and a finite constant β≥0 such that cost_A(σ;C_0)≤k·OPT(σ;C_0)+β for every finite request sequence σ∈M*? The rule and β may depend on M,d,k,C_0, but neither may depend on future requests or on the length of the request sequence.
cards.definitions: The metric is symmetric, has finite real distances, is zero exactly on equal points, and satisfies the triangle inequality; the space may be finite or infinite and is known to the online rule. There are exactly k interchangeable, unweighted servers, whose current positions form a multiset. A request r_t must be served before r_{t+1} is revealed. If a server is already at r_t, no movement is needed; otherwise the rule chooses one of the k servers and moves it to r_t, paying the metric distance. Restriction to these lazy moves loses no competitive power. A deterministic online rule is a function of the known metric, initial placement and revealed request prefix, with arbitrary memory and no access to future requests; this card imposes no running-time bound. OPT is the minimum total movement cost of an offline rule serving the same finite sequence from C_0 with the same k servers and advance knowledge of the sequence. The additive β must be fixed before requests arrive and cannot grow with the number or cost of requests. Randomization, advice about future requests, and extra servers are not supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated exact k-competitive guarantee on every metric space, using any deterministic online rule, or refute it by showing that some k, metric and initial placement admit no such rule with any finite additive constant. Proving that the work-function algorithm or a particular potential-function family fails is insufficient for a negative answer about all algorithms. A (k+ε)-competitive guarantee for every ε>0 does not by itself prove attainment of ratio k.
cards.context:
The problem isolates the price of making placement decisions without seeing future demand. Servers can represent cache slots, mobile resources or copies of data; a movement pays for changing which demand locations are covered. On a uniform metric, where every distinct pair has distance one, serving a request is precisely the paging problem. The online rule and the offline optimum have the same number of servers. Their difference is information about the future, not available capacity.

The proposed factor k is a sharp target, already forced by paging lower bounds. The classical work of Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator establishes the lower-bound framework and settles the two-server case on general metrics. An additive constant is included so that a fixed initial placement does not distort asymptotic performance. Allowing that constant to depend on the request sequence would make the definition vacuous, which is why its quantifiers are explicit.

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou prove that the work-function algorithm is (2k−1)-competitive on every metric space. Its work function records the minimum offline cost of serving the already revealed prefix and ending in each possible server configuration. The algorithm uses these values to weigh movement against how well a configuration fits the past. This provides a single general strategy and leaves a factor approaching two between the known guarantee and the conjectured optimum.

It is widely conjectured that the same algorithm is actually k-competitive. Proving that stronger statement would settle this card, but the card permits a completely different algorithm. Similarly, failure of one proposed potential function only identifies a gap in that proof method. A potential proof typically compares changes in a quantity assigned to the current work function with the online and offline costs, so that the inequalities telescope over an arbitrarily long request sequence.

Several geometric settings attain the target. Chrobak and Larmore give k-competitive algorithms on tree metrics, covering line-like settings as well. Trees have unique connecting paths, which support movement rules unavailable in arbitrary metrics. This is substantial positive evidence, but arbitrary metric spaces can contain cycles and distance patterns that do not admit the same analysis.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle, with distance measured along the shorter circular arc. Their result first appeared in a 2022 preprint and was published in Theoretical Computer Science in 2024. They also give computer-assisted evidence excluding their defined canonical family of potential functions for the general three-server case. The geometric theorem and the limitation of that proof family are different conclusions.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani’s STOC 2023 theorem disproves the randomized O(log k) conjecture by constructing metrics with randomized competitive ratio Ω(log²k). It does not refute the deterministic target k: these are different claimed rates, and log²k is asymptotically smaller than k. The deterministic lower bound and the (2k−1) upper bound remain the relevant endpoints here.

Brilliantov, Bamas and Abbé’s April 2026 benchmark studies automated searches for potentials, particularly for four servers on a circle. A violated checked inequality refutes a candidate under the chosen formulation, while passing the finite checks is not a proof for every metric configuration and request sequence. Their experiments leave the open case unresolved. This offers concrete research tooling without changing the status of the conjecture.

cards.title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform interactive protocol (P,V) for the following promise problem? Input is an explicit quantum circuit C over {H,T,CNOT}, starting on all-zero qubits, with one designated output bit and binary description length N. Let p(C) be the probability of output 1. YES instances have p(C)≥2/3 and NO instances have p(C)≤1/3. V is a classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm and the honest P is a quantum polynomial-time algorithm; they exchange only classical messages. On every YES instance, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P]≥2/3. On every NO instance, for every computationally unbounded cheating prover P*, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P*]≤1/3. Both honest running times, the number of rounds and total communication must be polynomial in N.
cards.definitions: H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT is controlled NOT. The circuit explicitly specifies its qubits and gates, with at most N qubits. The promise excludes intermediate acceptance probabilities; no answer is required there. The two parties know C. The verifier may use private classical random coins, but has no trusted quantum memory, operations or measurements. The honest prover starts without an input-dependent advice state and uses a uniform polynomial-size quantum computation with classical control. All communication is through a single classical interface to one prover. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary adaptive response strategies with no computational bound; probabilities include the verifier’s coins and any prover randomness or measurements. There is no trusted setup, shared secret, second noncommunicating prover or cryptographic assumption. Fixed constant completeness and soundness gaps are the target; no constant-round requirement is imposed. This circuit promise problem expresses verification for arbitrary BQP computations.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol and prove its completeness, information-theoretic soundness and honest-party efficiency, or prove that none exists. A cryptographically sound argument against efficient cheaters, an interactive proof requiring a superpolynomial-time honest prover, or a protocol with quantum verifier operations does not meet the specification. A lower bound for a restricted number of rounds or a particular construction does not refute all polynomial-round protocols.
cards.context:
A user who can run only classical computations would like to check the answer returned by a quantum computer. Repeating the same claimed computation on the same untrusted device gives no independent reason to trust it. Interactive verification instead lets the user issue challenges whose answers constrain whether the reported result is correct. The survey by Gheorghiu, Kapourniotis and Kashefi organizes approaches according to what the verifier can do and which resources or assumptions establish trust. This card fixes the most restrictive physical verifier: entirely classical.

The usual inclusion BQP⊆IP does not settle the question. Since quantum polynomial time is contained in polynomial space, Shamir’s IP=PSPACE theorem supplies a classical interactive proof with an unrestricted prover. However, a proof system whose honest prover must carry out much harder auxiliary computations cannot be implemented merely by running the quantum computation being certified. Requiring the honest prover to be quantum polynomial time is therefore substantive.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev show that a verifier with a small quantum register can verify arbitrary efficient quantum computations. Quantum authentication lets a weak client protect data while delegating its processing. This demonstrates that a very limited quantum capability can be enough, but its communication and trusted operations do not satisfy the all-classical interface specified here. Their 2017 paper supplies the completed journal treatment of work first reported in 2008.

Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani provide another route: a classical verifier interacts with separated quantum devices sharing entanglement. Correlations in nonlocal games can force the devices to implement the required states and measurements. Isolation is crucial because it prevents the devices from coordinating arbitrary answers during the test. Combining both devices into one freely communicating prover removes that constraint, so the multiprover result cannot simply be reused for this card.

Mahadev’s 2018 breakthrough gives classical verification with one efficient quantum prover under the hardness of Learning With Errors for quantum algorithms. Cryptographic structure conceals information needed to cheat in the measurement tests. Its soundness is computational: the theorem protects against efficiently implementable attacks under the assumption. The present question deliberately quantifies over unbounded cheating strategies, which may break the underlying cryptography.

Recent work continues to refine these neighboring models. Kalai, Khurana and Raizes’s February 2026 construction verifies computations using one reusable QMA witness without destroying it, with negligible errors under post-quantum LWE. This is useful when the input quantum state cannot be copied. It retains the computational soundness assumption and therefore does not supply an unconditional protocol for the simpler BQP target here.

Kashefi, Leichtle, Music and Ollivier’s May 2026 journal article achieves information-theoretic verification without trusted state preparations or measurements. Its client still applies trusted quantum gates: one construction uses single-qubit Z rotations and bit flips. Removing two particular hardware requirements is meaningful progress, but a client performing these gates is not a purely classical verifier.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi explicitly retain the single-prover question in April 2026. They prove BQP^O⊆MIP^O for every classical oracle O using an exponentially long classical proof queried in polynomially many locations. Their theorem concerns multiple classical provers and does not establish efficient honest provers. Relativization is proposed as a way to investigate the difficulty, rather than as an equivalence that resolves it.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient quantum computation has an equally efficient, purely classical way to establish trust without computational hardness assumptions or isolated extra devices. A resolution would identify a basic boundary between producing quantum answers and certifying them.

importance.reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.

cards.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
cards.formal: For every fixed integer c≥1, does there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm A_c with the following guarantee? Given n≥2, a nonsingular rational n×n matrix A with m nonzero entries, a nonzero rational vector b, and an integer 1≤p≤c·ceil(log_2 n), output an explicit rational vector x̂ such that ||Ax̂−b||_2≤2^(−p)||b||_2 with probability at least 2/3. Each numerator and positive denominator of A and b has at most c·ceil(log_2 n) binary digits, and the spectral condition number κ_2(A) is promised at most n^c. The worst-case running time must be O_c(m log^(d_c)n) for some constant d_c independent of the input.
cards.definitions: The input lists the row index, column index and rational value of each nonzero coefficient, without duplicate positions, together with the n entries of b; hence n≤m≤n². The Euclidean norm is ||v||_2=(Σ_i v_i²)^(1/2), and κ_2(A)=σ_max(A)/σ_min(A), the ratio of its largest and smallest singular values. Nonsingularity makes the denominator positive. A may be nonsymmetric, indefinite and unrelated to a graph Laplacian. The algorithm need only meet its guarantee on promised inputs; it is not asked to certify the condition-number promise. Computation uses a word RAM with Θ(log n)-bit words, conventional arithmetic, comparison, bit operations and memory access; all operations on longer numbers, preprocessing, random-bit generation and writing the output are charged. No operation on an arbitrary real number has unit cost. Converting word operations to bit operations changes only polylogarithmic factors. Constants and the fixed program may depend on c, but neither nonuniform advice depending on n nor a supplied inverse or preconditioner is allowed. Here ε=2^(−p); this is the polynomial-condition, inverse-polynomial-accuracy regime of the near-input-size target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such a finite-precision algorithm for every fixed c, or prove that the specified guarantee is impossible for some fixed c. A conditional lower bound must state its unproved assumption and is progress rather than an unconditional negative answer. An exact-real arithmetic count, performance only on a structured matrix class, implicit quantum-state output, or a bound with polynomial dependence on κ instead of only polylogarithmic overhead in this regime does not settle the question.
cards.context:
Solving Ax=b is a basic operation inside scientific simulation, optimization and data analysis. A sparse input can be read and multiplied by a vector without scanning all n² matrix positions. The question is whether solving one system can always be comparably inexpensive, up to powers of logarithms. Peng and Vempala frame the general complexity problem around exploiting sparsity while also controlling numerical precision, rather than treating arithmetic on exact real numbers as free.

The target fixes a residual norm because different meanings of approximate solution can conceal different costs. If x*=A^(-1)b, the elementary inequality ||x̂−x*||_2/||x*||_2≤κ_2(A)·||Ax̂−b||_2/||b||_2 relates residual error to forward error. Thus a tiny residual need not mean an equally tiny solution error. For instance, A=diag(1,δ), b=(1,δ) and x̂=(1,0) have residual δ while the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The condition promise and requested accuracy make this dependence explicit.

Nearly linear solvers already exist for major structured families. Spielman and Teng establish such algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant systems using preconditioning and graph structure. Their guarantee is naturally expressed in the matrix energy norm. For positive-definite systems, norm comparisons relate this guarantee to residual accuracy, with conditioning affecting the required tolerance. An arbitrary sparse matrix lacks the diagonal-dominance structure that supports this machinery.

Peng and Vempala’s SODA 2021 result breaks the matrix-multiplication barrier for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. They implement a randomized block Krylov approach using structured factorizations and a numerical-stability analysis. This is why merely asking for a sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication would be an obsolete open question. The stronger near-input-size target remains far beyond that theorem.

Nie improves the required anti-concentration bounds for random Krylov matrices. His STOC 2022 result yields a bound of Õ(m^((ω−2)/(ω−1))n²) in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. For m=Õ(n), this becomes Õ(n^((3ω−4)/(ω−1))). The paper’s numerical exponent 2.2716 uses the matrix-multiplication bound available at that time; it is not a claim about today’s best numerical value of ω. Either expression remains far above linear for very sparse inputs.

The distinction between a sparse matrix and a structurally easy sparse matrix is sharpened by Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang. They reduce general linear equations with polynomially bounded integer coefficients and conditioning to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes while preserving sparsity up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, extending graph-Laplacian techniques to those higher-dimensional Laplacians would already have general consequences. This is a completeness reduction, not an unconditional proof that a near-linear solver cannot exist.

The Simons workshop report, revised in August 2026, calls for broader classes of scalably solvable systems and studies the finite-precision behavior of iterative methods. Its benchmark questions are more focused than a universal worst-case solver, and its discussion of preconditioning makes clear that constructing a useful preconditioner is itself part of the computational task. The present card is an explicit editorial formulation of the general complexity target; it is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report.

The output requirement also matters. An explicit n-vector is compatible with nearly linear time because a nonsingular n×n input has at least n nonzeros. Returning only access to a vector, a few observables, or a quantum state encoding its normalized coordinates changes the task. Conversely, demanding an exact rational solution could introduce much larger output encodings; the specified numerical approximation avoids building that extra requirement into the question.
cards.why: This tests whether sparsity and moderate conditioning suffice for solving linear equations at essentially the cost of reading them. A resolution would clarify the limits of graph-based solvers, preconditioning and numerical subroutines used throughout algorithms and optimization.

importance.reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.

This is why merely asking for a sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication would be an obsolete open question. The stronger near-input-size target remains far beyond that theorem.

Nie improves the required anti-concentration bounds for random Krylov matrices. His STOC 2022 result yields a bound of Õ(m^((ω−2)/(ω−1))n²) in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. For m=Õ(n), this becomes Õ(n^((3ω−4)/(ω−1))). The paper’s numerical exponent 2.2716 uses the matrix-multiplication bound available at that time; it is not a claim about today’s best numerical value of ω. Either expression remains far above linear for very sparse inputs.

The distinction between a sparse matrix and a structurally easy sparse matrix is sharpened by Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang. They reduce general linear equations with polynomially bounded integer coefficients and conditioning to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes while preserving sparsity up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, extending graph-Laplacian techniques to those higher-dimensional Laplacians would already have general consequences. This is a completeness reduction, not an unconditional proof that a near-linear solver cannot exist.

The Simons workshop report, revised in August 2026, calls for broader classes of scalably solvable systems and studies the finite-precision behavior of iterative methods. Its benchmark questions are more focused than a universal worst-case solver, and its discussion of preconditioning makes clear that constructing a useful preconditioner is itself part of the computational task. The present card is an explicit editorial formulation of the general complexity target; it is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report.

The output requirement also matters. An explicit n-vector is compatible with nearly linear time because a nonsingular n×n input has at least n nonzeros. Returning only access to a vector, a few observables, or a quantum state encoding its normalized coordinates changes the task. Conversely, demanding an exact rational solution could introduce much larger output encodings; the specified numerical approximation avoids building that extra requirement into the question.

cards.title: Does every unsatisfiable Boolean formula have a short efficiently checkable certificate?
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a fixed polynomial p such that, for every Boolean CNF formula F, $F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\iff\exists\pi\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|F|)}:V(F,\pi)=1$, with V never accepting a certificate for a satisfiable formula? Equivalently, is NP=coNP? The verification algorithm and polynomial are fixed for all formulas.
cards.definitions: A CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals x or NOT x. Variables take values in {0,1}; unsatisfiable means that no assignment makes all clauses true. The formula is encoded explicitly in binary, and |F| is its total bit length, including variable names and all literal occurrences. Empty clauses and an empty conjunction have their usual false and true meanings. V halts in time polynomial in |F|+|pi| on every pair of strings and rejects malformed formula encodings. Certificates may be arbitrary binary strings; they are not restricted to any particular inference calculus. NP is the class of languages with polynomial-length certificates checked in deterministic polynomial time. coNP consists of complements of NP languages. No randomization, oracle, advice, or interaction with a prover is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a sound verifier and one polynomial length bound covering every unsatisfiable formula, or prove that no such verifier and bound exist. Equivalently, prove NP=coNP or NP≠coNP. A lower bound for a particular proof system is insufficient for separation, and an efficient algorithm for finding certificates is not required for equality.
cards.context:
A satisfiable formula has a direct certificate: a satisfying assignment. For an unsatisfiable formula, one must explain why every possible assignment fails. Listing all assignments and a violated clause for each gives a checkable certificate, but its length can be exponential. The question asks whether some fixed verification scheme can always compress this explanation to polynomial length.

Simple contradictions already have short certificates. For instance, the conjunction of the one-literal clauses x and NOT x has no satisfying assignment, which can be checked immediately. The difficulty is a universal guarantee over all formulas, including large contradictions whose structure does not reveal such a local conflict. The verifier must be sound even on adversarially chosen purported proofs.

Cook and Reckhow formalized proof systems by requiring efficient verification, soundness, and completeness. Their connection with complexity theory says that a polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists exactly when NP=coNP. The theorem permits any efficiently checked proof format. Restricting the allowed inference rules changes the problem to one about the power of that particular system.

This also distinguishes the question from P versus NP. If NP differs from coNP, then P differs from NP because deterministic polynomial time is closed under complement. The converse implication is not known. Equal certificate classes would still leave open whether those certificates can be found efficiently. Thus the target is symmetry between short evidence for yes and no answers, rather than an algorithm for deciding every NP problem.

Restricted lower bounds are nevertheless instructive. The pigeonhole principle has exponentially long resolution refutations in its usual encoding, while stronger Frege reasoning has polynomial-size proofs of the same principle. A formula family hard for one proof language therefore need not be hard for another.
cards.why: This asks whether every nonexistence claim with an efficiently verifiable positive counterpart also has concise evidence. It is a central bridge between computational complexity, the length of mathematical proofs, and the limits of automated reasoning.

importance.reason: A fundamental certificate-complexity question that implies P≠NP in the separation direction and motivates the entire general proof-complexity lower-bound program.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow establish the equivalence between NP=coNP and the existence of a polynomially bounded propositional proof system. This turns a complexity-class question into a precise proof-length target.

Haken proves an exponential resolution lower bound for pigeonhole formulas; Buss gives polynomial-size Frege proofs of the pigeonhole principle. These results demonstrate why lower bounds must account for the chosen proof system.

The ICTS program Circuits, Communication, and Proofs continues to present separation of NP from coNP as the goal of the Cook–Reckhow program. It describes current connections with circuit lower bounds and communication complexity; it announces no resolution of this question.

cards.title: Does a quantum witness have more power than a classical witness?
cards.formal: Is $\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QCMA}$? Both classes have a polynomial-time quantum verifier and bounded error. QMA permits a polynomial-size quantum witness; QCMA permits only a polynomial-length classical string. The question concerns the standard classes without an oracle.
cards.context:
A quantum state may encode a proof that has no short classical description. Oracle separations test this idea but do not separate the standard classes.

The same quantum verifier is used on both sides of the comparison. What changes is the proof supplied by a prover: either a classical string or a quantum state. A classical proof is still allowed to instruct the verifier to perform a sophisticated quantum computation, so this is not simply a comparison between classical and quantum algorithms.

To prove a separation, one needs a verification task whose positive instances admit useful quantum proofs but no comparably short classical proofs for any efficient quantum verifier. Observing that a particular state has a long classical description is not sufficient: a different classical argument might certify the same claim without describing that state.
cards.why: This identifies what kind of information might be intrinsically necessary for efficient verification.

progress.text: A separation relative to a classical oracle is known. The February 2026 paper gives a simpler construction. It leaves the unrelativized class question untouched.

cards.title: Can directed reachability be decided in deterministic logarithmic space?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine A and an absolute constant C such that, for every directed graph G on vertices {1,...,n} and every s,t, A decides whether t is reachable from s while using at most $C\log_2(n+2)$ work-tape cells? G is supplied explicitly as a read-only adjacency matrix, together with s and t. The machine must halt and be correct on every input. This is equivalent to L=NL.
cards.definitions: The graph may have self-loops; reachability allows a path of length zero, so s=t is a yes instance. Input access is two-way and read-only. Work tapes have a fixed finite alphabet; visited work-tape cells, including all counters and stored vertex identifiers, count toward space. The finite control and read-only input cells do not. There is no advice, random tape, oracle, writable copy of the input, or external storage. L is deterministic O(log N) work space on binary inputs of bit length N. NL uses the same space bound with nondeterministic transitions and accepts exactly when some computation branch accepts; all branches can be clocked to halt within polynomial time. Since the matrix encoding has N=Theta(n^2) bits, O(log N)=O(log n). A halting deterministic machine with this space bound automatically runs in polynomial time: it cannot repeat a complete configuration.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an always-correct deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm for all directed graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. By NL-completeness under deterministic logspace reductions, either direction settles L versus NL. An algorithm for undirected graphs, a nondeterministic algorithm, or an algorithm using a larger power of log n does not answer the stated question.
cards.context:
A graph search usually remembers which vertices it has visited. With only logarithmic space, it can store a constant number of vertex names and counters, but cannot keep a separate visited bit for every vertex. The input may be rescanned as often as necessary. The challenge is to organize those repeated scans so that arbitrary directed paths can be detected without retaining a large search frontier.

Nondeterminism gives a simple logarithmic-space procedure: keep the current vertex and a length counter, guess the next edge, and accept if t is reached within n−1 edges. Any reachable target has a simple path within that bound. For a general nondeterministic logspace computation, vertices can instead represent machine configurations. An accepting computation becomes a directed path, explaining why this graph problem captures the whole class NL.

Savitch’s algorithm recursively asks whether a path can pass through a candidate midpoint. It saves space by recomputing subproblems, but a logarithmic recursion depth with logarithmic information per level uses O(log² n) space. Its running time is quasipolynomial. Reducing the storage to a single logarithmic factor would also force polynomial time in the stated machine model.

For undirected graphs, Reingold already achieved the logarithmic target. Edge direction is therefore a substantive part of this card. Likewise, NL=coNL shows that nonreachability has a nondeterministic logspace procedure; it does not remove nondeterminism. Recent connections with random-walk estimation make the landscape richer, while leaving the same deterministic directed question.
cards.why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.

importance.reason: A central space-complexity separation expressed by a basic graph problem. The contrast with solved undirected reachability isolates a fundamental role of edge direction and nondeterminism.

progress.text: Savitch proves that nondeterministic space s can be simulated deterministically in O(s²) space, for s at least logarithmic. Directed reachability consequently has an O(log² n)-space algorithm.

Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. In particular NL=coNL, so both reachability and nonreachability admit nondeterministic logspace algorithms.
Reingold obtains deterministic logarithmic space for undirected connectivity, published at STOC 2005 and subsequently in JACM. Arbitrary directed graphs are outside that theorem.

Doron, Pyne, Tell, and Williams give two algorithms such that, on each directed graph, at least one succeeds: deterministic polynomial-time, polylogarithmic-space transitive closure, or nondeterministic logarithmic-space random-walk estimation. This per-graph alternative does not give the first algorithm on every graph or reduce its space to O(log n).

Bhadra and Tewari show NL-hardness even for directed graphs whose edges can be partitioned into two forests of directed paths of length at most two, including when the partition is supplied. Such a simple decomposition therefore does not make the general logspace obstacle disappear.

cards.title: How many k-element subsets can a line separate from a planar point set?
cards.formal: Let K₂(n,k) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets S⊆P of size k strictly separable from P\S by a line. Determine K₂(n,k) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers n≥2 and 1≤k≤⌊n/2⌋.
cards.definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with (a,b)≠(0,0), ax+by<c for every (x,y)∈S, and ax+by>c for every (x,y)∈P\S. The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression F(n,k) and absolute constants 0<c₀≤C₀<∞ such that c₀F(n,k)≤K₂(n,k)≤C₀F(n,k) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values n/2<k<n; k=0,n each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove an upper bound for every admissible planar point set and a lower-bound construction for each admissible n,k that match within absolute constant factors. Resolving only fixed k, only the balanced case k=⌊n/2⌋, or only the exponent while leaving an unbounded factor between the bounds is partial progress.
cards.context:
A line can realize only a small fraction of all choices of k points. The question measures the combinatorial capacity of one linear cut at a fixed output size. For example, when k=1 the separable points are the convex-hull vertices, and their maximum number is n. The difficult regime lets k increase with the input size.

Point-line duality translates changes of a separating line into the structure of levels in a line arrangement. A level tracks positions having a specified number of lines below them. These level bounds recur in geometric selection and in analyses of parametric optimization. Dey’s method also yields bounds for related level structures, convex chains, and parametric spanning-tree problems.

For even n, the balanced case is closely tied to halving edges: segments joining two input points whose supporting line leaves (n−2)/2 of the other points on each side. A halving edge is not itself a separating line, since it passes through input points. The correspondence between k-sets and directed (k−1)-edges gives K₂(n,n/2) equal to twice the maximum number of undirected halving edges.

The known planar upper bound is O(n k^(1/3)), whereas constructions give n exp(Ω(√log k)) subsets. In the balanced regime the latter grows faster than n times any fixed power of log n, yet slower than n^(1+ε) for each fixed ε>0. Thus neither a linear bound nor an ordinary polylogarithmic correction to linear growth can describe the worst case.

Sharper finite-size constructions and improvements to the additive terms of halving-line bounds are useful progress. They do not close the gap in asymptotic growth. Keeping this distinction explicit matters here: an improved upper bound may retain the same 4/3 exponent in the balanced case.
cards.why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.

importance.reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.

progress.text: Dey proves K₂(n,k)=O(n k^(1/3)) for 1≤k≤n/2 through a crossing-number argument. The balanced specialization gives an O(n^(4/3)) upper bound.
Tóth constructs planar point sets with n exp(Ω(√log k)) k-sets for n≥2k>0, improving the earlier n log k scale. This remains separated from the upper bound by an unbounded factor when k grows.
Nivasch gives a simpler halving-edge construction improving the constant in the square-root-log exponent. The construction does not produce n^(1+ε) halving edges for any fixed positive ε.

Alonso, López, and Rodrigo improve a linear subtractive term in the upper bound on the maximum number of halving lines for even n, and improve some finite-n bounds. The asymptotic upper exponent remains 4/3.
The revised Open Problems Project entry still lists the planar asymptotic gap as unresolved. A search through September 2026 did not locate matching general upper and lower bounds.

cards.title: The online Boolean matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
cards.context:
If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.

A small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.

The conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.

The graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.
cards.why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.
cards.definitions: The product uses OR and AND, not addition modulo two. The matrix remains fixed throughout the sequence. The word-RAM has logarithmic-size words. Success concerns the complete online computation. This is distinct from multiplying over a field, updating the matrix itself, or answering one query after an uncharged preprocessing phase.

progress.text: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak formulate OMv and derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems, including reachability and variants of connectivity.
Larsen and Williams give randomized online multiplication in total time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$. This improves the algorithmic baseline without refuting the conjecture.

Hu and Polak show fine-grained equivalences between Boolean OMv and several online non-Boolean products, including min-max, dominance, and equality. These broaden the supporting connections; they do not prove the conjecture.

cards.title: Is perfect matching in general graphs in deterministic NC?
cards.formal: Given a simple undirected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, can a deterministic parallel algorithm find a perfect matching, or report that none exists, in $(\log n)^{O(1)}$ time using $n^{O(1)}$ processors? A perfect matching is a set of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex. Equivalently, seek a uniform polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuit family for the search problem. Graphs may contain odd cycles; no bipartition is supplied or promised.
cards.context:
A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the open issue is the length of the dependency chain after work is spread across many processors. Following one augmenting path after another does not automatically give a polylogarithmic number of parallel steps. The processor bound matters too: solving many possibilities simultaneously is useful only if the total work remains polynomial.

Choosing matching edges independently is dangerous. On a four-cycle, every edge can be excluded while preserving some perfect matching. Removing all four edges at once nevertheless destroys every solution. A parallel construction must coordinate its choices around one compatible matching rather than around separate existence certificates.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite result is a major nearby advance. Its theorem covers bipartite graphs, including polynomially bounded weights. The present card deliberately asks for arbitrary graphs, where the deterministic polynomial-processor target remains unresolved in the checked literature.
cards.why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
cards.definitions:
NC permits polynomially many processors and polylogarithmic parallel time; quasi-NC permits a quasipolynomial processor count. Both conditions in the target are required. The algorithm must construct the matching when one exists, not merely recognize that the input has even order or satisfy a relaxation of the matching constraints.

Use Boolean circuits with bounded fan-in and logspace-uniform descriptions. An output lists matching edges or a distinguished symbol for nonexistence.

progress.text: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it.

Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap.
Chatterjee, Ghosh, Gurjar, Raj, and Thierauf prove an NC result for bipartite matching. This new preprint does not state the general-graph theorem sought here.

cards.title: Can directed reachability have near-linear work and polylogarithmic depth?
cards.formal: Given an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge directed graph and a source $s$, is there a randomized shared-memory parallel algorithm that outputs every vertex reachable from $s$ using $\widetilde O(n+m)$ total work and $(\log n)^{O(1)}$ depth, with high probability? Both bounds must hold on arbitrary inputs, including sparse graphs with long directed paths. Work counts all primitive operations across processors; depth is the longest chain of dependent operations.
cards.context:
A breadth-first search does little total work but exposes only the next frontier after processing the current one. On a directed path, that dependency chain is long. Matrix-based transitive closure can instead exploit massive parallelism, but it computes reachability for every pair and may do far more work than one-source search needs. The target asks for the useful properties of both approaches in one algorithm.

The size of the input and the size of its transitive closure are very different parameters. A one-way path has only $n-1$ edges but $\Theta(n^2)$ reachable ordered pairs. Thus an algorithm whose work is nearly linear in the closure size can still be quadratic in the input size. This remains true even though the requested one-source answer has only $n$ bits.

Shortcuts are a natural way to shorten dependencies: add an edge only when its endpoints were already connected by a directed path, then search the augmented graph. Constructing and storing these edges costs work too. Bounds on what a particular shortcut representation can achieve should not be mistaken for lower bounds on every parallel reachability algorithm.

The August 2026 result improves the polylogarithmic-depth side of the tradeoff using the size of the transitive closure as a parameter. It is relevant progress, but does not supply near-linear input work on all graphs. This distinction is essential when reading the phrase “faster than transitive closure.”
cards.why: I include this because reachability is one of the simplest linear-time sequential graph tasks, yet obtaining fast parallel time without wasting substantial work remains difficult. The two-resource formulation makes the goal precise: a faster wall-clock computation should not require polynomially more total computation.
cards.definitions:
The model is a standard word-based PRAM/shared-memory parallel model, with $O(\log n)$-bit words and concurrent access handled by standard PRAM conventions. Local primitive operations, auxiliary data construction, and shortcut generation count toward work. $\widetilde O$ hides polylogarithmic factors. High probability means $1-n^{-c}$ for a requested fixed $c>0$. The output is reachability, not shortest-path distances.

For definiteness fix a CREW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed, and concurrent writes to one cell are prohibited. Word operations are arithmetic, multiplication, bitwise operations, shifts, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of logarithmic-size words. The target permits the polylogarithmic overhead of simulating common alternative PRAM conventions.

progress.text: Jambulapati, Liu, and Sidford obtain almost-linear work with $n^{1/2+o(1)}$ depth for directed reachability.

Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg, and Saranurak improve the near-linear-work depth bound as graph density increases; their dense-graph reachability bound is $n^{0.136}$. The theorem does not give polylogarithmic depth for every density.

Kogan and Parter give polylogarithmic depth with $\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})$ work, where $T=|TC(G)|$ and $\omega$ is the matrix-multiplication exponent. Even the hypothetical $\omega=2$ gives work in terms of $T$, which may be quadratic for a linear-size input.

cards.title: Is Exact Matching on general graphs in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a simple undirected graph G on an even number n of vertices, each edge colored red or blue, and an integer $0\le k\le n/2$, determine whether G has a perfect matching containing exactly k red edges. The algorithm must be correct on every input. No bipartition is promised, and no randomness or computational hardness assumption is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that this decision problem belongs to P, or prove that it does not. A randomized polynomial-time algorithm, an approximation to the red count, or an algorithm restricted to bipartite graphs does not establish the positive answer.
cards.context:
Perfect matching already has efficient deterministic algorithms on general graphs. Requiring a prescribed number of red edges adds an exact constraint that the ordinary matching objective does not express. A minimum-red matching and a maximum-red matching only identify two ends of the attainable range; intermediate counts can be missing.

For example, color a six-cycle alternately red and blue. Its two perfect matchings have respectively three and zero red edges. Neither one nor two is attainable. This obstruction appears even in a bipartite graph; allowing odd cycles adds further structure that a general algorithm must handle.

A yes answer is easy to verify once a matching is supplied: check that every vertex is covered once and count the red edges. The difficulty is finding a deterministic procedure that also certifies no instances in polynomial time. The existing algebraic route uses random choices to prevent the cancellation that can hide a feasible matching.

The graph class is essential. A 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for bipartite Exact Matching, and the separate catalogue entry records that claim and its formalization limits. This card concerns all graphs. Even a validated bipartite theorem would need another argument before it could settle the proposition here.
cards.why: I include this because it is a concrete combinatorial derandomization target with a short, checkable definition. It asks whether randomness is necessary for an exact constraint on top of an otherwise tractable optimization problem, connecting matching algorithms to algebraic identity testing.
cards.definitions: P denotes languages decidable by a uniform deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the ordinary adjacency-list encoding and the binary encoding of k. A perfect matching is a set of disjoint edges covering every vertex. If a polynomial-time decision algorithm exists, a matching can also be recovered by polynomially many decisions on residual instances. This target concerns sequential polynomial time, not deterministic NC.

progress.text: Mulmuley, U. Vazirani, and V. Vazirani provide the randomized algebraic matching framework underlying polynomial-time Exact Matching algorithms.
El Maalouly surveys algorithms and related problems while retaining general deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.
Du claims a deterministic bipartite algorithm. Version 3 states eight explicit hypotheses in its Lean formalization. That paper does not claim a general-graph solution.

Sato and Yamaguchi’s revised preprint tests all possible red counts simultaneously with high probability using O(n^ω) finite-field operations, where ω denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent used by their algebraic routines. The algorithm remains randomized; the introduction explicitly retains deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.

cards.title: Hill’s conjecture for the crossing number of complete graphs
cards.formal: For every integer n≥3, is the minimum number of edge crossings in a drawing of the complete graph K_n in the plane exactly $H(n)=\frac14\prod_{i=0}^{3}\left\lfloor\frac{n-i}{2}\right\rfloor$? Edges may be arbitrary simple curves. Drawings with H(n) crossings are known for every n; the unresolved assertion is that no drawing has fewer.
cards.definitions: K_n has n vertices and one edge between each pair of distinct vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points of ℝ² to its vertices and represents each edge by a simple arc joining its endpoints, with no other vertex on the arc. Edge interiors intersect in finitely many points, all proper crossings; tangencies, shared subarcs and crossings of three or more edge interiors are excluded. Count intersection points of edge interiors, not shared graph endpoints. The crossing number cr(K_n) is the minimum over all these drawings and all vertex placements. Finite polygonal arcs suffice; restricting every edge to a single straight segment is a different problem. Allowing drawings on the sphere with arbitrary arcs gives the same minimum. H(n)=n⁴/64+O(n³), but the card asks for exact equality at every n, not just agreement of leading coefficients. For example H(5)=1, H(6)=3, H(12)=150 and H(13)=225.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove cr(K_n)≥H(n) for every n, or exhibit one valid drawing of some K_n with strictly fewer than H(n) crossings. An asymptotic ratio of 1 would settle only the asymptotic version; a lower bound for straight-line, two-page, or shortest-geodesic drawings does not by itself settle arbitrary drawings.
cards.context:
A complete graph asks every pair of vertices to communicate through a separate drawn edge. Planarity fails already at five vertices. The conjecture proposes an exact measure of the unavoidable interference as the number of vertices grows, independent of the choice of drawing coordinates or the shape of each edge.

The upper bound is constructive: there are systematic drawings with H(n) crossings. The challenge is universal. A lower bound must rule out every different way to route the edges, including configurations whose geometry bears little resemblance to the known constructions. Counting crossings in a visually natural drawing establishes only the upper bound.

The topological and geometric versions must be separated. Straight-line edges impose extra restrictions; shortest arcs on a sphere allow more freedom but still impose a geometric rule. Two-page drawings impose another rule: vertices lie on one spine and each edge stays on one of its two sides. Proving the formula for any of these families narrows the search for a counterexample without exhausting arbitrary curves.

General lower bounds are already close to the conjectured leading term. The flag-algebra approach derives inequalities from the frequencies and compatibility of small drawing configurations. Even a remaining gap of roughly one or two percent matters here: the goal is an exact extremal formula for all sizes, rather than a constant-factor estimate.

The April 2025 spherical-arc theorem is a substantial geometric advance: it establishes the conjectured lower bound for every shortest-geodesic drawing on the sphere. Its statement does not say that an optimal unrestricted drawing must be of this type. That missing reduction is why the original question remains open.
cards.why: This is a basic benchmark for universal crossing lower bounds. Its study links topological graph drawing, geometric configurations, and extremal counting methods, and supplies a reference family against which crossing inequalities for more general graphs are compared.

importance.reason: A foundational exact extremal problem for the most symmetric dense graph family. It tests the reach of general crossing-number lower bounds beyond drawing classes constrained by a particular geometry.

progress.text: Hill’s constructions and subsequent work give drawings with H(n) crossings. The general assertion that these are optimal became the Hill or Harary–Hill conjecture, also known as Guy’s conjecture.
Ábrego, Aichholzer, Fernández-Merchant, Ramos, and Salazar prove that the two-page crossing number of K_n equals H(n). The unrestricted crossing number minimizes over a larger drawing class.

Balogh, Lidický, and Salazar use flag algebras to show an asymptotic general lower bound of at least 0.985H(n). This substantially improves the earlier general asymptotic ratio, while leaving a positive gap from the conjectured value.
The Gasarch–Hayes–Ostuni–Park column states the unrestricted formula as Conjecture 4.6. The linked manuscript is dated 4 January 2025, correcting the legacy record’s 2022 source year.

Streltsova and Wagner prove the lower bound H(n) for all spherical shortest-geodesic drawings, with equality for coneighborly configurations. Their introduction still lists the unrestricted conjecture as open and verified through n=12.

cards.title: Do single-pair shortest paths require cubic-size min-plus circuits?
cards.formal: For n >= 2, assign an arbitrary nonnegative real weight x_{ij} to every unordered edge {i,j} of the complete undirected graph on vertices 1,...,n. Define $f_n(x)=\min_{P:1\leadsto n}\sum_{e\in P}x_e$, where P ranges over simple paths. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input gates x_{ij} and optional constants 0 and infinity, binary gates min(a,b) or a+b, unrestricted reuse of gate outputs, and one designated output. Its topology depends on n but not on x, and it must compute f_n exactly for every permitted weight assignment. Let s(n) be the minimum number of binary gates in such a circuit. Is s(n)=Omega(n^3)? Equivalently, do there exist constants c>0 and n0 such that every such circuit has at least c n^3 gates for every n>=n0?
cards.definitions: A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences x_{ij} and x_{ji} denote the same input, because the graph is undirected. Infinity is an optional internal constant with min(a,infinity)=a and a+infinity=infinity; all input edge weights are finite and nonnegative. The circuit has no subtraction, tests with separate Boolean outputs, conditional routing, or input-dependent memory access. A min gate directly returns the smaller of its two numerical arguments. Input gates, wires, and reuse of an already computed value are free; binary arithmetic gates are counted. Circuits need not be generated uniformly by an efficient algorithm, so the proposed lower bound is nonuniform and imposes no depth restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified cubic lower bound, or refute it by proving its negation: for every c>0 and every n0 there is an n>=n0 with a correct circuit using fewer than c n^3 gates. An o(n^3)-size circuit family for all sufficiently large n would suffice for a negative answer. A lower bound for a more restricted circuit class, for all-pairs output, or for shortest paths allowing negative input weights does not establish this statement.
cards.context:
The numerical task is elementary to state: return one shortest-path distance. The difficulty is understanding what can be done by a fixed network of minimum and addition operations. An algorithm that chooses which vertex to process next using comparisons may use information to control its future computation. This circuit model cannot turn the identity of a minimum into arbitrary control flow. Consequently, a fast implementation of a graph-search algorithm does not automatically supply a circuit of comparable size.

A concrete upper bound comes from repeated relaxation. Initialize d_0(1)=0 and d_0(v)=infinity otherwise, and compute d_k(v)=min(d_{k-1}(v), min over u distinct from v of d_{k-1}(u)+x_{uv}). After n-1 layers, output d_{n-1}(n). Each layer uses O(n^2) gates. Nonnegative weights ensure that deleting cycles cannot increase a walk’s cost, so these layers suffice for the simple-path optimum. This gives O(n^3) gates.

Every edge can influence the answer: choose a simple source-to-target path through that edge, make its other edges cheap, and all edges outside the path expensive. Thus dependence on the quadratic number of inputs gives a quadratic lower bound, but does not charge separately for repeated reuse of intermediate computations. The missing factor n is the substantive issue.

For all-pairs shortest paths, a cubic lower bound is known in the same general min-plus framework. Its many required outputs are essential to the usual argument; requesting only the distance from 1 to n leaves room for different sharing. The database formulation places the question in absorptive semirings, where adding an unnecessary detour is absorbed. This card fixes the nonnegative tropical instance so that its allowed operations and output are unambiguous.
cards.why: This is a basic unconditional lower-bound question for dynamic programming. A resolution would clarify whether the standard cubic relaxation computation is intrinsically necessary even for one distance when computation is restricted to minimum and addition, and would illuminate why monotone lower-bound methods struggle with paths of varying lengths.

importance.reason: A central explicit lower-bound problem for tropical circuits, linking shortest paths, pure dynamic programming, and provenance computation. The gap concerns a basic polynomial-time task rather than a specialized graph family.

progress.text: Jukna gives the O(n^3) min-plus upper bound and explicitly asks for a cubic lower bound for the single-pair connectivity polynomial; his framework distinguishes nonnegative tropical evaluation from formal polynomial production.

The author’s book supplements discuss the known cubic all-pairs lower bound and the unresolved single-source and single-pair optimality questions. The all-pairs argument does not directly settle one output.

Koutris restates the question for complete undirected graphs over absorptive semirings, recording the O(n^3) upper bound and the quadratic input-dependence lower bound, with the gap open already over the tropical semiring.

cards.title: Quantum 3-coloring of cycles in o(log* n) rounds
cards.formal: Is there a uniform quantum-LOCAL algorithm that, for every n≥3 and every identifier assignment to an n-cycle, outputs a proper 3-coloring with global probability at least 1−1/n in $T(n)=o(1+\log^* n)$ communication rounds? Every node is given n, its own identifier from [n²], and a consistent clockwise/counterclockwise orientation. Initial quantum registers are unentangled across nodes.
cards.definitions: The network is a simple cycle; the orientation only identifies predecessor and successor, and communication is allowed in both directions. Nodes do not receive their numerical position in the cycle, a leader, or the list of other identifiers. They run one finite classical control program which may perform arbitrary finite local quantum computations, then exchange finite but unbounded numbers of qubits with each neighbor in each synchronous round. For a concrete uniform model, local quantum operations are finite circuits over H, T, and CNOT, fresh |0⟩ ancillas, and computational-basis measurements with adaptive classical control. Register size, message size, and local computation time are not charged, but are finite on every branch. Initially the joint quantum state is a product of local |0⟩ registers; the given classical local input may affect subsequent operations. No shared randomness, initial entanglement, or graph-dependent advice is supplied. The protocol may generate entanglement by sending qubits during its counted rounds. Every node eventually outputs one color in {1,2,3}. Success means that every cycle edge has differently colored endpoints, simultaneously. T(n) bounds all branches of the protocol, not its expected time. The little-o condition is T(n)/(1+log* n)→0 as n→∞; log* counts iterated base-2 logarithms down to at most 1. This card fixes the standard directed-cycle input variant, while allowing communication in either direction.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol with a proof of its worst-case round bound and global success probability, or prove that no such protocol exists. A constant-round protocol would answer yes. An anonymous zero-error lower bound, a two-color lower bound, or a lower bound using unbounded-degree trees does not by itself answer this high-probability three-color cycle question.
cards.context:
A cycle is the simplest network in which many nearby choices must be coordinated. Two colors encode a global parity constraint, but three colors allow a much more local solution. In classical distributed computing, the exact deterministic cost of this symmetry breaking is Θ(log* n).

Naor’s lower bound shows that classical randomization with high-probability correctness still needs Ω(log* n) rounds. Quantum messages can create correlations unavailable to classical messages, but a coloring algorithm still has to return ordinary classical colors. The question is whether those correlations allow neighboring processors to agree on a valid local pattern faster than the classical symmetry-breaking threshold. The orientation and identifiers are explicit inputs, so no lower bound may rely on their absence.

There is a fundamental obstacle to arguments based only on causality. Finitely dependent proper colorings exist: far-separated sets of outputs can be independent while all adjacent colors differ. Consequently, the output distribution of a hypothetical constant-round quantum coloring algorithm need not violate a general no-signaling or finite-dependence constraint. Existence of such a distribution does not provide a quantum protocol that samples it.

The August 2026 result attacks the quantum implementation itself using matrix-product-state structure and a teleportation-based reduction. It proves a linear lower bound for anonymous finite-qubit protocols that must always succeed. Its Section 1.4 explicitly identifies the extension to high-probability correctness as the remaining problem. That is precisely the error regime retained on this card.

A separate July 2026 paper proves a log-star lower bound for 3-coloring rooted trees through growing-degree instances, and a linear lower bound for 2-coloring even cycles. Neither theorem handles the combination here: degree exactly two, three available colors, and small nonzero failure probability.
cards.why: This is a canonical test of quantum advantage for a natural distributed symmetry-breaking task. A faster protocol would improve one of the basic local coordination primitives; a lower bound would have to explain a limitation of quantum realizability that mere causal consistency does not capture.

importance.reason: A central concrete benchmark for quantum distributed computation, with an elementary output condition and a sharp classical threshold. The recent zero-error breakthrough leaves the practically standard high-probability regime unresolved.

progress.text: Cole–Vishkin and subsequent algorithms give O(log* n) classical coloring. Linial proves a matching deterministic lower bound. These classical bounds also give a quantum upper bound by running a classical protocol.
Naor proves the classical randomized ring-coloring lower bound, preserving the log-star obstruction when small failure probability is allowed.
Holroyd and Liggett construct finitely dependent colorings. These establish the barrier to deriving the desired quantum lower bound solely from finite dependence or causality.
Fraigniaud, Magniez, and Ziccardi give quantum lower bounds for rooted-tree 3-coloring and even-cycle 2-coloring. Their rooted-tree lower bound uses degree as a growing parameter.

Coiteux-Roy and coauthors prove that for any fixed c≥3, anonymous quantum-PN c-coloring of an even directed n-cycle with probability 1 needs more than floor(n/2)−2 rounds. They explicitly leave high-probability correctness open.

cards.title: Can distributed MIS be solved in sublogarithmic time on every graph?
cards.formal:
In the randomized LOCAL model, does there exist an algorithm that finds a maximal independent set in $o(\log n)$ rounds on every $n$-vertex simple graph? Its output $I\subseteq V$ must satisfy $(u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\{u,v\}
subseteq I$ and $v
otin I\Rightarrow N(v)\cap I
e\varnothing$. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each fixed constant $c>0$, allowing the constant in the running time to depend on $c$. The bound must hold uniformly over all maximum degrees $\Delta\le n-1$.
cards.context:
A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.

Maximal means that no further vertex can be added. It does not require the largest possible independent set. For example, on a star, either the center alone or all leaves is a valid answer. The challenge is to choose consistently across a general network, rather than to optimize the number of selected vertices.

Degree-sensitive algorithms achieve $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds. This is already sublogarithmic when the degree is sufficiently small; the unresolved target includes polynomial-degree graphs. Repeatedly making only constant-factor progress leaves a logarithmic running time.

Recent work breaks that pattern on graphs with no cycles of length at most six. It does not extend to arbitrary graphs. Together with stronger lower bounds, this leaves a concrete question: can local choices still make sufficiently rapid progress when short cycles create dependencies between nearby decisions?
cards.why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.
cards.definitions:
The network is the input graph. Rounds are synchronous; each edge can carry an arbitrarily large message in each direction. Vertices may have distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifiers and private random bits. Every vertex outputs its own membership bit. The measured time is the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, not the number of rounds in which an individual processor stays awake.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree. Both the algorithm and the asymptotic time bound are uniform over input graphs and valid identifier assignments.

progress.text: Ghaffari gives the degree-sensitive MIS algorithm. With subsequent deterministic finishing routines, the standard bound is $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$.

Khoury and Schild give a randomized lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\log\Delta,\sqrt{\log n}\})$ for maximal matching and, by reduction, MIS on general graphs. This implies an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ worst-case barrier, not an $\Omega(\log n)$ barrier.

Their separate degree-reduction paper obtains $O(\log\Delta/\log(\log^{*}\Delta)+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds for girth at least seven. Its Open Question 1 asks for the general-graph improvement.
