cards.title: One cycle versus two: is logarithmic time necessary in low-memory MPC?
cards.formal: For every fixed $0<\delta<1$, must every randomized MPC algorithm distinguishing one n-cycle from two vertex-disjoint (n/2)-cycles use $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds in the worst case over even n and input placement? Each machine has $O(n^\delta)$ words and total memory is O(n) words. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each requested fixed $c>0$. An $o(\log n)$-round algorithm for one fixed $\delta<1$ would refute this lower-bound conjecture.
cards.context:
Both promised inputs have exactly n vertices and n edges, and every vertex has degree two. Counting vertices, counting edges, and checking degrees therefore gives the same answer. The difference is how those edges join into components. Vertex identifiers are arbitrary, so the labels do not reveal where a cycle begins or whether two pieces belong together.

A sequential scan with graph traversal solves the problem in linear time. With the edge list spread across machines, no one machine can store the whole instance. Repeatedly joining path fragments or doubling the length represented by a pointer gives a natural logarithmic-round approach. The conjecture says that general distributed computation cannot compress this process into asymptotically fewer communication rounds under the stated memory limits.

It is tempting to justify the conjecture by saying that information travels only one graph edge per round. That would be incorrect here. Any machine may send to any other machine, and local computation between exchanges is unrestricted. The restriction is how much information a machine can store, send, and receive at once. A valid lower bound must cope with arbitrary encodings and nonlocal communication.

Extra geometric structure can change the answer. The 2025 grid-connectivity algorithm uses an embedding with bounded edge lengths to obtain constant rounds in its parameter regime. An arbitrarily labelled cycle does not provide that embedding, so the geometric result does not refute this promise-problem conjecture.
cards.why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.
cards.definitions: Words have $O(\log n)$ bits. The input edge list is distributed across machines without exceeding their local memory. Each synchronous round allows arbitrary local computation followed by sending and receiving at most $O(n^{\delta})$ words per machine. The desired success probability is $1-n^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. This card fixes linear total memory; variants allowing more total space must be stated separately.

progress.text: Nanongkai and Scquizzato develop equivalence classes and conditional-hardness connections around this cycle problem and logarithmic-space computation. Their reductions have explicit global-memory requirements; those should be checked before transferring them to the linear-total-memory variant here.

Gan, Wirth, and Zhang explicitly state the linear-total-memory 2-CYCLE conjecture while giving a constant-round algorithm for embedded grid graphs. The promised arbitrary-cycle problem is left unresolved.

cards.title: Constant non-signaling locality beyond deterministic log-star LOCAL
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed locally checkable labeling problem Π on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree Δ, with finite input and output alphabets, that admits a zero-error non-signaling outcome of constant locality, but has no deterministic LOCAL algorithm using $O(1+\log^* n)$ rounds? The degree bound, checking radius, alphabets, and non-signaling locality must all be independent of n.
cards.definitions: An LCL is specified by an integer Δ≥2, a fixed radius r≥1, finite input/output alphabets, and a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhoods with input/output labels, degrees, and ports. A labeling is valid when every vertex sees a permitted pattern. Legality does not depend on identifiers or n. Inputs range over all simple undirected n-vertex graphs of maximum degree at most Δ, all finite-alphabet input assignments, all port numberings, and all injective identifiers from [n²]; disconnected graphs are included. For one constant integer R, a non-signaling outcome assigns each input a joint probability distribution on all vertex outputs, supported entirely on valid labelings. For every vertex subset S and any two inputs of the same size, an identifier-, input-, and port-preserving isomorphism of their radius-R neighborhoods of S must carry one marginal output distribution on S to the other. This condition applies to every subset, not only to individual vertices. Arbitrary real probabilities and correlations are allowed; there is no requirement that the outcome be sampled by a classical or quantum protocol. Exact n may be used. In deterministic LOCAL every node initially knows n, its identifier, its input, degree, and ports, follows one finite computable program, and exchanges arbitrarily long messages with neighbors in synchronous rounds. Local computation is unrestricted but must terminate. The negative classical condition is: for every correct algorithm A and constant C, arbitrarily large inputs require more than C(1+log* n) rounds. Here log* counts base-2 logarithms needed to reduce n to at most 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Exhibit one finite LCL specification and a constant-locality family of non-signaling distributions, and prove that no deterministic O(log* n)-round solver exists; or prove that every LCL with such a distribution has a deterministic O(log* n)-round solver. This card fixes the all-bounded-degree-graphs, zero-error formulation of the saved question. A family whose degree grows with n, or an outcome of logarithmic locality, does not establish the required separation.
cards.context:
A distributed algorithm can only react to information that has reached it. Non-signaling keeps this causality requirement but removes the demand for a physically implementable algorithm. It asks whether the joint output probabilities could exist without letting a distant input change the observations of any group of nearby or far-apart observers. This makes it a useful setting for proving strong communication lower bounds.

Requiring consistency only for one vertex would be much too weak. For example, choosing the two colors of a connected bipartite graph with a random global flip makes each vertex individually uniform. The correlation between two vertices can nevertheless reveal whether their distance has even or odd parity. The marginal condition for every subset is what detects such hidden signaling.

The iterated logarithm marks an established symmetry-breaking regime. Every LCL solvable there by a deterministic LOCAL algorithm has a constant-locality, finitely dependent solution distribution, and therefore a constant-locality non-signaling distribution. The question asks whether constant non-signaling locality reaches further than this classical regime.

The rooted-tree case is constrained by a simulation theorem: sufficiently small non-signaling locality leads back to a deterministic O(log* n)-round algorithm there. That theorem cannot simply be extended to unrooted trees or arbitrary graphs. The corrected February 2026 manuscript explicitly withdraws an earlier claim about unrooted trees.

Recent quantum separations show that the models can differ for a fixed LCL, but at a larger time scale. The August 2026 revision gives a quantum O(log n) upper bound and a classical randomized lower bound of Ω(log n·(log log n)^0.99). These rates leave the constant-locality threshold on this card unresolved.
cards.why: A resolution would locate the boundary of what causality alone permits for locally verifiable tasks. It would either extend a fundamental symmetry-breaking classification to arbitrary non-signaling correlations, or provide a concrete obstruction to such a classification and a benchmark for quantum lower bounds.

importance.reason: A foundational boundary question between local computation and causal output distributions. The fixed degree and constant locality requirements isolate an unresolved structural issue beyond the already known logarithmic quantum separations.

progress.text: Akbari and coauthors prove that deterministic O(log* n) LCLs admit constant-locality finitely dependent distributions. They also show that o(log log log n) randomized online locality in rooted trees implies deterministic O(log* n), which covers non-signaling outcomes through their simulation.

Suomela’s updated problem list still asks for an LCL with constant non-signaling locality and classical deterministic complexity beyond the log-star regime. This card fixes zero error and a finite specification on all bounded-degree graphs.

Balliu and coauthors strengthen the established quantum separation to O(log n) versus Ω(log n·(log log n)^0.99). Their general simulation also bounds the power of finitely dependent distributions; finite dependence imposes an extra independence condition absent from general non-signaling outcomes.

cards.title: Quantum versus classical nonuniform advice
cards.formal: Is $\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}=\mathrm{BQP/poly}$? Advice for inputs of length $n$ depends only on $n$: a state on $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ qubits on the left, or $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ classical bits on the right. The computation must succeed on every input of that length.
cards.context:
Advice is not a witness chosen for an individual input. It is one nonuniform information resource shared by an entire input-length class.

For a fixed input length, the advice must support all inputs of that length. It cannot be tailored after seeing the particular instance. This makes it different from a witness, which is chosen to establish a claim about one input. A fresh copy of the same quantum advice state can be supplied for each computation.

The possible advantage is not that a measurement reveals an arbitrary amount of classical information from a few qubits. Instead, the algorithm might use the input to choose which computation to perform with the advice. The open question is whether polynomial-length classical advice can always support an equally effective computation for every input.
cards.why: This distinguishes two basic ways to store auxiliary information for computation. It is different from QMA versus QCMA.

progress.text: The source gives the first separation of these advice classes using a standard classical oracle. It does not claim an unrelativized separation.

cards.title: Does worst-case Nearest Codeword hardness imply low-noise LPN hardness?
cards.formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
cards.context:
LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.
cards.why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.

progress.text: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.

cards.title: Can deterministic LOCAL algorithms find an MIS in O(log n) rounds?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that outputs a maximal independent set on every $n$-vertex simple graph in $O(\log n)$ synchronous communication rounds? Each vertex has a distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifier, and the guarantee must hold for every valid identifier assignment and every maximum degree. The output must be independent, and every vertex outside it must have a neighbor inside it. No random bits are available.
cards.context:
Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.

Randomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.

Network decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.

The 2024 improvement reaches approximately $\log^{5/3}n$ rounds and avoids the log-squared cost of the standard decomposition-based route. Closing the remaining gap requires more than optimizing the constants of that route. The 2026 coloring reduction still uses this improved MIS bound as its benchmark.
cards.why: This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An O(log n) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.
cards.definitions:
LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output. The target is uniform over arbitrary graphs, not restricted to bounded degree, planar graphs, or trees.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree; the time guarantee must still be O(log n) uniformly over degrees.

progress.text: Balliu and coauthors prove a deterministic lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})$. In particular, the general worst-case complexity cannot be substantially below logarithmic up to a log-log factor.
Rozhoň and Ghaffari obtain polylogarithmic deterministic network decomposition and consequently polylogarithmic deterministic MIS.
Ghaffari and Grunau improve MIS to $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ rounds, where the hidden factors are polylogarithmic in $\log n$.
Bourreau, Brandt, and Nolin use the same deterministic MIS benchmark to improve Δ-coloring; their result does not give an O(log n) MIS algorithm.

cards.formal: Is there a Turing algorithm D that, given a finite description of a locally checkable labeling problem Π on trees of maximum degree Δ, always halts and decides whether Π has a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that solves every allowed input instance in at most t communication rounds, for some constant t depending only on Π? Trees are unrooted, arbitrary finite input labels are allowed, and each node knows the exact number n of nodes.
cards.definitions: The input description is (Δ,r,Σ_in,Σ_out,C), with integers Δ≥2,r≥1, finite nonempty input and output alphabets, and a finite list C of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhood types. Neighborhoods record input/output labels, degrees and incident port numbers, but not processor IDs or n. Ports at a degree-d node are numbered 1,…,d; the two port numbers of an edge need not agree. A labeling is valid precisely when every node’s radius-r neighborhood is isomorphic, preserving this data and its center, to a type in C. Instances range over every finite nonempty simple undirected tree of degree at most Δ, every input labeling, and every port numbering. Processors additionally have distinct IDs in {1,…,n²}. Initially a node knows its own input, ID, degree, ports, n, and Π. In each synchronous round it can send arbitrary finite messages to its neighbors; local computation is unrestricted in cost but must be computable and terminate. The same finite program runs at every node and works for all n and all ID assignments. No distinguished global root, parent pointers, randomness, or additional advice is supplied. D itself is centralized, with no running-time bound. Descriptions with an unsolvable instance are no instances of the decision problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an always-terminating decider for exactly the described constant-round solvability property, or prove that no such decider exists. A procedure that eventually recognizes every positive instance but may run forever on negative instances is insufficient. This is an explicitly chosen binary subproblem of the saved broader question about deciding the entire asymptotic complexity.
cards.context:
An LCL is specified by local rules rather than a global objective. Proper coloring and maximal independent set illustrate the distinction: a completed labeling can be checked from small neighborhoods, yet finding a valid labeling may require substantially more communication. Here the input to the decision procedure is the rulebook itself, not one network to label.

The question asks whether a finite rulebook reveals that a bounded communication radius will always suffice. The radius may be enormous and may depend on the rulebook, but it cannot grow with the network. Testing small trees alone cannot certify this property; a procedure must account for every larger tree, every input labeling, and every assignment of identifiers.

The possible round complexities and the ability to recognize them are separate issues. Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt prove that an LCL on bounded-degree trees with o(log* n) complexity actually has constant complexity. Their paper nevertheless explicitly leaves constant-time decidability open. A gap theorem supplies a separation between cases without automatically providing a test for which case applies.

Positive instances can be recognized by searching the finite local-rule candidates associated with each fixed radius. If a suitable radius exists, this search eventually finds it. The missing part is a terminating certificate or other method for the negative answer. The full complexity-classification question would also need to distinguish further classes, so an affirmative answer here is only one stage of that larger goal.

Rooted-tree classification results use the supplied parent-child direction to organize their certificates. An arbitrary port numbering on an unrooted tree provides no such globally consistent direction. Recent results also show that knowledge of network size and the computability of local state transitions can matter. This card fixes both assumptions rather than silently moving between models.
cards.why: This asks whether one can automatically recognize when local verification can be converted into truly local construction on the simplest branching networks. A decider would be a basic ingredient of distributed algorithm synthesis; undecidability would expose a limit that persists even on trees.

importance.reason: A core decidability boundary for local distributed computation, linking finite specifications, algorithm synthesis, and lower-bound certificates on trees. It isolates a fundamental unresolved stage of full complexity classification.

progress.text: Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt close the o(log* n)-to-O(1) gap on bounded-degree trees. Their Section 1.4, Question 1.7, explicitly asks whether constant-time solvability is decidable and explains why recognizing positive instances is not the missing direction.

Balliu, Brandt, Chang, Olivetti, Studený, and Suomela classify the O(log n)-versus-polynomial region efficiently for their regular-tree formalism. Their abstract explicitly leaves finer classification in the O(log n) region open for unrooted trees.

Cruciani and coauthors show that computable and arbitrary local transition functions give the same round complexity for LCLs when a bound on n is supplied. Without such knowledge they can differ. The exact-n convention of this card avoids that ambiguity.

Balliu and coauthors show that weakening exact network-size knowledge changes the tree complexity landscape. Their result motivates keeping that assumption fixed; it does not decide constant-round solvability from an arbitrary LCL description.

Piombi extends decidable polynomial complexity gaps to a more general logical formalism on unbounded-degree rooted trees. The paper still identifies the lower-complexity classification of unrooted LCLs as an unresolved boundary.

cards.title: Can randomized O(log log n) LOCAL solvability on trees be decided?
cards.formal: Does there exist an always-terminating Turing algorithm that, given a finite locally checkable labeling specification Π on unrooted bounded-degree trees, decides whether Π admits a randomized LOCAL algorithm using O(1 + log log(n+2)) rounds and producing a globally valid labeling with probability at least 1 − 1/(n+1) on every n-node input? Nodes know the exact n. The implicit constant may depend on Π, but not on n or the input instance.
cards.definitions: A specification consists of integers Δ≥2 and r≥1, finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhood types. Types record input/output labels, degrees and incident port numbers, but do not mention identifiers or n. All finite nonempty simple unrooted trees of maximum degree Δ, all input labelings, and all port numberings are allowed; a degree-d vertex has ports 1,…,d, independently of ports at the other endpoint. Every node must output one symbol, and the labeling is valid when every node sees a permitted neighborhood. Nodes have distinct identifiers in {1,…,n²}, initially know their own input, ID, ports, degree, Π and n, and use independent private fair random bits. A single finite computable program operates at every node. Communication is synchronous with arbitrary finite messages and unrestricted terminating local computation. The round bound holds for every random tape; the success requirement is joint over the entire labeling, for each fixed input and ID assignment. There is no supplied root, shared random advice, or graph-dependent preprocessing. A specification with an unsolvable instance is a negative instance of the decision problem. Logs have base 2.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a total decider for this exact property, or prove its undecidability. A classification for one fixed specification, a promise of solvability, or only a test for O(log n) algorithms does not answer the question. This card explicitly specializes the saved full-classification question to one binary threshold; it does not claim this threshold alone decides every complexity class.
cards.context:
A local rulebook describes what a solution should look like near each node. Here a centralized program receives that rulebook and must decide whether random local decisions can coordinate a valid solution within a doubly logarithmic number of communication rounds. It is a question about automatically understanding algorithms, rather than running a particular algorithm on one tree.

On trees under the usual network-size convention, randomness can produce an exponential improvement: sinkless orientation has logarithmic deterministic complexity and doubly logarithmic randomized complexity. Other locally checkable problems remain logarithmic with randomness. Thus the threshold in this card distinguishes real algorithmic behaviors; it is not simply asking whether random bits can be removed.

The known landscape has substantial empty intervals. A gap theorem can tell us that no problem occupies an interval without giving an effective way to determine which side a supplied rulebook occupies. The regular-tree classification paper explicitly marks the gap between randomized doubly logarithmic and logarithmic complexity as having unknown decidability.

The answer required from the decider is only yes or no. On a negative input it need not compute the exact larger complexity, and on a positive input it need not distinguish constant, iterated-logarithmic, and doubly logarithmic algorithms. This avoids hiding an undefined symbolic representation of an arbitrary asymptotic function inside the output requirement.

A small failure probability at one vertex is not the same as a small chance of any error in the network. The statement fixes the latter, and also fixes exact knowledge of n. The 2026 network-size results show that changing this knowledge can change the relationship between randomized and deterministic complexities.
cards.why: Recognizing this threshold would give a general test for fast randomized coordination on branching networks. Undecidability would instead establish a limit on automated classification despite the remarkably sparse list of possible round complexities.

importance.reason: A basic recognition problem at the boundary where randomization yields exponential speedups on trees. It connects local specifications, algorithm synthesis, and effective lower-bound theory.

progress.text: Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt establish the complete standard tree complexity landscape, including the randomized doubly logarithmic class; knowing the possible classes does not decide membership.

Balliu and coauthors give polynomial-time classification of the logarithmic-versus-polynomial region in their regular-tree formalism. Figure 1(c) leaves recognition of the randomized O(log log n) threshold open.

Suomela’s updated primary problem list continues to ask for randomized complexity decidability for LCLs with inputs on unrooted trees. This card selects a concrete threshold within that broader request.

Balliu and coauthors show that weakening exact knowledge of n changes the tree landscape and the circumstances in which randomness helps. Those variants are not silently substituted for this card’s model.

Piombi’s discussion still identifies only the polynomial gaps as known decidable for unrooted trees. The new main results concern a logical generalization on rooted trees, rather than the randomized threshold here.

cards.title: Can every fixed-dimensional Tarski problem be solved with O(log² n) queries?
cards.formal: Let Q(n,k) be the minimum worst-case number of adaptive deterministic value queries needed to find any fixed point of an unknown monotone function $f:[n]^k\to[n]^k$, where [n]={1,...,n} and monotonicity is with respect to coordinatewise order. A query at x reveals the entire vector f(x). Is it true that for every integer k>=1 there is a constant C_k such that $Q(n,k)\le C_k(1+\log_2 n)^2$ for every n>=2? Arbitrary finite computation between queries is allowed. Constants may depend on k but not on n or f. This asks for an exponent independent of the fixed dimension, not a polynomial bound on C_k.
cards.definitions: For x,y in the grid, x<=y means x_i<=y_i for every coordinate i. The oracle is promised to satisfy x<=y implies f(x)<=f(y). A valid output is any x with f(x)=x; no minimum or maximum fixed point is required. An adaptive query procedure can choose each query using all earlier queries and answers, and must terminate correctly for every promised oracle. Equivalently, Q(n,k) is the minimum depth of a finite deterministic oracle decision tree whose leaves output valid fixed points for every monotone function consistent with that leaf. Neither a circuit description nor the table of f is part of the input. Query cost is one per returned vector, and places no restriction on the bit complexity of choosing the next query. The finite product grid is a complete lattice, so a fixed point always exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the bound for every fixed k, or show that there is a fixed k for which Q(n,k)/(1+log_2 n)^2 is unbounded as n grows. A growing factor depending only on k is permitted. A bound whose logarithmic exponent grows with k does not answer yes. A lower bound obtained only by letting k grow with n does not answer no unless it implies failure at some fixed k.
cards.context:
Starting at the bottom of the grid and repeatedly applying f gives a nondecreasing chain until a fixed point is reached. This directly proves existence constructively, but the chain can contain a number of steps proportional to n times the dimension. Since the coordinates need only log n bits to describe, dependence on n can be exponentially larger than dependence on the coordinate description length.

One-dimensional search can exploit order by repeatedly discarding a large interval. In a product order, two points can be incomparable: one coordinate is larger and another smaller. The oracle’s monotonicity then does not directly compare their images. The question asks whether these multidimensional interactions must eventually increase the power of log n, or whether they can be absorbed into a dimension-dependent constant.

The first surprise was that dimensions two and three both have Theta(log^2 n) query complexity. Chen, Li, and Yannakakis extend this equality to dimension four in their March 2026 preprint. Their more general upper bound is O(log^(ceil((k-1)/3)+1) n) for fixed k. The concluding discussion explicitly raises a bound of the form f(k) log^2 n, which is the target on this card.

Query complexity and computational efficiency must be separated here. The 2026 algorithm uses expensive intermediate search and counting; its authors leave a time-efficient implementation open. Even a positive answer to this card would only limit how much oracle information is needed. Obtaining a polynomial-time algorithm when both k and log n are input parameters would require additional control of the constants and the work between queries.
cards.why: This probes the information cost of finding a guaranteed fixed point under monotonicity, a basic organizing principle in algorithms, semantics, and equilibrium computation. The same sharp bound in dimensions two, three, and four makes the dependence on dimension a substantive structural mystery rather than just a loose analysis of one algorithm.

importance.reason: A broad oracle-complexity question about monotone fixed points, with a surprising low-dimensional pattern and connections to equilibrium search. It distinguishes intrinsic information requirements from implementation time.

progress.text: Etessami, Papadimitriou, Rubinstein, and Yannakakis prove an Omega(log^2 n) lower bound already in two dimensions, including for randomized algorithms; the 2022 seminar records this starting point.
Fearnley, Pálvölgyi, and Savani give an O(log^2 n)-query algorithm in three dimensions, matching the two-dimensional lower bound.
Brânzei, Phillips, and Recker prove randomized query lower bound Omega(k log^2 n / log k) for n,k>=2. For fixed k this remains quadratic in log n, so it does not rule out the card’s target.

Chen, Li, and Yannakakis obtain O(log^2 n) queries in four dimensions and improve the exponent in every fixed dimension. Section 9 proposes the possibility of a generic dimension-dependent constant times log^2 n.

context_blocks.text: Starting at the bottom of the grid and repeatedly applying f gives a nondecreasing chain until a fixed point is reached. This directly proves existence constructively, but the chain can contain a number of steps proportional to n times the dimension. Since the coordinates need only log n bits to describe, dependence on n can be exponentially larger than dependence on the coordinate description length.

One-dimensional search can exploit order by repeatedly discarding a large interval. In a product order, two points can be incomparable: one coordinate is larger and another smaller. The oracle’s monotonicity then does not directly compare their images. The question asks whether these multidimensional interactions must eventually increase the power of log n, or whether they can be absorbed into a dimension-dependent constant.

The first surprise was that dimensions two and three both have Theta(log^2 n) query complexity. Chen, Li, and Yannakakis extend this equality to dimension four in their March 2026 preprint. Their more general upper bound is O(log^(ceil((k-1)/3)+1) n) for fixed k. The concluding discussion explicitly raises a bound of the form f(k) log^2 n, which is the target on this card.

Query complexity and computational efficiency must be separated here. The 2026 algorithm uses expensive intermediate search and counting; its authors leave a time-efficient implementation open. Even a positive answer to this card would only limit how much oracle information is needed. Obtaining a polynomial-time algorithm when both k and log n are input parameters would require additional control of the constants and the work between queries.

cards.title: Does sublinear deterministic volume always collapse to O(log* n)?
cards.formal: For every locally checkable labeling problem Π on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree Δ, does the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm A with V_A(n)=o(n) imply the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm B with V_B(n)=O(1+log* n)? Algorithms know the exact size of their input graph, and node identifiers are distinct integers in {1,…,|V(G)|²}. Here V_A(n) is the maximum number of distinct vertices visited to determine one vertex’s output, over all allowed instances with at most n vertices and all requested vertices.
cards.definitions: An LCL is specified by fixed Δ≥2, a fixed verification radius r≥1, finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite set of permitted rooted radius-r labeled neighborhoods. Rules may inspect degrees and local ports, but not n or IDs. Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree Δ, possibly disconnected, every input labeling and every port numbering. A labeling is valid exactly when all neighborhoods satisfy the rules. A deterministic VOLUME computation for a requested vertex v starts with v’s ID, degree, input, ports, Π and the exact |V(G)|, and visited set {v}. It may adaptively choose a visited vertex w and one of its incident ports, learning the neighbor u, its ID, degree, input and incident port names, then add u to the visited set. Arbitrary jumps to unseen IDs are forbidden. Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including v, is charged; local computation must terminate but its time and temporary space are unrestricted. Queries at different vertices run independently with no preprocessing or shared mutable state. Their outputs must jointly form a valid labeling for every input and ID assignment. Each algorithm is one finite computable program for all graph sizes. log* n is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1; the added 1 handles small n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication, or specify one fixed LCL with a sublinear-volume deterministic algorithm and prove it has no O(log* n)-volume deterministic algorithm. Precisely, the latter lower bound means that for every correct B, every C>0 and every n₀, some n≥n₀ satisfies V_B(n)>C(1+log* n). This gap formulation fixes the asymptotic quantifiers without assuming an optimal algorithm or an arbitrary symbolic complexity function exists.
cards.context:
A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.
cards.why: This tests whether deterministic access to local solutions has only a tiny-information regime and an essentially global regime. Either outcome would substantially constrain the design and possible complexity classes of deterministic local computation algorithms.

importance.reason: A proposed collapse of an entire deterministic complexity interval, rather than a bound for one task. It clarifies the power of adaptive exploration and the role of randomness in local computation.

progress.text: Rosenbaum and Suomela introduce the distance-versus-volume framework and pose the deterministic intermediate-volume question as Question 7.1. Their examples establish several randomized intermediate scales while retaining linear deterministic volume.

Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň show that randomized local computation below o(√log n) can be sped up to deterministic O(log* n). Their results also give linear deterministic volume lower bounds for fixed-color tree-coloring tasks in the relevant bounded-degree setting. These do not cover every LCL.
Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt close the gap between constant and iterated-logarithmic VOLUME complexity. The much larger interval above log* n remains the issue here.
Suomela’s updated problem list retains the question of deterministic volume strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear.

Peng gives randomized VOLUME and LCA constructions of complexity Θ(log^k n) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to logarithmic factors. Section 1.1 explicitly leaves the deterministic gap unresolved.

cards.title: Does sublogarithmic randomized volume collapse to deterministic log-star?
cards.formal: For every fixed locally checkable labeling problem Π on all bounded-degree graphs, does a randomized VOLUME algorithm with worst-case volume $o(\log(n+2))$ and global success probability at least 1−1/(n+1) imply a deterministic VOLUME algorithm with volume $O(1+\log^* n)$? The degree bound, checking radius, and finite input/output alphabets are fixed independently of n.
cards.definitions: An LCL is a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhoods with input/output labels, degrees, and local ports, for fixed integers Δ≥2 and r≥1. All finite nonempty simple undirected graphs of maximum degree at most Δ, all input labels, all port orders, and all distinct identifiers from [|V(G)|²] are allowed; disconnected graphs are included. Legality depends on the finite neighborhoods, not on IDs or n. The query algorithm knows exact |V(G)| and starts at the requested vertex with its ID, degree, ports and input. It may follow any port of any visited vertex, revealing the next vertex and its local data; the visited set remains connected. Volume counts distinct visited vertices, including the queried one. Each graph vertex has its own independent infinite sequence of fair random bits, sampled once and used consistently by every query that visits it. A query may read finitely many bits from visited vertices, but has no access to a separate shared random tape. There is no preprocessing or mutable memory shared between queries. With probability at least 1−1/(|V(G)|+1), the answers to all vertex queries together must be a valid labeling. For a fixed algorithm A, V_A(n) is the maximum number of visited vertices over graphs of at most n vertices, all queries and all random tapes. Every computation must terminate; temporary space and local computation time are unrestricted. Both algorithms are uniform finite programs. log* is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every fixed LCL, or give one finite LCL specification with a sublogarithmic-volume randomized solver and prove that every deterministic solver fails every O(log* n) volume bound on arbitrarily large inputs. The known speedup below √log n makes deterministic and randomized O(log* n) equivalent for this purpose, so a counterexample would supply the missing intermediate randomized regime.
cards.context:
A randomized local oracle can decide which parts of a graph to inspect using random choices. Its separate answers still need to fit together into one valid solution. The card samples one random tape per graph vertex and reuses it across queries, so an answer cannot evade an inconsistency by drawing fresh, unrelated randomness each time.

The cost is a worst-case information budget, with failure probability assigned to correctness. Bounding only the expected exploration size would be a different question. Likewise, success at one requested vertex is weaker than saying that all answers are simultaneously correct. These distinctions are significant when small failure probabilities are amplified across an entire graph.

There is already a strong speedup theorem: below √log n, randomized local computation can be replaced by deterministic O(log* n) computation. The conjectured threshold is log n. A candidate at, for example, (log n)^(3/4) would escape the existing theorem while remaining strictly below the proposed threshold.

Logarithmic randomized volume really occurs. The Lovász local lemma and sinkless orientation provide benchmark behavior at that scale in the cited work. The question is whether the whole interval immediately below log n is empty, beyond the familiar tiny-information symmetry-breaking regime.

Peng’s July 2026 constructions provide Θ((log n)^k) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to polylogarithmic factors. Since the smallest exponent k is one, these do not insert a problem into the sublogarithmic interval. Figure 2 of that paper continues to mark the interval from √log n to log n as unknown.
cards.why: A gap theorem would classify every sufficiently small randomized local computation as ordinary deterministic symmetry breaking. A counterexample would reveal a new scale of useful random exploration. This is a general complexity-landscape question, with consequences extending beyond any one coloring or matching algorithm.

importance.reason: An unresolved universal speedup threshold for randomized local computation. It isolates the remaining gap between a proven square-root-logarithmic threshold and the first established logarithmic examples.

progress.text: Rosenbaum and Suomela formalize randomized VOLUME with connected exploration and per-vertex random strings, and construct logarithmic and larger intermediate randomized complexities.

Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň prove the o(√log n) → deterministic O(log* n) speedup in Theorem 1.2. Their Conjecture 1.3 proposes the stronger o(log n) threshold for LCA; the VOLUME question considered here is explicitly tracked by later sources.
Suomela’s list asks whether an LCL can have randomized volume strictly between the log-star and logarithmic regimes.
Peng’s Theorem 1 fills the positive-integer polylogarithmic scales, and Theorem 2 gives rational polynomial exponents. Section 1.1 and Figure 2 retain the unknown interval from √log n to log n.

cards.title: What is the deterministic round complexity of maximum independent set in the congested clique?
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as n grows, the optimal worst-case number $T_{\mathrm{MIS}}(n)$ of synchronous communication rounds needed to output an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex graph in the deterministic unicast congested-clique model below. For every vertex v, its processor must output one bit indicating whether v belongs to the chosen set. Local computation and local storage are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. Here maximum means largest cardinality, not merely inclusion-wise maximal.
cards.definitions: There is one processor for each vertex in {1,...,n}. Initially every processor knows n, all processor identifiers, its own identifier, and exactly the edges incident to its vertex. The communication network is the complete graph regardless of which input edges exist. In each synchronous round, each processor may send a different message of at most $b=\max\{1,\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\}$ bits to each other processor; messages sent in a round become available at its end. Protocols are deterministic and must terminate correctly on every input. An independent set S contains no edge with both endpoints in S; maximum requires |S| >= |I| for every independent set I of the input graph. Define T_MIS(n) as the minimum round bound among protocols for n processors in this model. No polynomial bound is imposed on the computation between rounds. The deterministic and fixed-bandwidth conventions specialize the broader seminar question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give asymptotically matching upper and lower bounds: identify an explicit asymptotic function f(n), construct protocols taking O(f(n)) rounds on every graph, and prove that every correct deterministic protocol requires Omega(f(n)) rounds on some n-vertex graph for all sufficiently large n. Bounds separated by a logarithmic factor or a result only for maximal independent sets do not settle this target.
cards.context:
The graph being optimized and the network carrying messages are different objects. Two vertices that are not adjacent in the input can still communicate directly. This removes distance as an obstacle while retaining a limit on how much information a processor can receive in one round. The task asks how much this distributed information limits exact optimization.

A simple baseline is to collect the entire graph at processor 1. Each other processor sends its n-bit adjacency row along its direct link, in blocks of b bits. These transmissions happen simultaneously and take O(n / log n) rounds for n >= 2. Processor 1 then enumerates subsets locally, chooses a largest independent set, and sends each processor its membership bit. This is an elementary upper bound for the stated model, rather than a claim that centralizing the graph is optimal.

The unlimited local computation is essential to interpreting this baseline. The exponential subset enumeration has no communication cost. Conversely, a faster centralized algorithm does not by itself reduce the number of rounds needed to assemble the input. The question isolates information movement from the ordinary running-time difficulty of exact independent set.

Lower bounds are especially delicate in the unicast clique. Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman relate this model to powerful circuit computations, explaining why familiar sparse-network bottleneck arguments do not transfer directly. Chechik nevertheless identifies exact maximum independent set as a concrete round-complexity question. The catalogue has a separate constant-round question for a maximal independent set; that weaker output requirement must not be substituted here.
cards.why: This places a canonical exact graph optimization problem in a model where computation is free but communication is limited. Understanding its round complexity would help distinguish the benefit of distributing information from merely gathering the graph at one processor.

importance.reason: A canonical exact optimization task testing the communication power of the congested clique. Its relevance extends beyond symmetry breaking, although the chosen deterministic model is one specific frontier.

progress.text: Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman establish circuit-simulation connections and distinguish unicast from broadcast congested cliques. Their work supplies model context, not a tight bound for the present task.
Chechik explicitly asks for the communication rounds necessary to compute a maximum independent set in the congested clique.

cards.title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
cards.formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and k≥1 and one deterministic VOLUME algorithm that computes a maximal matching on every bipartite graph of maximum degree at most Δ, inspecting at most C(Δ+1)^k distinct vertices per queried vertex, independently of the number n of graph vertices? A proper input two-coloring specifying the bipartition is supplied. Answers to all vertex queries must describe the same matching.
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph, arbitrary local port orders, a supplied proper two-coloring, distinct identifiers in [n²], and known integers n and Δ≥1 bounding its size and degrees as stated. A query at v must output either ⊥ for unmatched or the local port of its matching edge. If v names u then u must name v. Every edge must have at least one matched endpoint, which is equivalent to maximality by inclusion. Initially the algorithm sees only v’s identifier, degree, color, ports, n, and Δ. It may adaptively follow a port at any already visited vertex; doing so reveals the neighbor’s identifier, degree, color, and reciprocal port. Count all distinct visited vertices, including v. The explored set is connected: arbitrary jumps to identifiers are forbidden. Each query starts afresh, with no preprocessing or memory retained between queries. Repeating a query must give the same answer regardless of other queries or their order. Local computation and temporary memory are unrestricted but finite, and only the number of distinct visited vertices is charged. One finite deterministic program must work for all n, Δ, graphs, identifiers, and port orders; the constants C,k are universal. There is no additional log n or log* n term in the allowed volume.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the uniform polynomial-in-Δ algorithm with globally consistent matching answers, or prove that every correct deterministic algorithm violates every such polynomial bound on some valid input and query. A randomized bound, expected volume, an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal, or a polynomial bound containing a factor depending on n does not settle this formulation.
cards.context:
A matching is maximal when there is no edge that can be added while keeping its endpoints disjoint from the current matching. It can be much smaller than a maximum matching. The local output is only one port or an unmatched symbol, so the difficulty is the information needed to make this small answer consistent with answers elsewhere.

The supplied bipartition lets the two sides play different roles. A simple distributed procedure has unmatched vertices on one side propose along a new incident edge, while vertices on the other side accept at most one proposal and remain matched thereafter. After O(Δ) rounds this yields a maximal matching. Gathering a whole neighborhood to simulate those rounds can inspect Δ raised to a linear-in-Δ power many vertices.

Volume asks whether that exploration can be made much narrower. A vertex may follow a few carefully chosen dependencies far into the graph, instead of collecting every branch of a large ball. But it cannot simply choose a convenient partner in isolation: when that partner is queried separately, the answers must agree. The lack of shared mutable query state makes this coordination part of the algorithm itself.

The independence from n is essential. For each fixed Δ, even an enormous function such as Δ^(2Δ) is constant as n grows. This question compares those constants uniformly as Δ grows, asking for a single polynomial. It is therefore different from obtaining logarithmic dependence on n for fixed degree or from studying only a single fixed-degree LCL.

Known round lower bounds force at least linear dependence on Δ when n is sufficiently large. They leave a large interval between that obstruction and full-neighborhood simulation. Suomela conjectures an exponential degree dependence for volume, so even deciding whether a polynomial is possible would determine which side of that major gap is achievable.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether a fast distributed symmetry-breaking algorithm can be evaluated locally without exploring an exponentially branching dependency structure. A polynomial bound would give a small deterministic oracle for a fundamental graph primitive; a superpolynomial lower bound would expose an information cost that round complexity alone does not capture.

importance.reason: A fundamental maximal-matching oracle question that isolates degree dependence and the difference between distance and volume. It asks for a qualitative polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification with no network-size term.

progress.text: Brandt and Olivetti sharpen the degree dependence of bipartite maximal matching in LOCAL. In the identifier model, the deterministic Ω(min{Δ,log n/log log n}) lower bound gives an Ω(Δ) obstruction to any degree-only volume bound by choosing sufficiently large n.

Rosenbaum and Suomela formalize connected adaptive exploration and explain why an f-round LOCAL algorithm gives a Δ^O(f)-volume algorithm. Combining this with the bipartite O(Δ)-round procedure gives the baseline Δ^O(Δ) volume.
Suomela explicitly asks whether bipartite maximal matching admits polynomial volume in Δ, and conjectures 2^Θ(Δ) as the correct dependence. The conjecture is not a proved lower bound.

cards.title: Can bipartite 3-coloring be maintained with logarithmic recoloring radius?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm and a universal constant C such that, for every n and every adversarial sequence of edge insertions into an initially edgeless graph on [n], with every intermediate graph bipartite, the algorithm maintains a proper coloring with colors {1,2,3} while changing colors only within distance C log₂(n+2) of an endpoint of the newly inserted edge? Distance is measured in the graph immediately after that insertion. The algorithm sees the entire current graph and may retain arbitrary state, but has no knowledge of future insertions.
cards.definitions: The vertex set [n] and n are supplied initially. The graphs are finite, simple and undirected, and maximum degree is unrestricted. An insertion adds one previously absent edge {u,v}; no edge deletions or supplied bipartition are included. The adversary may select its next insertion after inspecting the algorithm’s previous colors. Before any insertion the algorithm chooses a color for each isolated vertex. After update i it must output c_i:[n]→{1,2,3} with c_i(x)≠c_i(y) for every edge {x,y} of G_i. If min(dist_G_i(w,u),dist_G_i(w,v))>⌈C log₂(n+2)⌉, then c_i(w)=c_{i−1}(w); vertices in other components have infinite distance. All colors must be valid after every update. One computable program works for all n and terminates on every update. Global reading, computation time, memory and the number of recolorings inside the permitted neighborhood are unrestricted. The resource being bounded is the worst-case spatial radius of changed output, not amortized update time or communication rounds. This fixes the incremental edge-update convention of dynamic-LOCAL.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm with a proof valid for every bipartite insertion sequence, or prove that no deterministic algorithm has an O(log n) worst-case recoloring radius. A bound only for trees, only on the number of recolored vertices, or for a model with advance access to future edges does not settle this formulation.
cards.context:
Every intermediate graph has a two-coloring, but a maintained coloring commits to choices before future edges are known. Two separately colored components may later be joined with incompatible parities. With only two colors, repairing that conflict can force a change across a large component. A third color offers additional ways to create a local transition between regions.

The question measures where a repair spreads. It does not limit how much of the graph the algorithm may inspect to decide on that repair. In particular, an algorithm could perform expensive global computation and still have small dynamic locality if only nearby output labels change. Conversely, a fast data structure could recolor a distant vertex and violate the radius bound.

The online-LOCAL model has a different source of power: when a vertex must be colored, a neighborhood in the eventual input graph is revealed. The ICALP 2023 algorithm uses logarithmic visibility to 3-color bipartite graphs. That result is a useful benchmark, but does not provide a logarithmic repair radius when edges themselves arrive without such advance visibility.

The later logarithmic lower bound for online-LOCAL already holds on grids and transfers to the weaker dynamic-LOCAL setting. Therefore an affirmative answer here would attain the correct asymptotic order. It remains possible that repairing a sequence of past commitments requires a substantially larger radius than choosing a color with a view into the eventual graph.

The corrected February 2026 comparison paper still lists a logarithmic lower bound and a roughly square-root upper bound for dynamic-LOCAL bipartite 3-coloring. It also withdraws an earlier general claim about derandomizing LOCAL in dynamic-LOCAL. The card uses the corrected version when describing the relationship between the models.
cards.why: Bipartite 3-coloring is a simple test of whether global information and local repairs can match the power of online lookaround. A tight answer would clarify a basic separation between dynamic and online computation without hiding the issue in expensive local processing.

importance.reason: A canonical coloring task that tests the power of maintaining solutions under local changes. The logarithmic target matches a known lower bound, and its resolution would clarify the relationship between two general locality models.

progress.text: Akbari and coauthors define incremental dynamic-LOCAL and give an O(log n)-locality online-LOCAL algorithm for 3-coloring bipartite graphs. The online algorithm is not a dynamic repair algorithm.

Chang, Mishra, Nguyen, Yang, and Yeh establish an Ω(log n) deterministic online-LOCAL lower bound even for grids. Together with the model simulation, this supplies the same lower bound for dynamic-LOCAL.

The corrected v4 of Online Locality Meets Distributed Quantum Computing retains Õ(√n) versus Ω(log n) in the dynamic-LOCAL entry of Table 1. Its corrections section withdraws a claimed general dynamic derandomization theorem from earlier versions.
Suomela’s updated open-problem page explicitly asks whether dynamic-LOCAL can 3-color bipartite graphs with O(log n) locality.

cards.status_note: The February 2026 primary problem list retains the logarithmic-radius question, consistently with the corrected v4 comparison table. No later resolution located through 10 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Every intermediate graph has a two-coloring, but a maintained coloring commits to choices before future edges are known. Two separately colored components may later be joined with incompatible parities. With only two colors, repairing that conflict can force a change across a large component. A third color offers additional ways to create a local transition between regions.

The question measures where a repair spreads. It does not limit how much of the graph the algorithm may inspect to decide on that repair. In particular, an algorithm could perform expensive global computation and still have small dynamic locality if only nearby output labels change. Conversely, a fast data structure could recolor a distant vertex and violate the radius bound.

The online-LOCAL model has a different source of power: when a vertex must be colored, a neighborhood in the eventual input graph is revealed. The ICALP 2023 algorithm uses logarithmic visibility to 3-color bipartite graphs. That result is a useful benchmark, but does not provide a logarithmic repair radius when edges themselves arrive without such advance visibility.

The later logarithmic lower bound for online-LOCAL already holds on grids and transfers to the weaker dynamic-LOCAL setting. Therefore an affirmative answer here would attain the correct asymptotic order. It remains possible that repairing a sequence of past commitments requires a substantially larger radius than choosing a color with a view into the eventual graph.

The corrected February 2026 comparison paper still lists a logarithmic lower bound and a roughly square-root upper bound for dynamic-LOCAL bipartite 3-coloring. It also withdraws an earlier general claim about derandomizing LOCAL in dynamic-LOCAL. The card uses the corrected version when describing the relationship between the models.

cards.title: Bipartite Exact Matching: deterministic polynomial time
cards.formal: Given a bipartite graph $G=(L\cup R,E)$ with $|L|=|R|=n$, a red/blue coloring of its edges, and $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, decide whether $G$ has a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The historical question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the ordinary bit encoding of $(G,k)$. An April 2026 preprint claims such an algorithm. This entry records that claimed resolution and its verification limits; it is no longer labeled as a confirmed open problem.
cards.context:
An ordinary perfect matching assigns every left vertex to a different right vertex. Here an additional equality constraint counts how many selected edges are red. Minimizing or maximizing the red-edge count does not decide whether a particular intermediate count is attainable.

Consider two left vertices and two right vertices, with every possible edge present. Color the two diagonal edges red and the two off-diagonal edges blue. The only perfect matchings have either two red edges or none. There is no perfect matching with exactly one red edge, although one lies between the minimum and maximum attainable counts. Even this small example defeats an interval-based feasibility test.

The randomized algebraic approach encodes matchings in a polynomial and tests whether a relevant coefficient vanishes. Finding a deterministic replacement has made the problem a particularly concrete meeting point of graph algorithms and polynomial identity testing. Approximation results relax the equality constraint and therefore answer a different question.

Du’s April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for every bipartite graph. Version 3 describes its Lean formalization as reducing the main theorem to eight explicit hypotheses, rather than independently checking all ingredients. The paper states that these hypotheses correspond to mathematical results proved there or in prior work. That qualification matters when assessing the original version’s stronger formal-verification wording.
cards.why: I retain and expand this entry because exact cardinality constraints can remain difficult even when unconstrained optimization is easy. It is also a useful status correction: a research catalogue should preserve the problem and the claimed advance, while distinguishing an attributed preprint theorem from a proof that has been independently checked.
cards.definitions: A perfect matching consists of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex. Exactly k is an equality constraint, not an upper bound or an approximation target. This card concerns sequential deterministic polynomial time. Ordinary bipartite perfect matching in NC and Exact Matching on general graphs are separate questions.

progress.text: El Maalouly’s survey develops algorithms and reductions around Exact Matching while describing deterministic polynomial time as unresolved.
Du’s first preprint version claims a deterministic $O(n^6)$ algorithm for all bipartite graphs and describes its proof as formally verified.

Version 3 states $O(n^6)$ arithmetic complexity and qualifies the Lean result: the main theorem is reduced to eight explicit hypotheses. The claimed mathematical resolution and the formalization scope must be assessed separately.

cards.title: Do splay trees support deque operations in constant amortized time?
cards.formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing $n$ ordered keys, and perform $m$ legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always $O(n+m)$, with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
cards.context:
A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.
cards.why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.
cards.definitions: Splaying uses the standard zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rules. Deletions are allowed only on a nonempty tree, and an inserted key must be outside the current key range at the specified end. Amortized cost is a bound on the total sequence, not a worst-case guarantee for each deletion. The initial tree may have any shape.

progress.text: Pettie proves $O((n+m)\alpha^*(n+m))$ total cost, where $\alpha^*$ counts how many iterations of the inverse-Ackermann function reduce the argument to a constant.
Levy and Tarjan connect the deque conjecture to a subsequence property sufficient for dynamic optimality. This provides a structural route to a proof, not the required linear bound itself.
The new analysis of splay competitiveness still describes the deque guarantee as nearly constant per operation. Its general search bound does not supply constant amortized deque cost.

cards.title: How many rounds does triangle detection require in CONGEST?
cards.formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct O(log n)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate O(log n)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. On a triangle-free graph all vertices must output NO; otherwise at least one must output YES. The joint answer must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input and identifier assignment. The algorithm is uniform, has private random bits, and may know n. The currently established bounds are $\Omega(\log\log n)$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$.
cards.context:
Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. Consequently, a lower bound driven by the volume of listed output does not automatically apply to detection. The near-optimal listing algorithm supplies a detection upper bound, but leaves this distinction unresolved.

The 2025 lower bound rules out every fixed number of rounds, including randomized protocols. It changes the old question of whether even two rounds are necessary into a quantitative gap. Conventional two-party communication reductions encounter barriers here, making stronger lower bounds a problem about proof techniques as well as about graph algorithms.
cards.why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
cards.definitions: $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. Local computation is unrestricted, vertex identifiers have $O(\log n)$ bits, and the communication graph is exactly $G$, not an all-to-all overlay. Nodes may know $n$. The output convention avoids charging the graph diameter merely to inform every vertex of a remote triangle. The triangle is a subgraph on three distinct mutually adjacent vertices.

progress.text: Chang, Pettie, Saranurak, and Zhang give $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$-round algorithms for triangle enumeration, counting, and detection. The matching enumeration lower bound does not establish the same detection lower bound.
Assadi and Sundaresan prove an $\Omega(\log\log n)$ lower bound for deterministic and randomized detection, providing the first lower bound beyond a single round.
Censor-Hillel’s ADGA survey explicitly retains the round complexity of CONGEST triangle detection as an open problem after incorporating that lower bound.

cards.title: Can pointer-machine working-set heaps have constant amortized insertion and decrease-key?
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic online priority queue in the pointer-machine model below and an absolute constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations, starting from an empty queue, has total cost at most $C(M+\sum_{x\ \mathrm{extracted}}\log \Gamma(x))$? The operations are insert, find-min, decrease-key, and extract-min. For an extracted item x, define $\Gamma(x)=1+$ the number of insertions strictly after x was inserted and before it was extracted, including inserted items that have already been removed. An insertion creates a distinct item and returns its handle; decrease-key receives that handle and its new key. Require exact answers for all sequences; melding is not required.
cards.definitions: Keys are opaque values in a totally ordered set and can only be compared; ties are broken by a fixed order on item identities. Find-min returns the minimum live item; extract-min also removes it. Decrease-key changes the key of an existing item to a no-larger value and does not reset its insertion time. A pointer machine has records containing O(1) pointers and O(1) auxiliary bits, together with the supplied key records. A fixed program operates through O(1) pointer registers. Charge one step for a key comparison, a pointer traversal or change, a constant-bit operation, or allocation of one constant-size record. It cannot perform address arithmetic or unit-cost operations on an unbounded auxiliary integer; larger counters must be explicitly represented and manipulated. All work between requests is charged. Amortization is over every finite sequence, including sequences leaving items in the queue.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct one queue meeting the displayed total-cost bound for every sequence, or prove that every queue in this model has sequences with an unbounded ratio between its cost and that budget. Constant decrease-key with a growing insertion cost does not establish the positive answer. Neither does a word-RAM implementation using operations absent from the stated model.
cards.context:
The usual priority-queue guarantee charges for extraction according to the number of stored items. A working-set guarantee instead takes account of how recently the extracted item entered the queue. For example, keep a large collection of expensive items present, repeatedly insert one smaller item, and immediately extract it. Each of these recent items has Gamma equal to one, so the proposed budget charges only a constant per such pair of requests. This illustrates the adaptive behavior that the question asks the implementation to exploit.

Fast decreases matter independently of these insertion times. A graph algorithm can discover a better tentative distance for an item that has been waiting for a long time. The interface gives the algorithm a handle to that item, but the queue still has to update the organization used to find its next minimum. Efficient extraction alone therefore does not settle the requested operation sequence bound.

The pointer restriction isolates the contribution of machine operations to this adaptivity. The July 2026 revision of van der Hoog and coauthors gives constant amortized insertion and working-set extraction, with inverse-Ackermann amortized decrease-key. That remaining factor is very slowly growing, but is asymptotically different from a constant.

A separate July 2026 construction achieves constant decrease-key with a stronger, stack-like extraction guarantee, while charging an iterated-log-star overhead to insertion. Its different trade-off is useful progress, but the joint constant-update target here still requires another argument. This card fixes the insertion-count definition of the working set and expresses the amortized question as a single total-cost inequality.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether temporal adaptivity and cheap priority changes can coexist without word-level machine tricks. A solution would clarify a model distinction in a fundamental graph-algorithm primitive. The small remaining factor makes it a sharper structural question than simply asking for a faster heap.

importance.reason: A concrete model-power gap for adaptive priority queues, with consequences for shortest-path methods that rely on both locality and cheap priority changes. It is more focused than general dynamic optimality.

progress.text: Iacono states the pointer-model working-set/decrease-key problem at the Adaptive and Scalable Data Structures seminar.

The revised pointer-machine construction achieves O(1) amortized insertion, O(alpha(n)) amortized decrease-key, and O(1 + log Gamma(x)) worst-case extraction. Its introduction explicitly leaves removal of the inverse-Ackermann overhead open.

Haeupler, Hladík, Rozhoň, and Tarjan obtain constant amortized decrease-key and stack-like extraction, with insertion bounded by any fixed iteration of log-star. This is not a constant insertion bound.

cards.title: Strong quantum IOPs with polynomial communication
cards.formal: Does every QMA promise problem admit a constant-round strong quantum interactive oracle proof with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, total prover-message length polynomial in the input length n, total query complexity O(1), completeness at least 2/3, and soundness at most 1/3? The strong access model is defined below. The prover may be computationally unbounded, and soundness quantifies over all prover strategies.
cards.context:
A quantum proof can be much larger than the portion a verifier actually inspects. An interactive oracle proof lets a prover supply such messages over several rounds, with the verifier charged for the qubits it touches. Communication volume and access complexity are therefore different resources.

The strong model requires the verifier to hand each received quantum message back in full and forbids sending an additional quantum message of its own. It still has private workspace. Returning a message does not mean undoing the measurement or channel applied to the queried qubits; the resulting state can be returned.

For example, a protocol might inspect only two qubits from an enormous register. That has constant query complexity but still transmits the enormous register.
