cards.title: Can a congested clique find a maximal independent set in constant rounds?
cards.formal: Is there a randomized algorithm that, on every n-vertex simple input graph, finds a maximal independent set in O(1) rounds in the Congested Clique model, with success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for every requested fixed $c>0$? Processor v initially knows its identifier and incident input edges. Every ordered pair of processors may exchange an O(log n)-bit message per synchronous round, whether or not the input edge exists. Each processor outputs whether it belongs to an independent set that dominates every vertex outside it. The algorithm must be uniform across inputs; it cannot be chosen after seeing the graph.
cards.context:
This changes the communication network while leaving the graph problem unchanged. A vertex can contact a distant processor immediately, so graph distance no longer limits the spread of information. Bandwidth still matters: one processor can receive only $O(n\log n)$ bits per round, whereas a general graph can contain $\Theta(n^2)$ independently specified edges. Sending the entire input to one leader is therefore not a constant-round solution.

That bottleneck is not itself a lower bound for MIS. A complete graph has many edges but is easy: a designated vertex can join the independent set and all others can stay out. The sought algorithm only needs enough information to coordinate a valid answer; it need not reconstruct every edge in one place.

Known algorithms exploit this by solving suitably sparse sampled subgraphs and reducing the remaining degrees. The general upper bound is $O(\log\log\Delta)$ rounds. The central question is whether a bounded number of communication phases can remove the need for repeated sparsification.

A closely related relaxation is already possible in constant rounds: a 2-ruling set remains independent but only has to put every vertex within distance two of a selected vertex. MIS requires distance one. This supplies a precise nearby success case against which to assess the unresolved target.
cards.why: I include this beside the LOCAL MIS problem because it tests a different limitation of distributed computation: restricted bandwidth despite universal communication. A constant-round algorithm would show that exact local domination needs only a bounded number of global exchanges. A lower bound would have to explain why distributed processing cannot avoid the bottleneck.
cards.definitions: Here $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of the input graph, not of the communication network. Messages to different recipients may differ. Local computation is unrestricted. $O(1)$ means independent of both $n$ and $\Delta$, with constants allowed to depend on the requested failure exponent. This is the unicast Congested Clique, rather than the weaker broadcast variant.

progress.text: Ghaffari, Gouleakis, Konrad, Mitrović, and Rubinfeld obtain the $O(\log\log\Delta)$-round MIS bound using sparsification.
Cambus, Kuhn, Pai, and Uitto obtain constant rounds for the 2-ruling-set relaxation.

Censor-Hillel, Even, Flin, and Halldórsson obtain constant rounds, for example, when average degree is at most $2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$. They also identify graph families on which existing sparsification methods require $\Omega(\log\log n)$ iterations. That restriction applies to those methods, not to all Congested Clique algorithms.

cards.title: Does splaying every BST preorder take linear total time?
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant C such that, for every n and every two binary search trees A and B on the same n distinct ordered keys, searching for the keys of preorder(B), in order, using bottom-up splaying starting from A costs at most Cn? Define preorder recursively as root, then left-subtree preorder, then right-subtree preorder. Every key is searched once. Charge one unit per visited search-path node and one per single rotation; perform no insertions or deletions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a universal linear bound for all pairs (A,B), or show that the ratio of this cost to n is unbounded over a family of such pairs. A bound requiring the traversal tree B to be balanced does not settle the proposition.
cards.definitions: A binary search tree stores one key per node, all left descendants smaller and all right descendants larger. On a search for x, first follow comparisons from the root to x. Then repeatedly splay x: if its parent is the root, rotate x over its parent (zig); if x and its parent are both left children or both right children, rotate the parent over the grandparent and then x over the parent (zig-zig); otherwise rotate x over its parent and then over its former grandparent (zig-zag). The same node x remains the splayed node until it becomes root. The arbitrary starting tree A and the tree B defining the permutation are separate inputs to the mathematical claim; splay receives only the search requests.
cards.context:
This asks about a particularly structured access sequence, rather than every possible sequence in the dynamic-optimality conjecture. A traversal visits each key exactly once, but its order reflects a second tree that may be quite different from the tree currently being searched. The proposed linear total bound says that this hidden structure is enough for splaying to adapt efficiently.

For example, the preorder of a balanced tree on seven keys can be 4, 2, 1, 3, 6, 5, 7. This is not a sorted scan: after finishing one subtree, the sequence can jump to a distant part of the key order. If the starting tree is a long chain, even the first requested key can be far from the root. The question concerns the total cost, so a single expensive access is harmless if later savings pay for it.

The distinction between access and insertion matters. Building a tree by inserting the preorder keys into an empty splay tree is a different operation sequence, and that version is known to be linear. Linear access bounds are also known when the tree defining the preorder is weight-balanced. Neither restriction covers all traversal trees.

This is a useful intermediate target because the input family is precise and recognizable. A proof can exploit the recursive order of the permutation; a counterexample would have to show that this order still permits repeated expensive restructuring.
cards.why: I include this as a concrete test of whether a local restructuring rule detects global order in requests without being told that order. It isolates a major obstacle in understanding adaptive search trees while avoiding the full freedom of arbitrary repeated-access sequences.

progress.text: The traversal conjecture originates in the introduction of splay trees, as recorded in the later primary studies.
Levy and Tarjan prove linear-time preorder and postorder insertion into an empty tree, and linear access when the traversal tree is weight-balanced.
The new splay competitive analysis still records traversal optimality only in special settings. Its competitive factor is not constant.

cards.title: Does the specified weighted temporal logic express every weighted FO sentence over natural numbers?
cards.formal: For every finite alphabet Sigma and every closed weighted first-order expression E in the fragment defined below, with weights in the semiring (N,+,times,0,1), does there exist a weighted temporal expression H in the specified grammar such that E(w)=H(w,1) for every nonempty finite word w over Sigma? The weighted temporal grammar is $H ::= 0\mid Ls\mid\langle s\rangle H\mid s\,U_w\,H\mid H+H\mid\operatorname{if}(\varphi,H,H)$, where s is a finite conditional expression returning a natural-number constant and phi is an ordinary Boolean LTL formula with both future and past. Its exact semantics and the source weighted-FO grammar are given in Model & notation. No additional weighted operator may be introduced. This fixes the natural-number instance of the weighted Kamp question discussed in Gastin’s December 2025 slides.
cards.definitions:
Words w have positions 1,...,N, with N=|w|>=1. Boolean FO formulas theta use letter predicates a(x), equality, order, Boolean connectives, and quantification over positions. A step-FO expression s_F is a natural constant r or if(theta,s_F,s_F). Weighted FO expressions have grammar E ::= 0 | product_x s_F | sum_x E | E+E | if(theta,E,E). A sum or product ranges over every word position and binds x; conditionals select the indicated branch according to ordinary Boolean truth. Products are permitted only over step expressions, not arbitrary weighted expressions. E is closed when all position variables are bound.

Boolean LTL guards phi use true, letter tests, negation, disjunction, strong next X, strong previous Y, until U, and since S. X phi is false at the last position and Y phi false at the first. At i, phi U psi holds if some k>=i satisfies psi and every j with i<=j<k satisfies phi; since is the reverse-time counterpart. Guards are evaluated on the entire word, at the indicated position. A step-temporal expression s is a natural constant or if(phi,s,s).

Write s(w,i) for its value. The weighted semantics is: 0 has value zero; addition is pointwise ordinary addition; conditionals select one branch. (Ls)(w,i)=s(w,i) if i=N and zero otherwise. (<s>H)(w,i)=s(w,i) H(w,i+1) if i<N and zero otherwise. Finally, $(s\,U_w\,H)(w,i)=\sum_{k=i}^{N}(\prod_{j=i}^{k-1}s(w,j))H(w,k)$, with empty product one. This U_w is a numerical summation operator, distinct from Boolean until inside a guard. A temporal expression denotes the function w -> H(w,1). Arbitrary multiplication of weighted expressions and weighted past operators are absent from the grammar. All expressions are finite, with any fixed natural constants allowed; equality is exact on every word, not approximation or equality only of nonzero supports.
cards.answer_criterion: Translate every closed expression of the specified weighted FO fragment into the specified weighted temporal grammar, or give an expression E and prove that no temporal expression in that grammar agrees with it on all nonempty finite words. It is enough for a negative answer to use one finite alphabet. Changing the semiring or adding a new weighted operator does not answer this fixed question. Agreement only on the underlying Boolean language is insufficient.
cards.context:
Classical first-order logic and temporal logic can describe the same finite-word languages despite using different means of referring to positions. Weighted expressions ask for an exact number associated with a word. A position quantifier can now add contributions from many witnesses, rather than merely asserting that a witness exists. The question is whether a temporal expression can reproduce those totals without explicit position variables.

The source FO fragment deliberately restricts products to step expressions. Permitting products of arbitrary weighted sums would define a stronger language and change the question. Similarly, weighted until has a step expression on the left: it accumulates products along an interval and adds the possible endpoint contributions. These restrictions are part of the mathematical target, not choices left to a proposed translation.

For intuition, a weighted FO sentence can count occurrences of factors belonging to a chosen FO-definable language L. It sums one over pairs x<=y whenever the substring between those positions belongs to L. A temporal formulation must reproduce the same multiplicity, including overlapping occurrences. Ordinary Boolean temporal tests can decide many properties of prefixes and suffixes, but that alone does not give a way to sum over two independently chosen endpoints.

The February 2025 seminar leaves the appropriate weighted LTL formulation unspecified. Gastin’s later slides give an explicit grammar and semantics, establish equivalences in unambiguous and finite-ambiguity fragments, and mark the full weighted-FO/weighted-LTL equivalence with a question mark. This card uses that later formulation and fixes the natural-number semiring. Thus an answer concerns a particular expressive-power claim, rather than whether some future language definition would be considered adequate.
cards.why: This asks whether the classical equivalence between variable-based and temporal descriptions survives exact quantitative aggregation. It could identify a basic limit of temporal specification languages and clarify which operations are needed to describe the counts and weights recognized by aperiodic automata.

importance.reason: A quantitative analogue of a central expressiveness theorem, connecting finite-word logic with aperiodic weighted automata. The fixed natural-number setting makes the question concrete while retaining the difficulty of counting multiple witnesses.

progress.text: Droste and Gastin characterize the relevant weighted FO fragment using aperiodic polynomially ambiguous weighted automata, with finer correspondences when first-order and binary sums are removed.
The Dagstuhl problem discusses extending the classical star-free, aperiodic, FO, and LTL equivalences to weighted languages; the temporal-language definition is still part of its research direction.

Gastin gives explicit weighted LTL syntax and semantics. Slides 25–28 establish restricted-fragment equivalences and leave the full weighted FO versus weighted LTL correspondence open; slide 30 highlights counting factors as a test example.

cards.title: Can deterministic (Delta+1)-coloring beat square-root dependence on degree?
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that properly colors every simple n-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$ with colors in $\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}$ in $O(\Delta^{0.499}+\log^* n)$ synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers and know n and Delta. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The constant in the round bound must be independent of both n and Delta.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm with the specified uniform round bound, or prove that no deterministic LOCAL algorithm attains it. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent one-half does not meet the target.
cards.context:
A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

The target chooses a specific exponent strictly below one-half, as in Suomela’s list. The numerical improvement is small; its purpose is to cross the apparent degree barrier while keeping the optimal-size palette. Allowing more colors, randomness, or a larger n-dependent term gives separate questions.
cards.why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
cards.definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target.

progress.text: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette.
Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence.

The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.

cards.title: Two anticomplete paths with unrestricted terminal pairing
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple undirected graph G and four distinct pairwise nonadjacent vertices a,b,c,d, decides whether G contains two vertex-disjoint paths with no edge between their vertex sets, whose four endpoints are exactly a,b,c,d? Any of the three pairings of the four terminals is accepted.
cards.definitions: The input is an n×n adjacency matrix together with four vertex indices. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with an edge between each consecutive pair. The two paths must have disjoint vertex sets P and Q and satisfy E(G)∩(P×Q)=∅. Each terminal is the endpoint of exactly one path; none is an internal vertex. The accepted endpoint pairings are {ab,cd}, {ac,bd}, and {ad,bc}, with no prescribed source/sink partition. Paths can equivalently be required to be induced: replace either path by a shortest path between its endpoints in its own vertex set. This does not create an edge to the other path. Polynomial time means that one uniform deterministic Turing machine answers correctly on every valid input in at most C(n+1)^k steps for fixed constants C,k. Invalid encodings or nonindependent terminal sets are rejected by this formulation. There are no restrictions on the degree, genus, or connectivity of G.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such a polynomial-time algorithm with a proof, or prove that none exists. An NP-hardness proof for this exact unrestricted-pairing language would establish a negative answer under P≠NP, and must be labelled conditional accordingly. Hardness for a single prescribed pairing or for a prescribed source/sink partition is insufficient.
cards.context:
Ordinary disjoint routing prevents the paths from sharing vertices. Here even an unused graph edge between the two routes is forbidden. Thus one path must avoid the entire neighborhood of the other, and deciding which vertices to reserve can constrain a distant part of the graph.

The freedom to choose partners is the point of the question. Four terminals have three perfect pairings. A graph is accepted if at least one pairing works. A hard instance for a prescribed pairing may have an easy solution using another pairing; therefore simply invoking the hardness of any individual pairing does not classify their union.

The stable-terminal restriction isolates the unresolved case in Trotignon’s question. To see why an edge between two terminals helps, its endpoints would have to lie on the same solution path. That path can be shortened to the edge itself, leaving a reachability test for the remaining two terminals after deleting the closed neighborhoods of the first pair. Testing terminal edges handles these nonindependent cases.

This is a small routing primitive relevant to detecting induced minors, where a model must preserve both adjacency and nonadjacency between its connected pieces. An algorithm would allow a search to postpone the choice of which terminal belongs with which other terminal. A hardness proof would show that this flexibility still cannot overcome the anticompleteness constraint.

There are useful tractable restrictions. For graphs of any fixed bounded genus, polynomial algorithms for prescribed induced paths also solve this question by trying the three pairings. Conversely, the 2025 hardness theorem even for string graphs concerns prescribed pairs or a source/sink partition. The latter permits only two of our three pairings.
cards.why: This isolates a basic difference between specifying two routes and merely asking for two separated connections among four terminals. It is a compact test of how much freedom in terminal assignment can change the complexity of induced graph structure detection.

importance.reason: A concrete four-terminal primitive at the boundary of tractable routing and induced-containment hardness. Its importance comes from a missing basic complexity classification and its role in induced-minor detection, rather than from a large parameter range.

progress.text: The problem is in NP: the two vertex sequences form a certificate of length O(n log n), and adjacency, disjointness, terminal coverage, and absence of cross edges can all be checked in polynomial time. This is an immediate consequence of the stated definition, not a polynomial-time decision algorithm.

Trotignon explicitly asks for the complexity of the four-terminal problem with no prescribed pairing in Section 4.5 of the Dagstuhl report, printed page 140. The card makes its polynomial-time membership question explicit.

Aboulker, Bonnet, Picavet, and Trotignon prove NP-completeness for induced two-path routing even in a restricted class of string graphs. Their stronger flow theorem fixes two source terminals and two sink terminals. It does not automatically classify the language accepting all three perfect pairings.

The exact unrestricted-pairing question remains supported by its 2019 open-problem source. The checked recent theorem concerns different terminal constraints; no subsequent primary-source resolution of this exact question was located.

cards.title: Does recursively splitting a splay tree always take linear total time?
cards.formal: Start with an arbitrary n-node binary search tree. A split operation receives a current component tree and a key x in it, searches for x, splays x to that component’s root, and deletes x, leaving its left and right subtrees as separate components. Is the total cost of every legal sequence of n splits O(n)? Count all searches, rotations, and constant-time component bookkeeping. The input to each operation supplies the component’s root handle; identifying which component contains x is not a separate search problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove one universal linear bound for every initial tree and legal split order, or prove that total cost divided by n is unbounded over such inputs. A bound with any unbounded multiplicative factor is partial progress.
cards.context:
Ordinary search adjusts one tree and keeps all its keys available. A split removes its accessed key and permanently separates the keys on its two sides. Subsequent operations happen independently in the resulting components. Every original key is accessed as a pivot exactly once, but it can participate in rotations caused by earlier pivots.

For example, splitting at the median key first separates the two halves of the key order. Continuing recursively with medians gives a balanced pattern of subproblems. Another legal sequence repeatedly chooses an extreme key and leaves almost the entire tree in one component. The conjecture must cover both, including mixtures chosen from different components.

There are only n requested pivots, which explains the linear target, but not a linear upper bound for the actual implementation. A key may lie deep in the current tree. The proof must show that restructuring work can be charged globally without repeatedly charging the same surviving material too much.

This differs from the deque conjecture: a deque deletes only an extreme, whereas a split may select any internal rank and produce two nonempty trees. The July 2026 analysis gives a new nearly linear bound for this splitting process, making the remaining multiplicative gap explicit.
cards.why: I include this because recursive partitioning is a basic way to organize ordered data. The conjecture asks whether splaying pays only for the number of objects eventually removed, regardless of the partition order. It is a sharply delimited test of the amortization techniques used for adaptive search trees.
cards.definitions: Keys have a fixed total order and are compared rather than arithmetically manipulated. Splaying uses zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations. Each key is removed exactly once; no insertions occur. The sequence can choose any currently nonempty component. The bound is a worst-case bound on total cost over complete sequences, not a per-split worst-case bound.

progress.text: Pettie records Lucas’s split conjecture and distinguishes it from traversal and deque workloads. Even the deletion-only extreme-key case captures a restricted form of the deque question.
Chmel and coauthors prove total split cost $O(n\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)$ in Appendix D. The O(n) bound remains the target.

cards.title: Is 3-colorability polynomial-time decidable on diameter-two graphs?
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every finite simple connected undirected graph G of diameter at most 2, decides whether there is a map c:V(G)→{1,2,3} such that c(u)≠c(v) for every edge uv?
cards.definitions: The input is the adjacency matrix of an n-vertex graph. Distance counts edges in a shortest path, and diameter is the maximum distance between any two vertices. The graph has no loops or parallel edges. For a singleton the diameter is 0. The algorithm must correctly decide existence of a coloring, including on graphs that are not 3-colorable; it is not supplied with a coloring or a promise of 3-colorability. The color set has fixed size three and there are no vertex lists, precolored vertices, degree bounds, or forbidden-subgraph assumptions. A polynomial-time algorithm has worst-case running time C(n+1)^k for constants C,k independent of G. One may equivalently define a total language that rejects disconnected or diameter-greater-than-two graphs, since the diameter promise can be checked in polynomial time. Restricting to diameter exactly two gives the same polynomial-time question: diameter-zero and diameter-one connected graphs are complete and their colorability is immediate.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that such an algorithm exists, or that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-completeness proof would establish the conventional hardness classification and imply a negative answer under P≠NP. A subexponential algorithm or an algorithm requiring an additional graph restriction does not settle this question.
cards.context:
The 2019 source discusses several diameter-restricted coloring problems. This card selects its central explicit question, with three colors and diameter two. The same section also asks about triangle-free inputs and about coloring claw-free graphs with an input-dependent number of colors; these are distinct extensions, not additional requirements hidden in this question.

Bounding diameter means every pair of vertices is close, but it does not bound the amount of global information encoded by the graph. Diameter-one graphs are complete and trivial to color. Mertzios and Spirakis show that 3-colorability is already NP-complete at diameter three, even for triangle-free graphs. Diameter two is the remaining boundary between these neighboring cases.

A tempting hardness reduction adds a universal vertex to an arbitrary graph. This makes the diameter at most two, but the new vertex consumes a color that none of the old vertices can use. It transfers general 3-colorability to 4-colorability, so it does not prove hardness of the fixed three-color target. Conversely, when a diameter-two instance already has a universal vertex, its 3-colorability reduces to checking that the remaining graph is bipartite.

The best general upper bound identified in the July 2026 source is subexponential: Dębski, Piecyk, and Rzążewski give time 2 raised to O(n^(1/3) log² n). Their algorithm combines branching, reductions to 2-SAT, and a structural observation proved probabilistically. The remaining gap is between this bound and polynomial time; the existence of a subexponential algorithm does not exclude NP-completeness.

Murakami’s July 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time list 3-coloring when the diameter-two graph contains no four-cycle even as a non-induced subgraph. Its discussion explicitly leaves the general diameter-two case open. The distinction matters: forbidding every four-cycle is stronger than forbidding only induced four-cycles, and neither condition is imposed here.
cards.why: Three-colorability is a basic constraint-satisfaction problem, and diameter is one of the simplest measures of graph connectivity. This single unresolved boundary tests whether very short distances enforce exploitable structure without any sparsity assumption. Either an algorithm or a hardness reduction would explain a fundamental limit of structural restrictions in graph algorithms.

importance.reason: A longstanding concrete tractability boundary for a canonical NP-complete problem: two colors and diameter one are easy, while three colors at diameter three are hard. It supports the broader study of algorithms on structurally restricted graphs.

progress.text: Mertzios and Spirakis obtain a 2^{O(sqrt(n log n))} algorithm for diameter two and NP-completeness for diameter three, including triangle-free inputs.
Paulusma records the diameter-two three-color question as the exceptional unresolved (number of colors, diameter) pair.
Dębski, Piecyk, and Rzążewski improve the diameter-two upper bound to $2^{O(n^{1/3} \log^2 n)}$. Their abstract states that polynomial-time solvability remains open.
Murakami proves polynomial-time list 3-coloring for graphs of diameter two with no four-cycle as a subgraph. Sections 1 and 7 leave unrestricted diameter-two 3-colorability open.

cards.title: Can reachability diameter be approximated within a constant in near-linear time?
cards.formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least 2/3 in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving D(G)=0 on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
cards.context:
A directed graph need not be strongly connected. Taking the maximum over all ordered pairs then produces infinity as soon as one pair is unreachable, concealing the lengths of the routes that do exist. Reachability diameter discards unreachable pairs. On a one-way path of five vertices it is four, even though most ordered pairs have no directed route.

A familiar undirected idea is to search from an arbitrary vertex and use a farthest vertex as a witness. Directionality breaks its guarantee. Consider a long one-way path and an extra sink reached by an edge from the first path vertex. Searching from that sink sees no other vertex; searching toward it sees only the first path vertex. Both searches reveal a distance of one while the reachability diameter can be arbitrarily large. This is an illustrative counterexample to that particular pivot choice, not a lower bound against every sampling algorithm.

There is also a distinction between additive and multiplicative error. An estimate within $k$ of the truth is useful when $D(G)$ is much larger than $k$, but gives little information when the diameter is small. The question requires a useful relative guarantee on every input, including graphs whose longest finite shortest path has only a few edges.

The 2026 paper makes this a fine-grained algorithmic question and leaves a substantial gap for unweighted graphs. Its strong hardness results for weighted graphs do not settle the unit-weight case.
cards.why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.
cards.definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.

progress.text: Theorem 9 gives an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in near-linear time. Theorem 7 gives additive error $k$ in $O(nm/k)$ time; these guarantees leave the constant-factor near-linear target unresolved.

Corollary 5 conditionally excludes better-than-two approximation below the Boolean-matrix-multiplication exponent; its combinatorial version excludes truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms under combinatorial BMM. These results do not exclude every constant approximation.

cards.title: Is weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that solves the following problem? The input consists of an unambiguous DNF $F=\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j$ over n Boolean variables, nonnegative integer weights w_1,...,w_n encoded in binary, and an integer threshold t encoded in binary. Decide whether there exists $a\in\{0,1\}^n$ such that $F(a)=0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\ge t$. Each T_j is an explicitly listed conjunction of literals. Unambiguous means that no assignment satisfies two distinct terms simultaneously.
cards.definitions: A literal is either x_i or its negation. A term is true exactly when all its literals are true; the DNF is true when at least one term is true. Contradictory terms can be discarded. For the remaining terms, unambiguity is equivalent to every pair containing opposite literals on some variable, so this promise is itself checkable in polynomial time. Weights are exact integers, with no rounding. The running time must depend polynomially on their bit lengths rather than on their numerical sum. The threshold uses at least, not exactly; a strict-threshold formulation is equivalent by shifting the integer threshold by one. The output is a yes/no answer. A tautology has no falsifying assignment and always gives no, regardless of the threshold.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all such inputs, or prove that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-hardness proof would provide a negative answer conditional on P differing from NP; its assumption must be stated. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a method only for unweighted assignments, or hardness after changing the comparison to exact equality does not settle the specified question.
cards.context:
Unambiguity makes the satisfying regions disjoint. This is useful for counting: after fixing the literals of one consistent term, every remaining variable is free, and the term’s satisfying assignments can be counted directly. Summing across terms gives the total without any inclusion-exclusion correction. Subtracting that count from 2^n decides whether a falsifying assignment exists at all.

The weighted version asks where the complement lies relative to an additive score. Knowing how many points lie outside the DNF does not reveal whether even one of them has a large score. For example, take F=(x AND y) OR ((NOT x) AND z), whose two terms are incompatible. With weights 8, 3, and 5, the assignment (1,0,1) falsifies F and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has larger score 16 but satisfies F, so unconstrained maximization does not answer the question.

There is an important asymmetry between maximizing over satisfying and falsifying assignments. To maximize over satisfying assignments, optimize each term separately by setting every unrestricted positive-weight variable to one, then take the best result. To falsify the DNF, every term must fail at once, and choices made to destroy one term can interact with all the others.

Dynamic programming over achievable scores gives a pseudopolynomial algorithm; it becomes polynomial when weights are unary. The missing guarantee is polynomial dependence on binary descriptions of potentially large weights. Amarilli also explains a connection to complementing compiled Boolean representations: efficient complementation into a representation supporting weighted maximization would give an algorithm, while suitable hardness would obstruct that route.
cards.why: The problem separates easy counting from optimization on the complement of a simple disjoint representation. It tests whether unambiguity retains its algorithmic value when a compactly encoded additive objective is introduced, and it bears on the power of knowledge-compilation representations under negation.

importance.reason: A focused but structural tractability question connecting unambiguous representations, binary-weight optimization, and complementation. It has a clear gap between polynomial unweighted methods and an unresolved weighted case.

progress.text: Monet formulates the binary-weight optimization problem and records NP membership of its decision version, polynomial-time weighted satisfaction, and a pseudopolynomial dynamic program for falsification.
The Dagstuhl seminar on database representation and provenance presents this exact question by linking to Monet’s formulation. The catalogue’s separate TCS-0485 record comes from that link.

Amarilli’s maintained list still asks for a polynomial-time weighted-falsifiability algorithm and discusses its connection to complementation of d-DNNFs. Monet’s original question has no posted answer at this check.

Summing across terms gives the total without any inclusion-exclusion correction. Subtracting that count from 2^n decides whether a falsifying assignment exists at all.

The weighted version asks where the complement lies relative to an additive score. Knowing how many points lie outside the DNF does not reveal whether even one of them has a large score. For example, take F=(x AND y) OR ((NOT x) AND z), whose two terms are incompatible. With weights 8, 3, and 5, the assignment (1,0,1) falsifies F and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has larger score 16 but satisfies F, so unconstrained maximization does not answer the question.

There is an important asymmetry between maximizing over satisfying and falsifying assignments. To maximize over satisfying assignments, optimize each term separately by setting every unrestricted positive-weight variable to one, then take the best result. To falsify the DNF, every term must fail at once, and choices made to destroy one term can interact with all the others.

Dynamic programming over achievable scores gives a pseudopolynomial algorithm; it becomes polynomial when weights are unary. The missing guarantee is polynomial dependence on binary descriptions of potentially large weights. Amarilli also explains a connection to complementing compiled Boolean representations: efficient complementation into a representation supporting weighted maximization would give an algorithm, while suitable hardness would obstruct that route.

cards.title: Can the final survivors of an offline heap sequence be found with linear comparisons?
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic comparison algorithm and an absolute constant C that, for every legal sequence of N insert and delete-min operations starting from an empty priority queue, determines exactly which inserted items remain after the entire sequence using at most CN key comparisons? The complete operation sequence and all inserted keys are available before computation begins. Only the final membership vector is required; the algorithm need not output the items removed at intermediate delete-min operations or their removal order.
cards.definitions: Each insert introduces a distinct item with a key in an opaque totally ordered universe; all inserted keys are pairwise distinct. A delete-min removes the currently present item of smallest key. Legality means that in every prefix the number of delete-min operations is at most the number of inserts. If I is the total number of inserts, the output is an I-bit vector in insertion order, marking exactly the items still present after all N operations. The algorithm may examine any part of the input sequence at any time. Its only access to key values is by pairwise order comparisons; operation positions and item identities carry no information about key order. Count every key comparison, including preprocessing comparisons. Ordinary computation on indices and comparison outcomes is not the cost measure, but the algorithm must terminate and be correct on every input.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a uniform deterministic algorithm meeting the CN comparison bound for every legal sequence, or prove that every such algorithm requires a superlinear number of comparisons on a family of inputs. Sorting all removed items or simulating the queue online would solve stronger tasks; a lower bound for those stronger tasks is not a negative answer here.
cards.context:
A usual priority queue must identify each minimum when the corresponding request arrives. The offline task can postpone every decision and return only a final set. For example, after insert(8), insert(2), delete-min, insert(1), the survivors are 8 and 1. This is not simply the set of the two largest inserted keys: 2 disappeared before 1 became available. The interleaving still matters even though the intermediate outputs are discarded.

One upper bound is to simulate a comparison heap and mark its remaining elements, using O(N log(N+2)) comparisons. At the other extreme, when all insertions precede all deletions, one linear-time selection suffices to find the surviving upper part of the key order. The question asks whether arbitrary temporal interleaving can be handled without losing that linear comparison bound.

The ordinary heap sorting lower bound depends on recovering the entire order of the extracted keys. Here, if I items were inserted, there are at most 2^I possible membership vectors. Counting outputs therefore does not give the usual factorial number of leaves needed for sorting. This observation only removes one lower-bound argument: a small output space by itself is not a construction of a shallow comparison decision tree.

A successful approach can exploit future deletions and later insertions, because the complete schedule is known. It need not maintain any particular heap representation. That freedom makes the problem a useful test of how much information an algorithm really needs when only a summary of a dynamic process is requested. The formulation deliberately asks about comparisons, leaving a linear total running time as a stronger goal.
cards.why: This isolates a basic gap between maintaining a dynamic process and computing its final outcome. It connects offline data structures with selection and comparison lower bounds, in a small enough model that both algorithms and adversaries can be stated precisely.

importance.reason: A clean offline-versus-online information question for the priority-queue primitive. It could reveal a general way to avoid reconstructing unneeded intermediate outputs, while remaining narrower than model-wide dynamic lower bounds.

progress.text: Kozma explicitly asks whether final heap survivors can be computed in o(N log N), or even O(N), comparisons. The source identifies the all-insertions-first case as solvable by linear-time selection and notes that the usual sorting argument does not apply.

cards.title: Can an acyclic subgraph preserve a constant fraction of the optimal reachable pairs?
cards.formal: For a finite directed graph G=(V,E), let $R(D)=|\{(u,v)\in V^2:u\ne v,\text{ a directed path from }u\text{ to }v\text{ exists in }D\}|$ and $\mathrm{OPT}(G)=\max\{R((V,F)):F\subseteq E,\ (V,F)\text{ is acyclic}\}$. Do there exist a constant alpha>0 and a deterministic algorithm running in time polynomial in |V|+|E| that, for every G, outputs F subset E with (V,F) acyclic and R((V,F)) >= alpha OPT(G)? The constant and polynomial exponent must be independent of G. This card selects constant-factor approximation as a precise target within the source’s broader optimization question.
cards.definitions: The input is an adjacency-list representation of an unweighted directed graph with labeled vertices 1,...,n, no self-loops, and at most one edge for each ordered pair. Oppositely directed edges may both be present. The algorithm may delete edges but may not add edges, reverse edges, identify vertices, or remove vertices. Reachability uses paths of positive length and counts ordered pairs of distinct vertices, not paths or retained edges. An acyclic graph has no directed cycle. Output is the list of retained edges. Polynomial time is measured in ordinary bit operations on the finite input; no oracle for reachability or optimization is free. When OPT(G)=0, any acyclic output satisfies the value requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a polynomial-time algorithm and prove one universal positive approximation ratio, or prove that no algorithm with the quantified guarantee exists. A conditional impossibility result must identify its complexity assumption. Guarantees on the number or weight of deleted edges, or empirical similarity to a reference hierarchy, do not establish the required guarantee on reachable pairs.
cards.context:
A directed edge can represent a declared relation between two concepts, while a path represents an implied relation. Removing one edge can therefore erase many implications even if almost every input edge remains. The objective counts the implications preserved after all cycles have been removed. The optimum in the denominator already obeys acyclicity, so the algorithm is not asked to retain mutually contradictory reachability in both directions.

For example, a directed path on n vertices has only n-1 edges but n(n-1)/2 reachable ordered pairs. Deleting a middle edge destroys roughly a quarter of all n^2 ordered pairs. Conversely, adding a shortcut between vertices that are already connected by a path increases the edge count without adding a new reachable pair. These examples explain why edge-count approximation guarantees cannot simply be reused for this objective.

Ajwani’s 2016 question asks for an acyclic edge subgraph whose transitive closure has maximum size, motivated by cleaning taxonomies assembled from multiple contributors. The source explicitly welcomes approximation algorithms and scalable heuristics but specifies no approximation threshold. The constant alpha target here is an editorial specialization, rather than an approximation conjecture quoted from the seminar.

The 2017 follow-up on noisy hierarchies develops practical cycle-removal heuristics and evaluates recovery of inserted noisy edges. It identifies deviation in transitive closure as a possible further measure. Those experiments do not provide a worst-case ratio for R(D). A 2026 ranking paper likewise uses reachability to make edge reinsertion cycle-safe, but optimizes edge-weight disagreement; that use of reachability does not turn its objective into this one.
cards.why: This isolates how much implied relational information can be retained when a cyclic dependency system must become a partial order. It is a structural approximation problem in which the value of an edge depends on all paths that use it, and it asks for a guarantee on that global effect.

importance.reason: A clean graph-optimization direction connecting acyclicity with preservation of global reachability. The constant-factor target captures a fundamental guarantee missing from the cited heuristic work, though its literature is narrower than core shortest-path and dynamic-graph frontiers.

progress.text: Ajwani formulates the transitive-closure maximization objective for acyclic subgraphs and asks for approximation algorithms as well as practical heuristics.

Sun and coauthors study cycle removal in noisy hierarchies experimentally. Their conclusion proposes transitive-closure deviation as another measure to investigate; no constant-factor theorem for the reachable-pair objective is supplied.

Vahidi studies ranking through weighted feedback-arc removal and exact cycle-safe reinsertion. The objective and stated guarantees concern edge weights and ranking inconsistency, so they do not settle this approximation target.

Ajwani’s 2016 question asks for an acyclic edge subgraph whose transitive closure has maximum size, motivated by cleaning taxonomies assembled from multiple contributors. The source explicitly welcomes approximation algorithms and scalable heuristics but specifies no approximation threshold. The constant alpha target here is an editorial specialization, rather than an approximation conjecture quoted from the seminar.

The 2017 follow-up on noisy hierarchies develops practical cycle-removal heuristics and evaluates recovery of inserted noisy edges. It identifies deviation in transitive closure as a possible further measure. Those experiments do not provide a worst-case ratio for R(D). A 2026 ranking paper likewise uses reachability to make edge reinsertion cycle-safe, but optimizes edge-weight disagreement; that use of reachability does not turn its objective into this one.

cards.title: Can deterministic LOCAL coloring use a near-linear palette in log-star n rounds?
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants K,C and one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that, for every simple n-vertex graph and supplied maximum-degree bound $\Delta\ge2$, outputs a proper coloring with at most $\lceil K\Delta^{1.001}\rceil$ colors in at most $C(1+\log^*n)$ rounds? Vertices know n and Delta and have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. Neither K nor C may depend on Delta or n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the uniform algorithm and constants, or prove that no such constants and algorithm exist. A log-star n bound with a degree-dependent hidden constant does not settle this proposition.
cards.context:
A fast coloring algorithm can allow itself more colors than a sequential greedy algorithm. The extra palette gives neighboring vertices more room to make independent choices. This question fixes an extremely short round budget and asks how much extra palette is actually necessary.

The exponent 1.001 makes the requested palette slightly superlinear in maximum degree. It is still much smaller than a quadratic palette for sufficiently large degree. Because the graph family ranges over every degree, hiding a large degree-dependent factor in the running time would erase the intended tradeoff.

For example, fixing degree first and then saying that an algorithm takes a constant number of rounds is insufficient: that constant might grow as the degree squared. The question instead requires one numerical multiplier on log-star n that works as both graph size and degree grow. This is why all the constants are quantified explicitly.

Classical color reduction reaches a quadratic-degree palette in iterated-logarithmic time. The source lists reducing the palette below that quadratic scale, and in particular to degree raised to 1.001, as unresolved. The card focuses on that one concrete target; optimal Delta+1 coloring with a larger degree-dependent round budget is a separate question.
cards.why: I include this because it separates the cost of symmetry breaking from the number of colors used to absorb local conflicts. A solution would clarify whether the quadratic palette in a foundational distributed primitive reflects an intrinsic limitation or merely the current method of reducing identifiers to colors.
cards.definitions: Proper means that every input edge has differently colored endpoints. Colors are integers from one shared palette. The identifier bound has a fixed polynomial range in n. Log-star uses base two. The target is deterministic worst-case elapsed rounds over graphs and valid identifier assignments. Delta is not treated as a fixed constant outside the asymptotic bound.

progress.text: Linial’s color reduction gives an $O(\Delta^2)$-coloring in $O(\log^*n)$ rounds. Symmetry-breaking lower bounds also show that the graph-size dependence cannot in general become o(log-star n) when degree is fixed.
Maus and Tonoyan revisit the local color-reduction method and extend it to list and conflict constraints. Their result does not establish the near-linear palette at the requested uniform round bound.
Suomela explicitly lists the Delta-to-the-1.001 palette target within O(log-star n) deterministic rounds.

cards.title: Is the known exponent for distributed even-cycle detection optimal?
cards.formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge3$, is $\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/k})$ a worst-case round lower bound for randomized detection of a simple cycle of length exactly 2k in the CONGEST model? The network is an arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex graph. Each vertex initially knows n, its distinct O(log n)-bit identifier, and its incident edges; each edge carries O(log n) bits per direction per synchronous round. If a cycle exists at least one vertex must output YES, and otherwise all must output NO. Require the joint answer to be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated lower bound for every fixed k at least three, or refute it for at least one fixed k. A randomized algorithm with a fixed improvement in the exponent for one such k would refute the conjecture. The k=2 case is already known and is not the open target.
cards.context:
Cycle detection asks whether information about a bounded number of vertices can be assembled somewhere in the network. With unbounded messages, a constant-radius neighborhood suffices for a fixed cycle length. With limited messages, a vertex may learn that there are many short paths without having enough information to combine compatible paths into a cycle.

A simple six-cycle uses six distinct vertices. Walking across one edge and back three times is also a closed walk of length six, but is not a valid witness. Conversely, a graph containing a six-cycle may also contain triangles or four-cycles. Computing only the shortest cycle length would therefore not answer the exact-length existence question.

The algorithmic exponent changes with the fixed requested length. The conjecture predicts two-thirds for six-cycles, three-quarters for eight-cycles, and progressively larger exponents for longer fixed even cycles. Constants may depend on the length; the question is about how the communication cost grows with network size.

The best known upper bound already works deterministically even when each vertex must broadcast the same message to all its neighbors. The proposed lower bound concerns the stronger model allowing different messages to different neighbors. Establishing it would show that neither private randomness nor this extra communication flexibility improves the exponent.
cards.why: I include this because it asks whether a simple pattern parameter determines a precise hierarchy of communication costs. The gap is not merely about derandomizing an algorithm: the upper bound is already deterministic, while the missing lower bound must exclude every randomized protocol in the stronger unicast model.
cards.definitions: The cycle need not be induced: additional edges between its vertices are allowed. Local computation is unrestricted and random bits are private. Here $\widetilde\Omega(n^a)$ means a lower bound $\Omega(n^a/(\log n)^b)$ for some fixed b; constants may depend on k and the algorithm, but not n. A worst-case bound ranges over input graphs and identifier assignments. k is known to all vertices and is fixed before n grows.

progress.text: Censor-Hillel and coauthors give improved algorithms for small even cycles and show that, already for six-cycles, a lower bound $\Omega(n^{1/2+\alpha})$ for fixed positive alpha would imply major circuit lower bounds.
Fraigniaud, Luce, Magniez, and Todinca obtain randomized $O(n^{1-1/k})$-round detection for every fixed k.
The same authors obtain deterministic $O(n^{1-1/k})$ rounds in Broadcast CONGEST. Their conclusion explicitly leaves optimality open for every k>2.

cards.title: Does ordinary median-of-medians selection with groups of three run in linear time?
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant C such that the fixed deterministic comparison algorithm Select3 below uses at most Cn key comparisons on every sequence A of n distinct ordered keys and every requested rank $1\le k\le n$? Its output must be the k-th smallest key. The question concerns the one-grouping-pass algorithm exactly as specified; all recursive pivot-selection comparisons count toward the same cost.
cards.definitions: Define Select3(A,k) as follows. If |A| <= 3, sort a copy by insertion sort and return its k-th element. Otherwise put the first $3q$ elements, where $q=\lfloor |A|/3\rfloor$, into consecutive disjoint triples. Obtain each triple's median by sorting a copy using compare-exchanges (1,2), (2,3), (1,2); this leaves A unchanged. Let B be these q medians in group order. Set $p=\mathrm{Select3}(B,\lceil q/2\rceil)$. Scan all of A, including its at most two ungrouped final elements, comparing each key with p and forming L of keys below p and R of keys above p, preserving their original order. If k=|L|+1 return p; if k<=|L| return Select3(L,k); otherwise return Select3(R,k-|L|-1). One comparison returns the relative order of two keys at unit cost. The algorithm stores subsequences explicitly and uses no randomization, arithmetic on keys, or reuse of comparison outcomes beyond this description. These rounding and base-case conventions make the source's algorithm fully specified.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated comparison bound for every input sequence and every requested rank, or give a family of inputs and ranks for which comparisons divided by n are unbounded. An O(n log n) upper bound alone is not a refutation of linear time. A different small-group selection algorithm is not a positive answer for Select3.
cards.context:
Selection asks for one position in sorted order without requiring the whole sorted sequence. The pivot controls how much work can be discarded: after finding it, only the side containing the requested rank is relevant. Here the pivot itself must be selected recursively from the medians of small groups. Its quality and the cost of obtaining it therefore have to be analyzed together.

The familiar three-group analysis bounds two recursive subproblems by roughly n/3 and 2n/3, plus a linear scan. This gives an O(n log n) upper bound. It does not exhibit an input on which both recursive calls repeatedly realize their separate worst cases. They are linked: the median list is made of elements from the very array that is partitioned. An adversarial construction cannot freely choose the two subproblems independently.

A useful distinction is between the grouping size and the number of grouping passes. The repeated-step method groups the medians into triples again before selecting a pivot recursively. That modified algorithm has a linear-time analysis, but it makes a different recursive call from Select3. The present question preserves the simpler, single-pass rule.

For a proof attempt, the stable ordering in L and R matters because it determines the triples at the next call. Fixing these details turns an informal discussion of small groups into one mathematical proposition. A positive answer would establish that the standard recurrence loses an asymptotic factor; a negative answer must capture actual coupled executions, rather than just solve the upper-bound recurrence.
cards.why: This is a compact fundamental algorithm-analysis problem: even for a textbook primitive, independently worst-case recursive bounds may not be simultaneously attainable. It provides a concrete place to develop sharper tools for dependent subproblems or an explicit adversary.

importance.reason: A basic unresolved analysis of a canonical selection rule, valuable for understanding dependent recursion. Its algorithm-specific scope places it below general adaptive-data-structure and compressed-access barriers.

progress.text: Chen and Dumitrescu give linear-time modified small-group algorithms and leave ordinary three-group selection unresolved. Their Conjecture 1 asks for o(n log n), which is weaker than the linear bound asked here.
Kozma restates the three-group question as open at the Adaptive and Scalable Data Structures seminar.

cards.title: Do pure pairing heaps support O(log log n) amortized decrease-key?
cards.formal: For the pure pairing heap defined below, is there a universal constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations starting with empty heaps costs at most $C[M+D(1+\log N)+K(1+\log\log(N+2))]$? Here D counts delete-min operations, K counts decrease-key operations, and $N\ge2$ is the maximum of 2 and the total number of live items across all heaps at any moment. The allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld, decrease-key, and delete-min. Count comparisons and pointer-machine steps; keys are distinct opaque values in a totally ordered set, compared at unit cost. Handles to the affected items and heaps are supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove this total-cost bound for the specified algorithm, or construct legal operation sequences for which its ratio to the displayed budget is unbounded. Changing the heap algorithm or obtaining the bound only for a different self-adjusting heap does not establish a positive answer.
cards.definitions: A heap is one rooted heap-ordered tree whose child lists are ordered from left to right. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger root the leftmost child of the smaller; cut removes a node with its subtree from its parent in constant time. Store O(1) pointers per item, with doubly linked child lists. Make-heap creates an empty tree; find-min returns its root; insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the roots and destroys the old heap handles. Decrease-key changes the supplied key and, if its node is not the root, cuts that node and links its subtree with the remaining root. Delete-min removes the root and scans its children left to right, linking disjoint adjacent pairs; an unpaired last child remains. Winners keep their positions in the root list. Identify its minimum-key remaining root v, remove v from that list, and prepend all other remaining roots in their existing order to the child list of v. The resulting tree is the heap. Use the ordinary constant-time list splice, rather than doing an additional recursive linking pass. All loops, comparisons, pointer accesses, and writes are charged. Logarithms have base two.
cards.context:
A decrease-key call changes an item that is already present. It may execute only a few pointer operations immediately, yet the structural disorder it creates can make later deletions more expensive. Its amortized cost measures this delayed effect. Counting only the instructions inside the decrease-key procedure would miss the question entirely.

The pure pairing heap simplifies deletion by pairing neighboring roots once and then attaching all survivors beneath the smallest survivor. It does not maintain a rank or balance invariant. The desired estimate asks whether this sparse restructuring still prevents expensive configurations from being recreated too often.

The operation budgets must be considered together. A sorting sequence already forces substantial comparison work when many minima are deleted, so the logarithmic delete-min allowance is intentional. The unresolved issue is how much additional work to attribute to key decreases while keeping insertions and melds cheap. Using the maximum live population N makes that accounting explicit for a whole finite sequence.

Other self-adjusting heaps already attain the desired decrease-key order. This makes the remaining gap an informative algorithm-analysis problem: is the simpler rule equally efficient, or does its exact restructuring lose something asymptotically? A bound for slim or smooth heaps does not answer this question about pure pairing heaps.
cards.why: This is a precise opportunity to separate an analysis gap from a structural limitation of a simple data structure. Priority-queue costs propagate into graph algorithms, and the problem tests how little explicit balancing information is sufficient for optimal amortized behavior.

progress.text: Iacono and Özkan prove an Omega(log log n) decrease-key lower bound in the pure heap model under logarithmic extract-min bounds. The model name refers to a class, not specifically the 2026 data structure.

Sinnamon and Tarjan establish optimal logarithmic-logarithmic decrease-key bounds for slim and smooth heaps, with a further log log log n factor for multipass pairing heaps. The journal version appeared in 2025.

Tarjan and Xu introduce pure pairing heaps and bound decrease-key by O(log log n times log log log n), retaining O(log n) delete-min and O(1) insert/meld amortized bounds. Section 10 explicitly leaves the remaining factor open.

cards.title: Can bipartite maximal fractional matching be found in sublinear-in-degree rounds?
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm and a function $f(\Delta)=o(\Delta)$ that, on every simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most Delta, outputs a maximal fractional matching within f(Delta) rounds, independently of n? Each edge e receives a nonnegative rational weight x_e, agreed upon by its endpoints. Require $\sum_{e
i v}x_e\le1$ for every vertex v, and for every edge uv require $\sum_{e
i u}x_e=1$ or $\sum_{e
i v}x_e=1$. The bipartition is supplied as an input two-coloring, nodes know n and Delta, and identifiers are distinct O(log n)-bit integers.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform algorithm with a degree-only bound whose ratio to Delta tends to zero, or prove that no such deterministic algorithm exists. An additive log-star n term, an almost-maximal solution, or a lower bound only for nonbipartite graphs does not settle this target.
cards.context:
A fractional matching divides one unit of capacity at each vertex among its incident edges. Maximality means that no single edge can have its weight increased without exceeding an endpoint’s capacity. It does not mean that the total edge weight is as large as possible.

For example, on a star one can place the entire unit on a single leaf edge or divide it equally among all leaf edges. Both assignments saturate the center and are maximal, even though many leaves are unsaturated. Allowing fractions gives the algorithm ways to share capacity that do not exist for ordinary integral matching.

Bipartiteness supplies a globally consistent division into two sides, and the card gives that division to the algorithm. This can remove symmetry obstacles that occur when a vertex does not know which role it should play. Nevertheless, neighboring choices still have to agree on edge weights and achieve exact saturation somewhere along every edge.

Approximate saturation is a different requirement: leaving a small amount of unused capacity at both endpoints violates the condition on that edge. The known linear-degree lower bound on general graphs therefore cannot simply be combined with an approximation algorithm or transferred to the supplied-bipartition setting. The source specifically leaves this bipartite case open.
cards.why: I include this because it asks whether relaxing discrete choices to fractional ones changes the intrinsic time needed for local coordination, once a bipartition is available. The constraints are simple, but exact maximality makes the question stronger than approximately solving a packing problem.
cards.definitions: LOCAL uses synchronous rounds with unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. Rational weights have finite encodings; there is no imposed output-bit bound. The algorithm must work for every identifier assignment and every valid supplied degree bound. The little-o statement concerns Delta tending to infinity and must hold uniformly over all graph sizes. Vertices output weights for all incident edges, with exact endpoint agreement.

progress.text: Åstrand and Suomela give local algorithms for approximating covering and packing problems, including the linear-degree maximal-fractional-matching upper bound used in subsequent work.
Göös, Hirvonen, and Suomela prove that o(Delta) rounds are impossible for maximal fractional matching on general graphs. This does not resolve the bipartite question as stated.
Suomela’s open-problem list explicitly asks for o(Delta) rounds on bipartite graphs and conjectures that the answer is negative.

cards.title: Does the expected redundancy of optimal alphabetic trees with random weights converge?
cards.formal: For each n >= 2, let $D=(D_1,\ldots,D_n)$ be uniform on the probability simplex, equivalently Dirichlet(1,...,1). Let $C_n(D)=\min_T\sum_{i=1}^n D_i d_T(i)$, where T ranges over full ordered binary trees with leaves 1,...,n in that left-to-right order and d_T(i) is the depth of leaf i, with root depth zero. Define $H(D)=-\sum_iD_i\log_2D_i$ and $r_n=\mathbb E_D[C_n(D)-H(D)]$. Does the real sequence r_n converge to a finite limit as n tends to infinity? This is a precise limit-existence target within the source’s broader request to determine the expected optimal cost.
cards.definitions: A full binary tree has exactly two children at every internal node. An ordered tree distinguishes left from right, and the fixed leaf order is the alphabetic constraint. Following left and right edges as bits gives an alphabetic prefix code: no leaf codeword is a prefix of another, and lexicographic codeword order agrees with symbol order. The tree is optimized separately after the probabilities D are realized; the expectation is taken afterward. To sample D, draw n-1 independent uniform points in (0,1), sort them, append endpoints 0 and 1, and take the n successive interval lengths. The weights are positive almost surely. For a fixed D, the cost is the expected number of binary decisions to find a leaf drawn with probabilities D; no random-tree distribution is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every epsilon > 0 there exists N0 such that |r_n-r_m| < epsilon for all n,m >= N0, or prove that this Cauchy property fails. A negative answer can be established by separated subsequential limits. Identifying the numerical value of a limit, if it exists, is useful further progress but is not required for the stated yes/no question. Bounded redundancy or finite Monte Carlo estimates alone do not settle convergence.
cards.context:
An alphabetic tree preserves the order of the symbols, so a search can branch according to comparisons with boundaries in that order. This constraint is useful for searching and ordered merging, but can prevent the tree from using exactly the codeword lengths it would choose if the symbols were freely permutable. Redundancy measures the extra expected decisions beyond the entropy lower bound.

There are two levels of averaging. Once the weights are fixed, the weighted leaf depths describe the cost of queries to one optimized tree. The question then averages that optimum over a random probability vector. Optimizing a tree for the mean weight vector would be a different operation: it would choose a tree before seeing which symbols are common in the realized distribution.

The standard alphabetic coding bound gives 0 <= C_n(D)-H(D) < 2, so r_n is bounded. Boundedness does not imply convergence. Integer codeword lengths make it especially important not to assume that a constant correction term exists without proof. The present target isolates that issue before asking for the complete expected-cost formula.

Wild’s source question concerns the expected cost under exactly these random spacings, motivated both by alphabetic compression and by comparison-efficient partitioning in Quicksort. Its broad formulation asks to compute or approximate the expectation. This card extracts the specific convergence question explicitly; it does not attribute a conjectured limit or a claimed asymptotic formula to the source.
cards.why: This asks whether the cost of optimal ordered searching has a stable average overhead beyond entropy under a canonical random-input model. It connects discrete codeword constraints with probabilistic analysis and separates a constant-order question from the much easier leading logarithmic growth.

importance.reason: A precise average-case structural question connecting optimal search trees and information theory. Convergence is a focused first target within the broader expected-cost problem, rather than a general data-structure complexity barrier.

progress.text: Wild formulates the random-probability redundancy question, distinguishes it from averaging over symbols under a fixed distribution, and records the standard entropy bounds.
The Dagstuhl problem specifies uniform random spacings and explains its connection to optimal alphabetic trees and Quicksort partitioning. The expected redundancy is left unresolved.

cards.title: Can circle–segment reporting on connected planar graphs have additive output cost?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic static data structure that preprocesses a connected straight-line planar graph with n >= 2 edges in $O(n\log^3 n)$ time and space and reports all k edges intersecting a query circle in $O(\log^3 n+k)$ worst-case time? The graph is embedded in the Euclidean plane: edges are nonzero closed line segments, distinct edge interiors are disjoint, and edges meet only at shared endpoints. A query supplies a center c and radius r > 0. Promise that the circle contains no graph vertex on its boundary and is tangent to no edge. Report each intersected input edge once. All hidden constants are independent of the graph, circle, and output size.
cards.definitions: The query circle is the boundary $\{p:\|p-c\|_2=r\}$, not the filled disk. An edge intersects it if at least one point of that segment lies on the boundary, including when both edge endpoints are outside the disk. k counts distinct reported edges, even if one segment has two intersection points. Connectivity is that of the graph with the specified endpoints as vertices; crossing edges without a shared vertex are excluded. Use a unit-cost real RAM with exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, square roots, and comparisons, together with random access and O(log n)-bit integer indices. Each stored real or integer occupies one cell; integer bit manipulation does not apply to arbitrary real values. Preprocessing includes construction of every auxiliary index. Queries return edge identifiers and use only the stored structure and the query. The target specializes the older connected-segment direction to planar input and removes a multiplicative output overhead from a later bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a data structure with all three stated worst-case bounds, or prove that no such data structure exists in this model. An O((k+1) log^3 n) query bound still incurs the overhead this proposition asks to remove. Improvements only for disks, approximate answers, or a restricted family of graph embeddings do not establish the positive answer.
cards.context:
A large circle can enclose many graph edges while crossing very few of them. Reporting every segment inside its disk can therefore be far more expensive than the requested boundary query. There is also a second geometric obstacle: a segment can cross the circle twice while both of its endpoints are outside. An index of endpoint locations alone does not identify every answer.

Connectivity gives the search more structure. If a connected piece of the graph contains vertices on both sides of the circle, then some edge crosses the boundary. This observation suggests organizing the input into connected pieces and using geometric tests to discard pieces containing no answer. Planarity is an additional promise in this card; the graph is not an arbitrary collection of crossing segments.

The ISAAC 2025 construction makes this strategy effective using a hierarchy of connected edge subsets. Its preprocessing depends on n plus the number of edge crossings, and its reporting bound is O((k+1) log^3 n), including the empty-output case. With planar input the crossing term disappears. The remaining target here is to pay the logarithmic search overhead once per query, then only constant additional cost per reported edge.

This is a sharper question than the broad direction recorded at the May 2025 seminar. The later paper already demonstrates that connectivity can improve the old bounds substantially. Its final section discusses faster repeated searches and lower bounds. The precise additive-output target, fixed preprocessing budget, and nondegenerate-query promise here are editorial choices that turn that remaining direction into a yes/no proposition.
cards.why: Output-sensitive reporting separates the unavoidable cost of listing answers from the cost of finding them. This question asks whether connected planar structure is strong enough to achieve that separation for a curved boundary query, combining topological promises with geometric searching.

importance.reason: A focused structural reporting problem: removing per-answer search overhead would clarify the algorithmic value of connected planar input. It is narrower than general range-searching trade-off questions.

progress.text: Storandt proposes exploiting connectivity for circle–segment queries. The stored draft originally described this broad direction without a fixed remaining target.

Afshani, Bosch, and Storandt obtain O((n+C) log^3 n) preprocessing time and space for C crossings, and O((k+1) log^3 n) reporting. Thus the historical direction has substantial positive progress; Theorem 8 is not the additive-output bound asked here.
