cards.title: Can four-sided skyline reporting match ordinary range reporting?
cards.formal: Preprocess a static set $P\subseteq[N]^2$ of $N$ points, with distinct coordinates in each dimension, on a word RAM with $\Theta(\log N)$-bit words. Is there a structure using $N\log^{O(1)}N$ words that reports the skyline of $P\cap([a,b]\times[c,d])$ in worst-case $O(\log\log N+k)$ time, where $k$ is the number of reported points? A point is on the skyline if no other point in the query rectangle is at least as large in both coordinates and strictly larger in one.
cards.context:
Think of records scored on two attributes, with larger values preferred. A range filter first selects the eligible records; the skyline then removes options that are worse on both attributes. For points (1,5), (3,3), (4,4), and (5,1), the full-set skyline excludes (3,3). A rectangle that includes (3,3) but cuts off (4,4) can make it a skyline point. Therefore, storing only the global skyline loses information needed for later queries.

The output can be much smaller than the number of points inside the rectangle. If a rectangle contains thousands of points and one dominates all others, the requested bound permits only $O(\log\log N)$ time beyond outputting that one point. Reporting every point and filtering afterward cannot meet it. The data structure must skip large dominated regions without paying for their contents.

Counting and reporting have different targets. Four-sided skyline counting needs $\Omega(\log N/\log\log N)$ query time at near-linear space. That does not directly refute fast reporting: counting by enumeration costs an additional $k$, which can be large. The known reporting upper bound pays the same logarithmic overhead as counting, plus the output size.

The 2026 paper distinguishes the top-open and bottom-open three-sided variants and explicitly leaves the four-sided reporting bound unresolved. The missing side of a rectangle can change the problem, so results for three-sided queries do not settle this card.
cards.why: This asks whether selecting only undominated answers imposes an inherent indexing cost beyond locating a range and emitting its output. I include it as a focused data-structure problem with a precise model, a concrete gap, and a useful distinction between counting, reporting, and output-sensitive computation.
cards.definitions:
Coordinates are already in rank space; this avoids hiding a separate predecessor-search cost for a larger universe. The set is static. Space is measured in machine words, not bits. The factor $\log^{O(1)}N$ has a fixed exponent. The output parameter $k$ is query-dependent, and no scan of all of $P\cap Q$ is allowed unless its cost fits the stated bound.

The target is deterministic exact reporting with polynomial preprocessing time, using the usual word-RAM operations: arithmetic, multiplication, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words.

progress.text: Brodal and Larsen obtain an $O(N)$-word counting structure with $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ query time and a matching cell-probe lower bound. Their reporting tradeoff includes $O(N\log^{\varepsilon}N)$ space and $O(\log N/\log\log N+k)$ query time for fixed $\varepsilon>0$.
Kushwaha and Nekrich ask whether near-linear-space four-sided skyline reporting can attain $O(\log\log N+k)$, the optimal ordinary four-sided range-reporting bound.

cards.title: Can lazy B-tree priority queues keep their I/O bounds with stable handles?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic comparison-based external-memory priority queue with a universal constant c of internal storage at most cB words that satisfies the following bounds for every capacity $N\ge B\ge2$? Starting empty and never holding more than N elements, it uses $O(1+N/B)$ external blocks, supports insertion and handle-based decrease-key in $O(1+\log_B\log_B N)$ worst-case I/Os, and supports extract-min in $O(1+B^{-1}\log_2 N+\log_B\log_B N)$ amortized I/Os. Every handle remains valid until its element is removed. All handle maintenance and lookup costs count. Each logarithm is truncated below at one.
cards.context:
A handle lets an algorithm change a particular queued object after that object has moved. For example, a graph algorithm may keep a reference to a vertex’s queue entry and lower its priority when a better route is discovered. The reference must still identify that entry after other insertions, extractions, and internal rearrangements.

Block transfers make this subtle. Moving $B$ consecutive records between a few blocks can cost only a constant number of I/Os. If each record has a reference stored in a different disk block, repairing those references can cost $\Theta(B)$ I/Os. An analysis of the records alone can therefore miss the operation that dominates the running time.

Adding an indirection table is a possible design choice, not a complete solution. It can keep the caller’s handle stable, but the structure must update the table when entries move and look up the correct location on later decreases. Those accesses can again be scattered. The question requires charging these costs to the same operation bounds.

The December 2025 revision explicitly corrects the conference claim about priority-queue performance. It identifies the cost of external references as unaccounted for and reports logarithmic extract-min cost for the straightforward implementation when every element has a reference.
cards.why: I include this because stable object identity is part of a data structure’s interface, and its cost can conflict with the locality that makes external-memory algorithms fast. The target is specific enough to attack with a representation or a lower bound, while the obstruction also matters for other structures that move records in blocks.
cards.definitions: One I/O transfers B consecutive words between internal and external memory. N is an announced upper bound on the number of live elements, fixed for the operation sequence. Words contain O(log N) bits; keys and handles occupy a constant number of words, and key values are accessed by comparisons. A returned handle must continue identifying the same object after internal relocation. Decrease-key receives a handle and a no-larger priority; extract-min returns and removes an element with minimum priority. All auxiliary tables count toward the space bound. Amortized extract-min cost means that total cost of any legal sequence is bounded by the sum of its stated operation budgets.

progress.text: Eenberg, Larsen, and Yu establish a general external-memory lower bound showing that adding decrease-key can increase priority-queue cost. This is background on the resource tradeoff; it does not resolve the particular handle-sensitive bounds on this card.

The revised Lazy B-Trees paper records the missing pointer cost. Its displayed priority-queue bounds explicitly exclude that cost, and therefore are not a solution to the fully charged interface above.

cards.title: Linear LOCAL versus constant dynamic locality for a promise-free LCL
cards.formal: Does there exist one promise-free LCL on bounded-degree graphs that has a deterministic incremental dynamic-LOCAL algorithm with O(1) repair radius, but requires Ω(n) rounds in deterministic LOCAL? Under the models below, the answer is no: combining the cited simulations gives a deterministic O(√n·polylog n)-round LOCAL algorithm whenever constant dynamic locality is possible.
cards.definitions: A promise-free LCL Π has one fixed degree bound Δ≥2, one fixed checking radius r≥1, finite vertex input/output alphabets, and a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r input/output neighborhoods. A labeling is legal exactly when all vertices pass this check. The problem must admit a legal output for every finite simple undirected graph of degree at most Δ and every input assignment, including disconnected graphs. Legality is invariant under isomorphism and does not depend on identifiers, port orders, or graph size. No assumption of bipartiteness, planarity, a rooted structure, or a special global input encoding is made. In deterministic LOCAL, vertices initially know n, their own input, degree, ports, and a distinct identifier in [n²]. They exchange unbounded messages with neighbors in synchronous rounds. One finite computable program must work on every input, with unrestricted terminating local computation. Round complexity is the worst case over input graphs, labels, ports, and identifiers. In incremental dynamic-LOCAL, a central deterministic algorithm starts with the empty graph and a known upper bound N on the eventual number of vertices. An adversary inserts isolated vertices with immutable input labels and identifiers, or inserts edges between existing vertices, always respecting Δ and the size bound. After every event the algorithm must maintain a legal output on the entire current graph. Existing outputs may change only within distance R(N) of an endpoint of the inserted edge, or of the inserted vertex, measured after the event. The algorithm may inspect the entire revealed graph and retain arbitrary state, but future vertices, inputs, and edges are unknown. The locality is the largest radius of any output change, not the number of changes or the update time. All algorithms are uniform finite programs, all local computation must terminate, and all guarantees are deterministic and worst case. A constant locality bound is independent of size and may depend only on the fixed problem. A linear lower bound means that for every correct algorithm A there are a constant c_A>0 and arbitrarily large size bounds with an input or update sequence forcing locality at least c_A times that bound. This infinitely-often formulation is already ruled out by a uniform sublinear upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer would require one finite total LCL specification, a constant-radius dynamic algorithm, and a linear deterministic LOCAL lower bound. A negative answer rules out this combination for every such LCL. The latter follows from the sublinear simulation described below; this is a derived corollary, not a claim that either cited paper states this exact saved question verbatim.
cards.context:
Dynamic computation retains the history of how a graph was built. This history can provide choices that a fresh synchronous computation has to establish through communication. The saved question asks whether local repairs could exploit that advantage so strongly that a constant repair radius replaces a linear number of communication rounds.

The requirement to work on every bounded-degree graph and every input matters. Special graph families may have global promises that affect what an algorithm can infer from a partial view. Here all intermediate graphs are valid inputs to the same total problem, so the simulations can build disjoint copies, delete edges, and introduce isolated vertices without leaving the problem’s domain.

A constant-radius dynamic algorithm yields a constant-locality online algorithm. On each online request, reveal a slightly larger constant-radius neighborhood and simulate its vertex and edge insertions. Once a requested vertex is labeled, later revelations are too far away to change it. This uses the incremental model beginning with an empty graph; unseen input labels are not supplied in advance.

The first step removes dependence on unrelated revealed components. Lemma 7.5 turns an online algorithm of locality T(n) into one whose decision depends only on its current revealed component, with locality T(2^O(n³)). If T is a constant, this enormous change of the size argument leaves locality constant. The family of all bounded-degree graphs satisfies the lemma’s closure assumptions.

The second step simulates that component-wise algorithm in sublinear deterministic LOCAL time. The clustering framework separates small-diameter regions with only O(√n) leftover vertices. Grouping nearby leftovers gives components of diameter O(√n) whose constant-radius views are mutually separate. Each such component can simulate the deterministic online rule on its leftovers independently; these simulations form one valid online prefix. Each remaining region can then choose a compatible completion by finite exhaustive search. Local checkability makes the separate completions compatible. The total communication radius is O(√n·polylog n). This explains the deterministic specialization of the component-wise simulation.

Combining these steps gives dynamic O(1) → online O(1) → deterministic LOCAL O(√n·polylog n). Since √n times any fixed polylogarithm is o(n), a linear LOCAL lower bound is impossible. Smaller separations can still exist; the result only rules out the specified linear-versus-constant target.
cards.why: The question probes the limits of using construction history to replace communication for locally verifiable tasks. Its negative resolution places a general upper bound on that advantage and demonstrates why exact size regimes and the absence of promises matter when comparing locality models.

importance.reason: A broad model-separation benchmark resolved through general simulation machinery. Retained for its structural meaning and traceability, with resolved status rather than counted as a remaining open problem.

progress.text: The locality framework establishes the simulations from LOCAL to incremental dynamic-LOCAL to online-LOCAL, and studies their differences for locally checkable tasks.

The updated problem list asks for a promise-free linear LOCAL versus constant dynamic separation. The corrected comparison paper provides the component-wise conversion needed for the later implication.

The revised quantum-advantage paper extends the clustering simulation to component-wise online locality on general graphs. Its deterministic constant-locality specialization has O(√n·polylog n) LOCAL complexity.

Composing dynamic-to-online simulation, the constant-locality component-wise conversion, and the sublinear LOCAL simulation rules out the requested witness. The card records the derivation explicitly; no withdrawn dynamic derandomization theorem is invoked.

cards.title: Linear dynamic versus constant online locality for a promise-free LCL
cards.formal: Does there exist one promise-free LCL on bounded-degree graphs with deterministic online-LOCAL complexity O(1), but deterministic incremental dynamic-LOCAL complexity Ω(n)? Under the models below, the answer is no: constant online locality implies deterministic O(√n·polylog n) LOCAL complexity and hence a sublinear dynamic repair radius.
cards.definitions: A promise-free LCL Π has one fixed degree bound Δ≥2, one fixed checking radius r≥1, finite vertex input/output alphabets, and a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r input/output neighborhoods. A labeling is legal exactly when all vertices pass this check. Legality is invariant under isomorphism and does not depend on identifiers, port orders, or graph size. No assumption of bipartiteness, planarity, a rooted structure, or a special global input encoding is made. In deterministic online-LOCAL, the eventual graph has n vertices, n is known, and an adversary requests every vertex once in an arbitrary order. At the request for v, the entire radius-R(n) neighborhood of v in the eventual graph is revealed, including input labels and edges in the accumulated revealed subgraph. The algorithm has global memory, but must choose v’s final output immediately and never change a previous output. All final outputs must be legal for every graph and request order. It has no advance access to the rest of the eventual graph. In incremental dynamic-LOCAL, a central deterministic algorithm starts with the empty graph and a known upper bound N on the eventual number of vertices. An adversary inserts isolated vertices with immutable input labels and identifiers, or inserts edges between existing vertices, always respecting Δ and the size bound. After every event the algorithm must maintain a legal output on the entire current graph. Existing outputs may change only within distance R(N) of an endpoint of the inserted edge, or of the inserted vertex, measured after the event. The algorithm may inspect the entire revealed graph and retain arbitrary state, but future vertices, inputs, and edges are unknown. The locality is the largest radius of any output change, not the number of changes or the update time. All algorithms are uniform finite programs, all local computation must terminate, and all guarantees are deterministic and worst case. A constant locality bound is independent of size and may depend only on the fixed problem. A linear lower bound means that for every correct algorithm A there are a constant c_A>0 and arbitrarily large size bounds with an input or update sequence forcing locality at least c_A times that bound. This infinitely-often formulation is already ruled out by a uniform sublinear upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer requires one finite total LCL specification, a constant-locality online algorithm, and a linear dynamic-radius lower bound for all deterministic maintenance algorithms. A negative answer excludes every such witness. The cited simulations imply the negative answer; the conclusion is an editorial composition of the results, with its reasoning given below.
cards.context:
Online lookaround reveals nearby parts of the eventual graph before a vertex commits to its output. Incremental dynamic computation instead sees the graph as it is built and repairs earlier outputs. The question asks whether even constant lookaround can prevent changes that would otherwise have to spread linearly far.

These are spatial resource bounds. A dynamic algorithm may examine the whole current graph and perform very expensive computation, yet its output changes must remain close to the update. An online algorithm may use all previously revealed information but cannot revise a requested vertex. Neither definition bounds ordinary centralized running time.

The first step removes dependence on unrelated revealed components. Lemma 7.5 turns an online algorithm of locality T(n) into one whose decision depends only on its current revealed component, with locality T(2^O(n³)). If T is a constant, this enormous change of the size argument leaves locality constant. The family of all bounded-degree graphs satisfies the lemma’s closure assumptions.

The second step simulates that component-wise algorithm in sublinear deterministic LOCAL time. The clustering framework separates small-diameter regions with only O(√n) leftover vertices. Grouping nearby leftovers gives components of diameter O(√n) whose constant-radius views are mutually separate. Each such component can simulate the deterministic online rule on its leftovers independently; these simulations form one valid online prefix. Each remaining region can then choose a compatible completion by finite exhaustive search. Local checkability makes the separate completions compatible. The total communication radius is O(√n·polylog n). This explains the deterministic specialization of the component-wise simulation.

A deterministic T(n)-round LOCAL algorithm also supplies a dynamic algorithm with repair radius at most T(n)+O(1). Recompute its prescribed outputs after each insertion. Farther vertices have unchanged input neighborhoods and therefore unchanged outputs. For growing graphs, use the fixed size bound N and pad unseen vertices as isolated vertices with fixed dummy inputs; the problem is total and its legality is independent of N, so outputs on the real components remain valid.

The complete implication is online O(1) → component-wise online O(1) → deterministic LOCAL O(√n·polylog n) → dynamic O(√n·polylog n). This excludes the requested linear dynamic lower bound. It does not prove that online and dynamic locality always agree, nor give a constant-radius dynamic simulation.
cards.why: This asks whether a small view into the eventual graph can eliminate a global repair cost. Its negative resolution is a useful constraint on future separation constructions: a promise-free LCL with constant online locality must already permit sublinear dynamic repair.

importance.reason: A structural comparison of online lookaround and dynamic repair, now bounded by a general sublinear simulation. Preserved as a resolved historical question, distinct from the separate LOCAL-versus-dynamic comparison.

progress.text: Akbari and coauthors formalize online lookaround and incremental dynamic locality and establish LOCAL → dynamic-LOCAL → online-LOCAL simulations.

The primary problem list records the promise-free linear-versus-constant separation target. Lemma 7.5 of the corrected comparison paper turns constant online locality into constant component-wise online locality on all bounded-degree graphs.

The general-graph clustering simulation yields a sublinear deterministic LOCAL algorithm from a constant-locality component-wise online algorithm. The revised paper explains the online extension in Section 1.6 and Appendix A.

Combine that sublinear LOCAL algorithm with local recomputation after updates. The resulting O(√n·polylog n) repair radius contradicts any linear dynamic lower bound, so the saved separation target has a negative answer.

cards.status_note: Resolved negatively in the specified promise-free deterministic models by composition of the cited simulations. The derivation is made explicit rather than attributed to an exact theorem statement about this catalogue ID. The conclusion concerns linear-versus-constant separation, not equivalence of the two models.

context_blocks.text: Online lookaround reveals nearby parts of the eventual graph before a vertex commits to its output. Incremental dynamic computation instead sees the graph as it is built and repairs earlier outputs. The question asks whether even constant lookaround can prevent changes that would otherwise have to spread linearly far.

These are spatial resource bounds. A dynamic algorithm may examine the whole current graph and perform very expensive computation, yet its output changes must remain close to the update. An online algorithm may use all previously revealed information but cannot revise a requested vertex. Neither definition bounds ordinary centralized running time.

The first step removes dependence on unrelated revealed components. Lemma 7.5 turns an online algorithm of locality T(n) into one whose decision depends only on its current revealed component, with locality T(2^O(n³)). If T is a constant, this enormous change of the size argument leaves locality constant. The family of all bounded-degree graphs satisfies the lemma’s closure assumptions.

The second step simulates that component-wise algorithm in sublinear deterministic LOCAL time. The clustering framework separates small-diameter regions with only O(√n) leftover vertices. Grouping nearby leftovers gives components of diameter O(√n) whose constant-radius views are mutually separate. Each such component can simulate the deterministic online rule on its leftovers independently; these simulations form one valid online prefix. Each remaining region can then choose a compatible completion by finite exhaustive search. Local checkability makes the separate completions compatible. The total communication radius is O(√n·polylog n). This explains the deterministic specialization of the component-wise simulation.

A deterministic T(n)-round LOCAL algorithm also supplies a dynamic algorithm with repair radius at most T(n)+O(1). Recompute its prescribed outputs after each insertion. Farther vertices have unchanged input neighborhoods and therefore unchanged outputs. For growing graphs, use the fixed size bound N and pad unseen vertices as isolated vertices with fixed dummy inputs; the problem is total and its legality is independent of N, so outputs on the real components remain valid.

The complete implication is online O(1) → component-wise online O(1) → deterministic LOCAL O(√n·polylog n) → dynamic O(√n·polylog n). This excludes the requested linear dynamic lower bound. It does not prove that online and dynamic locality always agree, nor give a constant-radius dynamic simulation.
